# Phase 1: Region Heap + Send Task Model

## Purpose
Make the “task tier” sound:
- allow `Send` tasks to migrate across workers
- preserve region ownership and lifetimes via region-owned allocation

This is the “soundness frontier” encoded into the runtime:
- fibers (Phase 0): borrow-friendly, same-thread
- tasks (Phase 1): `Send`, parallel, region-heap-backed

## Requirements
- Region-owned allocation arena that is reclaimed only after region close/quiescence.
- A `RRef<'r, T>`-style handle (or equivalent) to store data with region lifetime.
- Clear rules for what can be captured in a migrating task.

## Acceptance Criteria
- It is impossible (by construction or by runtime checks) for a migrating task to hold references that outlive the region heap.
- Region close safely reclaims region heap after quiescence.

## Testing
- Parallel tests that allocate in region heap, migrate tasks, and verify data remains valid.
- Leak tests: ensure region heap reclaimed only after close.

title: Implement join_all combinator (N-way join)
description:
# join_all (N-way Join)

## Purpose
Provide an N-ary join combinator derived from the primitive join semantics (⊗):
- run all branches
- wait for all to complete
- aggregate outcomes under policy

This should be a thin, lawful layer on top of Phase 0 kernel primitives.

## Semantics
Given futures `f[0..n)`:
1. spawn each as a child in a subregion (or equivalent structured grouping)
2. await all join handles
3. aggregate outcomes according to policy (default: max severity)

## Requirements
- Must not abandon any branch.
- Must preserve region close = quiescence.
- Must be deterministic in lab runtime.

## Acceptance Criteria
- All branches complete before join_all returns.
- If policy is fail-fast, siblings are cancelled/drained as specified.
- No task leaks and no obligation leaks.

## Testing
- Unit test: 3 tasks complete, join_all returns aggregated result.
- E2E: one branch errors under fail-fast policy; others cancelled and drained.
close_reason: Implemented JoinAll combinator with marker struct, JoinAllResult, JoinAllError, make_join_all_result(), join_all_to_result(), and 20 comprehensive tests. All 33 join module tests pass.

title: Add forward/backward compatibility for trace format
description:
## Overview

Ensure trace files can be read by newer runtime versions and optionally by older versions.

## Requirements

### Forward Compatibility
- Newer runtimes must read older trace files
- Unknown events skipped with warning
- Missing fields get default values

### Backward Compatibility
- Version header indicates minimum required version
- Clear error if trace requires newer runtime
- Optional: conversion tool for upgrading traces

### Migration System
```rust
pub trait TraceMigration {
    fn from_version(&self) -> u32;
    fn to_version(&self) -> u32;
    fn migrate(&self, events: Vec<TraceEvent>) -> Vec<TraceEvent>;
}

pub struct TraceMigrator {
    migrations: Vec<Box<dyn TraceMigration>>,
}

impl TraceMigrator {
    pub fn migrate_to_current(&self, trace: OldTrace) -> Result<Trace, MigrationError>;
}
```

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Version number in trace header
2. Forward compatibility for 2 major versions
3. Migration system for format changes
4. CLI tool: `asupersync trace upgrade <file>`
5. Tests with traces from each version

## Test Requirements
- Test reading v1 trace with v2 runtime
- Test reading v2 trace with v1 runtime (error)
- Test migration chain v1 -> v2 -> v3
- Benchmark migration performance

title: [bd-2ijqf] Split RuntimeState into Task/Region/Obligation tables
description:
Goal: restructure RuntimeState into separate tables with dedicated locks, reducing contention and clarifying ownership.

Background:
- RuntimeState currently serializes unrelated operations on a single lock.
- Region/obligation ops are less frequent; isolating them reduces interference with scheduling.

Scope / Deliverables:
- Introduce `RegionTable` and `ObligationTable` (or equivalents) encapsulating their arenas + mutation APIs.
- Move region/obligation mutation methods out of RuntimeState into these tables.
- RuntimeState becomes a thin container owning tables plus shared read-mostly state (time, trace handle, metrics, config).

Acceptance Criteria:
- Public RuntimeState API remains coherent (minimal churn to callers).
- Lock ordering documented and enforced in cross-table ops.
- Unit tests for RegionTable/ObligationTable invariants (region close → quiescence, no obligation leaks) with deterministic seeds and structured logging.

title: [AUDIT] Deep correctness audit: runtime/blocking_pool.rs + runtime/deadline_monitor.rs
notes:
VERDICT: SOUND — 0 bugs found

## blocking_pool.rs (1,329 lines)

### Concurrency primitives: 7 patterns
- AtomicUsize × 3: active_threads, busy_threads, pending_count
- AtomicU64 × 1: next_task_id
- AtomicBool × 3 patterns: shutdown (pool-level), cancelled (per-task), done (per-completion)
- Mutex<()> + Condvar × 2: pool parking (BlockingPoolInner), completion waiting (BlockingTaskCompletion)
- Mutex<Vec<ThreadJoinHandle>>: thread_handles
- crossbeam_queue::SegQueue: lock-free MPMC work queue

### CAS-guarded thread spawning (line 596-610)
spawn_thread_on_inner uses CAS loop on active_threads to atomically claim a slot before spawning. Prevents overshoot. Rollback on spawn failure (line 652-656).

### Worker loop lost-wakeup protection (line 698-772)
Queue checked under lock before condvar wait (lines 738, 762). Spawner holds lock for notify (lines 472-474). Serialization prevents: check empty → push → park → missed notification.

### try_claim_idle_retirement (line 678-694)
CAS loop to atomically decrement active_threads only if above min_threads. Prevents thundering herd.

### Panic handling (line 714-721)
catch_unwind(AssertUnwindSafe(task.work)) wraps execution. busy_threads decremented and signal_done called unconditionally. Prevents hanging waiters.

### retired_with_claim (line 639, 644-647)
blocking_worker_loop returns true if thread retired via CAS. Post-loop skips active_threads decrement (already done in CAS). Prevents double-decrement.

### BlockingTaskCompletion (line 157-206)
Mutex+Condvar with while-loop recheck. signal_done: store(true, Release) + lock + notify_all. wait: fast-path load(Acquire) + while(!done.load(Acquire)) condvar.wait. No lost wakeup.

### Ordering
- active_threads CAS: Relaxed in spawn (counter consistency only), AcqRel in retirement (synchronization)
- shutdown/cancelled/done: Acquire/Release (correct)
- busy_threads/pending_count/next_task_id: Relaxed (metrics/heuristics, correct)

## deadline_monitor.rs (1,154 lines)

### Concurrency primitives: ZERO
Pure &mut self data structure. Only external interaction: RwLock::read() on task.cx_inner (owned by task record). Guard dropped at line 344 before any self methods.

### check() dual interval gating (line 303-316)
Returns early only if BOTH logical time AND wall-clock time are below interval. Either advancing logical time (deterministic tests) or wall-clock time (real runtime) triggers scan. Correct.

### Warn-once semantics (line 401-425)
entry.warned = true before emission. Prevents duplicate warnings per task.

### Task cleanup (line 441)
retain() removes tasks no longer in scan. Prevents stale entry accumulation.

### DurationHistory::percentile_nanos (line 127-139)
Fixed-point rank (scaled × 1_000_000) avoids float imprecision for percentile calculation. Clamp 0.0-1.0, saturating_sub for idx.

### No bugs found in either module.
close_reason: done

title: [EPIC-PHASE] Phase 5 - DPOR and TLA+ Tooling
description:
## Overview
Phase 5 adds advanced testing and verification tools: Dynamic Partial Order Reduction (DPOR) for systematic schedule exploration and TLA+ model checking integration for formal verification.

## Goals
1. Systematic exploration of concurrent schedules
2. Optimal DPOR using Mazurkiewicz trace equivalence
3. TLA+ model extraction from runtime traces
4. Property-based testing integration

## Key Components

### 1. Schedule Exploration
Lab runtime already captures execution traces. Phase 5 adds systematic exploration:

```rust
pub struct ScheduleExplorer {
    known_traces: HashSet<TraceFingerprint>,
    pending_schedules: Vec<Schedule>,
    coverage: CoverageMetrics,
}

impl ScheduleExplorer {
    /// Run test under all "interesting" schedules
    pub fn explore<F: Fn(&mut LabRuntime)>(&mut self, test: F) -> ExplorationResult;
}
```

### 2. Dynamic Partial Order Reduction (DPOR)
DPOR avoids redundant schedule exploration:

**Key insight**: Two schedules are equivalent if they differ only in the order of *independent* operations. Independent operations commute; exploring both orderings is redundant.

**Mazurkiewicz traces**: Equivalence classes of schedules under commutativity. DPOR explores one representative per class.

**Algorithm**:
1. Run initial schedule, record trace
2. For each "race" (dependent operations), create alternative schedule
3. Prune schedules equivalent to already-explored traces
4. Repeat until no new schedules

### 3. Independence Relation
Define which operations commute:
| Op A | Op B | Independent? |
|------|------|--------------|
| Read x | Read y | Yes (any x, y) |
| Read x | Write y | Yes if x ≠ y |
| Write x | Write y | No if x = y |
| Send ch1 | Send ch2 | Yes if ch1 ≠ ch2 |
| Send ch | Recv ch | No (same channel) |

### 4. TLA+ Integration
Extract TLA+ models from runtime:

```rust
pub struct TlaExporter {
    // ...
}

impl TlaExporter {
    /// Export trace as TLA+ behavior
    pub fn export_trace(&self, trace: &Trace) -> TlaModule;
    
    /// Export runtime model (state machine)
    pub fn export_model(&self, runtime: &LabRuntime) -> TlaModule;
}
```

TLA+ enables:
- Temporal logic property checking (□ safety, ◇ liveness)
- Model checking with TLC
- Proof integration with TLAPS

### 5. Property-Based Testing
Integration with proptest/quickcheck:

```rust
#[proptest]
fn test_concurrent_counter(
    schedule: Schedule,
    operations: Vec<Op>,
) {
    LabRuntime::new(schedule).run(|| {
        // Execute operations
    });
    // Verify invariants
}
```

## Mathematical Foundation
From the spec:
- **Mazurkiewicz traces**: Partial orders over events, `≡` equivalence
- **DPOR correctness**: Explores all equivalence classes
- **Optimal DPOR**: Explores exactly one per class (no redundancy)

## Coverage Metrics
Track exploration completeness:
- Trace coverage: % of equivalence classes explored
- State coverage: % of reachable states visited
- Edge coverage: % of transitions exercised

## Dependencies
- Requires complete Phase 0-4 (all runtime features)
- Requires lab runtime trace capture
- Requires deterministic execution

## Testing the Testing Tools
Meta-testing:
- Known-buggy programs should have bugs found
- Known-correct programs should pass all schedules
- Coverage metrics should converge

## References
- asupersync_plan_v4.md: §7 Phase 5 (Tooling)
- DPOR papers (Flanagan, Godefroid)
- TLA+ (Lamport)
- PCT (probabilistic concurrency testing)
- Event structures and true concurrency

## Success Criteria
- Defines an independence relation over trace labels and a canonical trace normalization procedure.
- Schedule exploration explores one representative per equivalence class (optimal DPOR-class behavior).
- TLA+ export tooling can emit bounded models/behaviors from traces/state machine snapshots.
- Coverage metrics and reporting make exploration progress measurable and actionable.
close_reason: Core Phase 5 deliverables complete: independence relation, Foata canonicalization, DPOR race detection, schedule explorer, TLA+ exporter. Remaining children (59c.4-59c.6) are P4 research/tracking items that remain open independently.

title: [EPIC-INFRA] Hierarchical Timer Wheel
description:
## Overview

Implement a hierarchical timer wheel for O(1) timer operations, replacing naive linear timer storage. This is a performance-critical optimization for workloads with many concurrent timers.

## Strategic Value

**Problem Solved**: Current timer implementations (if using Vec or BTreeMap) have O(n) or O(log n) cost for timer operations. Servers handling thousands of connections each with timeouts need O(1) operations.

**Why Hierarchical**: Simple timer wheels have limited range. Hierarchical wheels (like Linux kernel) provide O(1) insert/cancel/expire across wide time ranges (milliseconds to hours).

**Production Necessity**: Any serious async runtime needs efficient timer management. This is foundational for production use.

## Algorithm Overview

### Timer Wheel Structure
```
Level 0: 256 slots, 1ms resolution (covers 256ms)
Level 1: 64 slots, 256ms resolution (covers 16.4 seconds)  
Level 2: 64 slots, 16.4s resolution (covers 17.5 minutes)
Level 3: 64 slots, 17.5min resolution (covers 18.6 hours)
```

### Operations
- **Insert**: Hash deadline to appropriate level/slot, O(1)
- **Cancel**: Remove from linked list at slot, O(1) with handle
- **Tick**: Process Level 0, cascade higher levels periodically

### Cascading
When Level 0 wraps, cascade Level 1 slot into Level 0. This amortizes the cost of long-duration timers.

## Design Considerations

### Memory Layout
- Intrusive linked lists for zero-allocation in steady state
- Timer handles store list pointers for O(1) cancel
- Cache-friendly slot arrays

### Precision Trade-offs
- 1ms base resolution is sufficient for network timeouts
- Sub-millisecond needs separate approach (spin loops, etc.)
- Configuration allows tuning resolution vs. memory

### Integration
- Replace current timer storage in time module
- Maintain same API (sleep, timeout, Delay)
- Lab runtime gets separate virtual time wheel

## Acceptance Criteria

1. O(1) insert, cancel, and per-tick expire operations
2. Supports at least 24-hour timer range
3. Memory overhead < 1KB for wheel structure
4. Benchmark shows 10x improvement over BTreeMap for 10K timers
5. No changes to public timer API

## Dependencies

- Standalone module, no major dependencies
- Benefits from good integration test coverage

## Priority Rationale

Ranked #7 because while important for production performance, it is primarily an internal optimization. Users benefit indirectly through better performance, but it does not add new capabilities.
close_reason: All 4 sub-tasks closed: gt1c (Lab virtual time wheel), jrrw (overflow and coalescing), h7as (comprehensive test suite), uyqb (benchmarks). HierarchicalTimerWheel in src/time/intrusive_wheel.rs, VirtualTimerWheel in src/lab/virtual_time_wheel.rs, TimerWheel in src/time/wheel.rs. O(1) operations, hierarchical 4-level design, tests passing, benchmarks complete.

title: Implement hedge combinator for latency hedging
description:
## Purpose
The hedge combinator implements latency hedging - start a primary task, and if it does not complete within a deadline, speculatively start a backup. Return whichever completes first. This is a key pattern for reducing tail latency in distributed systems.

## Motivation
P99 latencies often exceed P50 by 10-100x. Hedging trades compute cost for latency:
- Primary starts immediately
- If deadline expires without completion, backup launches
- First to complete wins; loser is cancelled and drained
- Total latency bounded by min(primary, backup) rather than max

## Semantic Model

```rust
pub async fn hedge<T, E>(
    cx: &mut Cx<'_>,
    primary: impl Future<Output = Result<T, E>>,
    backup: impl FnOnce(&mut Cx<'_>) -> impl Future<Output = Result<T, E>>,
    deadline: Duration,
) -> Outcome<T, E>
```

### Behavior
1. Spawn primary as region child
2. Start timer for deadline
3. Case A - Primary completes before deadline: return result, never spawn backup
4. Case B - Deadline fires: spawn backup as region child, race primary vs backup
5. Loser of race MUST be cancelled and drained (non-negotiable)
6. Return winner's result

### Budget Semantics
From the spec: hedge operations have combined budget = primary_budget + backup_budget + deadline
The deadline acts as a "grace period" before hedging kicks in.

## Cancellation Handling
- If caller requests cancel before primary completes: cancel primary, never spawn backup
- If caller requests cancel during race: cancel both, drain both
- Loser draining is mandatory regardless of outcome

## Implementation Notes
- Backup is a `FnOnce` closure, not a future - only create backup future if needed
- This avoids allocating/preparing backup work that may never execute
- The closure takes `Cx` to spawn into the same region

## Invariant Support
- **Losers always drained**: If backup spawned, exactly one loses and must drain
- **No orphan tasks**: Both primary and backup owned by hedge region
- **Quiescence**: Hedge region closes only when all spawned children done

## Testing Requirements
1. Primary fast path (completes before deadline)
2. Backup triggered path (deadline expires)
3. Both cases: winner returns, loser drained
4. Cancellation at each phase
5. Budget propagation verification
6. Deterministic lab runtime testing

## Example Usage

```rust
// Primary RPC with 100ms hedge to backup
let result = scope.hedge(
    cx,
    call_primary_server(cx, request.clone()),
    |cx| call_backup_server(cx, request.clone()),
    Duration::from_millis(100),
).await?;
```

## Real-World Applications
- Database reads with replica fallback
- RPC calls with backup endpoint
- DNS resolution with multiple resolvers
- Storage operations with tiered backends

## References
- asupersync_plan_v4.md: §5.7 Derived Combinators
- Google "The Tail at Scale" paper (Dean & Barroso)
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md: §3.2 Budget composition

## Acceptance Criteria
- Starts a secondary attempt after a deterministic delay (virtual time in lab) to reduce tail latency.
- Ensures only one winner is committed; losers are cancelled and drained.
- Uses cancel-safe primitives for any shared result publication.
- E2E tests cover determinism, cancellation, and no-obligation-leaks.

title: Implement first_ok combinator for fallback chains
description:
## Purpose
The first_ok combinator tries a sequence of operations, returning the first Ok result. If all operations fail, returns an aggregated error. This is essential for fallback chains, service discovery, and graceful degradation.

## Distinction from race
- **race**: Run all concurrently, first to complete wins (regardless of success/failure)
- **first_ok**: Run sequentially or with controlled concurrency, first SUCCESS wins

For Phase 0 (single-threaded), implement sequential first_ok. Concurrent variants in Phase 1.

## Semantic Model

```rust
pub async fn first_ok<T, E>(
    cx: &mut Cx<'_>,
    operations: Vec<impl Fn(&mut Cx<'_>) -> impl Future<Output = Result<T, E>>>,
) -> Outcome<T, Vec<E>>  // Returns first Ok or all errors
```

### Behavior (Sequential)
1. For each operation in order:
   a. Execute operation
   b. If Ok: return immediately (short-circuit)
   c. If Err: collect error, continue to next
2. If all fail: return Err(collected_errors)
3. If cancelled at any point: return Cancelled

### Behavior (Concurrent - Phase 1)
1. Spawn all operations
2. As results arrive:
   a. If Ok: cancel remaining, drain them, return Ok
   b. If Err: collect, continue waiting
3. If all complete with Err: return aggregated errors

## Error Aggregation
Two options for error return:
1. `Vec<E>`: All errors in attempt order
2. `FirstOkError<E> { errors: Vec<E>, attempted: usize }`: With metadata

The simple `Vec<E>` is preferred for Phase 0.

## Cancellation Handling
- Check cancellation before each attempt
- If cancelled: return Cancelled with errors collected so far
- Do not start new attempts after cancellation

## Use Cases
1. **Service fallback**: Primary → Secondary → Tertiary endpoint
2. **Configuration sources**: File → Environment → Defaults
3. **Parser fallback**: Try parsers in preference order
4. **Cache hierarchy**: L1 → L2 → L3 → Origin

## Invariant Support
- **Short-circuit**: First success returns immediately
- **Complete error context**: All failures preserved for debugging
- **Cancel-correctness**: Respects cancellation between attempts

## Testing Requirements
1. First operation succeeds (no fallback needed)
2. Middle operation succeeds (some fallbacks tried)
3. All operations fail (error aggregation)
4. Cancellation at various points
5. Empty operations list (edge case)
6. Single operation (degenerate case)

## Example Usage

```rust
// Try multiple DNS resolvers
let addr = scope.first_ok(cx, vec\![
    |cx| async move { resolve_dns(cx, "8.8.8.8", domain).await },
    |cx| async move { resolve_dns(cx, "1.1.1.1", domain).await },
    |cx| async move { resolve_dns(cx, "9.9.9.9", domain).await },
]).await?;

// Try config sources
let config = scope.first_ok(cx, vec\![
    |cx| async move { load_config_file(cx, "/etc/app/config.toml").await },
    |cx| async move { load_config_env(cx).await },
    |cx| async move { Ok(Config::default()) },  // Always succeeds as final fallback
]).await?;
```

## References
- asupersync_plan_v4.md: §5.7 Derived Combinators
- Railway-oriented programming
- Option::or_else chains in Rust
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md: §3.2 Error handling

## Acceptance Criteria
- Returns the first `Ok` result if any branch succeeds; otherwise returns aggregated failure information.
- All losing/failed branches are cancelled and drained before returning.
- Deterministic behavior in lab runs with explicit tie-breaking.
- E2E tests cover cancellation + loser draining and interaction with policies.

title: [EPIC-INFRA] Deterministic Replay Debugging
description:
## Overview

Deterministic Replay Debugging enables recording execution traces and replaying them exactly to debug issues. This is a unique capability enabled by asupersync's deterministic Lab runtime.

## Strategic Value

**Problem Solved**: Async bugs are notoriously hard to reproduce. Race conditions, timing-dependent failures, and heisenbugs often disappear when debugging is enabled.

**Why This Approach**: Because asupersync has a deterministic Lab runtime with controllable scheduling, we can record every scheduling decision, timer event, and I/O result, then replay them exactly. This transforms "unreproducible" bugs into deterministic test cases.

**Differentiation**: No other Rust async runtime offers this. Traditional runtimes use OS schedulers and real I/O, making exact replay impossible. Our Lab runtime's determinism makes this feasible.

## Architecture

### Recording Phase
- Instrument Lab runtime to emit trace events
- Capture: scheduling decisions, timer ticks, I/O results, RNG seeds
- Store in compact binary format (bincode or MessagePack)
- Include minimal metadata for versioning

### Replay Phase
- Load trace file, verify compatibility
- Create Lab runtime in replay mode
- Feed recorded decisions instead of making new ones
- Assert execution matches recorded state

### Debugging Integration
- Provide "step" and "continue" commands in replay
- Show region tree state at each step
- Highlight divergence if replay doesn't match

## Acceptance Criteria

1. RecordingTrace captures all non-determinism sources
2. Replay mode reproduces exact execution order
3. Trace file format is versioned and forward-compatible
4. Documentation includes debugging workflow examples
5. At least 3 complex test scenarios demonstrate value

## Dependencies

- Builds on existing trace module infrastructure
- May benefit from tracing integration (Epic #2)

## Priority Rationale

Ranked #6 because while powerful, it requires significant infrastructure and the target users (debugging complex issues) are a subset of all users.

title: [bd-2ijqf] Sharding Scope + Lock Ordering Spec
description:
Goal: produce a self-contained, implementation-ready spec for RuntimeState sharding, including boundaries, ownership, and lock ordering.

Background:
- Hot-path contention today is `Arc<Mutex<RuntimeState>>` in scheduler worker execute and LocalQueue push/pop/steal. These paths lock the entire RuntimeState just to touch `tasks` + `stored_futures` + wake_state.
- Region/obligation mutations are less frequent than polling; we should decouple them from hot-path locks.
- Determinism, cancel-correctness, and no ambient authority are non-negotiable.

Scope / Deliverables:
- Define the split into tables: `TaskTable` (tasks arena, stored_futures, wake_state access), `RegionTable`, `ObligationTable`, plus shared read-mostly config (trace handle, metrics, logical clock config, time).
- Specify exact lock ordering: `tasks -> regions -> obligations` and enumerate any allowed shortcuts (e.g., hot-path may lock tasks only).
- Enumerate all RuntimeState methods that must be rehomed to TaskTable or Region/Obligation tables (list of affected functions + files).
- Identify cross-table operations and how to avoid deadlocks (documented order + helper APIs that lock in order).
- Decide shard granularity: single global lock per table for Phase 1, optional per-shard sharding later (Phase 2).
- Include a callsite migration checklist (ties to the callsite-audit bead) so no full-state locks remain in hot paths.
- Produce a test coverage matrix that maps each table/API change to unit tests, lab tests, and the E2E harness (so all verification paths are explicit and self-contained).

Acceptance Criteria:
- Spec includes rationale for why each datum lives in a given table.
- Spec includes a “do-not-break” list: determinism, cancel-correctness, no ambient authority, and no extra hot-path allocations.
- Spec references the verification beads for unit/lab/E2E testing and logging.

Notes:
This bead must be completed before code changes. It is the canonical blueprint so future work never requires prior markdown or memory.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Spec document is self-contained and implementation-ready, covering table boundaries, ownership, and lock ordering.
2. Test coverage matrix maps changes to unit, lab, and E2E harness (bd-ecaeo) with structured logging requirements.
3. Includes a callsite migration checklist and a do-not-break invariant list (determinism, cancel-correctness, obligation linearity, no ambient authority).
notes:
Additional cross-table notes (from 1360-2100 region):
- mark_obligation_leaked(): obligations -> regions -> advance_region_state (needs canonical order or staged apply).
- handle_obligation_leaks(): invokes abort_obligation (obligations -> regions) — ensure ordering aligns with canonical order via staging.
- apply_policy_on_child_outcome()/cancel_sibling_tasks(): regions -> tasks; must be two-phase (snapshot region task_ids under RegionTable, then apply cancel under TaskTable with canonical order).
- can_region_finalize(): checks region.task_ids + task states + child region states; should be snapshot-based to avoid multi-lock holds.
- is_quiescent(): touches tasks, obligations, regions, io_driver; should use snapshot counts rather than holding multiple locks.
- drain_ready_async_finalizers(): regions + tasks; spawn_finalizer_task creates tasks — ensure canonical order or staging around task creation.

Suggested pattern templates:
1) Snapshot pattern: lock RegionTable, collect ids; unlock; lock TaskTable to mutate tasks; if obligation updates needed, lock ObligationTable last.
2) Two-phase apply: Phase A validates constraints in RegionTable (admission/limits), Phase B performs obligation/task mutation under canonical order, Phase C updates region counters (resolve_obligation / advance_region_state) under RegionTable.
3) Read-only queries: prefer per-table snapshot counts (live_task_count, pending_obligation_count, live_region_count) to avoid multi-lock holds; consider caching counts with atomic updates.

Needs mapping in spec:
- apply_policy_on_child_outcome + cancel_sibling_tasks.
- mark_obligation_leaked + handle_obligation_leaks.
- is_quiescent + can_region_finalize.
- drain_ready_async_finalizers + spawn_finalizer_task.

title: [SUB-EPIC-PHASE] Windows IOCP Reactor
description:
# Sub-Epic: Windows IOCP Reactor

## Overview

I/O Completion Ports (IOCP) is Windows' native async I/O mechanism. Required for cross-platform support.

## Why IOCP

- Native Windows async I/O (no polling)
- Completion-based (not readiness-based like epoll/kqueue)
- Scales to thousands of concurrent operations
- Integrated with Windows thread pool

## Key Differences from Unix Reactors

| Aspect | epoll/kqueue | IOCP |
|--------|--------------|------|
| Model | Readiness | Completion |
| When notified | "Socket CAN be read" | "Read HAS completed" |
| Buffer ownership | User owns buffer | OS borrows buffer during I/O |
| Cancellation | Close fd | CancelIoEx() |

## Design Challenge

IOCP is **completion-based**, not readiness-based:
- User initiates read with buffer
- OS notifies when read is complete (data in buffer)
- Buffer must remain valid until completion

Our `Reactor` trait is readiness-based. Options:
1. **Adaptation layer**: Start operations and track completions
2. **Separate trait**: `CompletionReactor` for IOCP
3. **Internal polling**: Use IOCP internally but expose readiness

## Recommended Approach: Hybrid

```rust
pub struct IocpReactor {
    iocp: HANDLE,
    /// Pending operations (buffer lives here until complete)
    pending: Mutex<HashMap<Token, PendingOp>>,
}

impl Reactor for IocpReactor {
    fn register(&self, source: &dyn Source, interest: Interest, waker: Waker) -> io::Result<Registration> {
        // Associate handle with IOCP
        CreateIoCompletionPort(source.raw_handle(), self.iocp, token, 0)?;
        
        // For readiness emulation, we may need to start a speculative operation
        if interest.contains(Interest::READABLE) {
            self.start_speculative_read(source, token)?;
        }
        
        Ok(Registration::new(token, ...))
    }
    
    fn poll(&self, events: &mut Events, timeout: Option<Duration>) -> io::Result<usize> {
        // GetQueuedCompletionStatus(Ex)
        // Convert completions to readiness events
    }
}
```

## Dependencies

```toml
[target.'cfg(windows)'.dependencies]
windows-sys = { version = "0.52", features = ["Win32_System_IO", "Win32_Foundation"] }
```

## Task Breakdown

1. IOCP handle management
2. Handle association with completion port
3. Completion queue processing
4. Readiness emulation layer
5. CancelIoEx for cancellation
6. AFD_POLL for socket readiness (alternative)
7. Overlapped I/O integration
8. Thread pool integration (optional)

## AFD_POLL Alternative

Windows actually has readiness notification via AFD_POLL (undocumented but stable):
- Used by libuv, tokio-iocp
- Closer to epoll semantics
- May be simpler than full completion-based IOCP

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] IocpReactor implements Reactor trait
- [ ] Passes same tests as Unix reactors
- [ ] Cancellation works correctly
- [ ] No buffer safety issues
- [ ] Benchmark comparable to Unix performance

title: Implement race_all combinator (N-way race with loser draining)
description:
# race_all (N-way Race with Loser Draining)

## Purpose
Generalize `race(a,b)` to `race_all(futures)`:
- first terminal outcome wins
- every loser is cancelled and drained to terminal

This is essential for timeouts, hedges, speculative execution, and quorum-style patterns.

## Semantics
1. spawn all participants in a subregion
2. wait for the first terminal completion
3. request cancellation on every loser
4. **drain** every loser by awaiting completion
5. return winner outcome

## Acceptance Criteria
- Winner is returned.
- Every spawned participant reaches a terminal state before `race_all` returns.
- Loser finalizers run.
- Loser obligations are resolved.

## Testing
- E2E: include a loser holding a permit/guard; verify it is released due to drain.

title: Sub-Epic: WebSocket Protocol Implementation
description:
# Sub-Epic: WebSocket Protocol Implementation

## Overview

Implement complete WebSocket (RFC 6455) support for both client and server roles, with proper integration into Asupersync's structured concurrency model.

## Why WebSocket Matters

WebSocket is essential for:
- Real-time applications (chat, notifications, live updates)
- Streaming APIs (financial data, IoT sensors)
- Bidirectional communication (gaming, collaboration tools)
- Long-lived connections (dashboards, monitoring)

**This is THE critical gap** - no WebSocket means no real-time apps.

## Design Principles

### 1. Cancel-Correct Close Handshake

WebSocket has a specific close handshake (close frame exchange). Unlike Tokio where dropping a WebSocket may leak the close, we ensure:
- Close frame sent on region close
- Wait for close acknowledgment (with timeout)
- Proper drain of pending messages

### 2. Region-Owned Connections

```rust
// WebSocket connection belongs to spawning region
let ws = WebSocket::connect(cx, "wss://example.com/ws").await?;

// When region closes, connection closes cleanly
cx.spawn(async move {
    while let Some(msg) = ws.recv(cx).await? {
        // Process messages
    }
});
// Region close -> ws.close() called automatically
```

### 3. Split Read/Write

Like TcpStream, WebSocket supports splitting:
```rust
let (rx, tx) = ws.split();
// rx and tx can be used in separate tasks
// Both owned by same region
```

### 4. Backpressure

Sending respects backpressure:
```rust
// Returns Pending if send buffer full
ws.send(cx, Message::Text("hello")).await?;
```

## Protocol Coverage

RFC 6455 requirements:
- [ ] HTTP upgrade handshake (client and server)
- [ ] Frame parsing (text, binary, ping, pong, close)
- [ ] XOR masking (client->server must mask)
- [ ] Fragmentation (large messages split into frames)
- [ ] Close handshake (bidirectional close frame exchange)
- [ ] Ping/pong keepalive

Extensions (optional):
- [ ] Per-message deflate (compression)
- [ ] Subprotocol negotiation

## Architecture

```
src/ws/
├── mod.rs           # Public API: WebSocket, Message, CloseCode
├── handshake.rs     # HTTP upgrade negotiation
├── frame.rs         # Frame codec (RFC 6455 wire format)
├── mask.rs          # XOR masking implementation
├── close.rs         # Close handshake state machine
├── message.rs       # Message types (Text, Binary, Ping, Pong, Close)
├── split.rs         # ReadHalf, WriteHalf
├── client.rs        # WebSocket::connect()
├── server.rs        # WebSocket::accept()
└── tests/
    ├── handshake_test.rs
    ├── frame_test.rs
    └── integration_test.rs
```

## Integration Points

- Uses existing TcpStream/TlsStream
- Uses existing HTTP/1.1 parser for upgrade
- Integrates with Cx for cancellation checkpoints
- Uses codec framework for framing

## Lab Runtime Considerations

- Virtual time for ping/pong intervals
- Deterministic frame ordering
- Simulated connection drops for close testing

## Dependencies

- Depends on: HTTP/1.1 (for upgrade handshake), TLS (for wss://)
- Blocked by: None (core infrastructure exists)

## Success Criteria

- [ ] Client can connect to standard WebSocket servers
- [ ] Server can accept WebSocket upgrades
- [ ] All frame types handled correctly
- [ ] Close handshake completes cleanly
- [ ] Cancellation triggers proper close
- [ ] Lab runtime tests deterministic
- [ ] Passes Autobahn test suite (industry standard)

## References

- RFC 6455: https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6455
- Autobahn test suite: https://github.com/crossbario/autobahn-testsuite
- tokio-tungstenite (reference): https://github.com/snapview/tokio-tungstenite

title: [ALIEN][PLAN] Semantics spec: trace-equivalence + side-condition schema
description:
## Purpose

Define what it means for two Plan IR programs to be "the same" in Asupersync, and define the schema that makes rewrite rules checkable.

This is the foundation for:
- e-graph search (we can only merge nodes if we know the equivalence notion)
- certificates + verifier (what exactly is being certified?)
- lab equivalence oracle (how we test equivalence deterministically)

## Equivalence notion (independence-aware, not schedule-identical)

We target observational equivalence up to the runtime's trace semantics.

Two plans P and Q are equivalent if, under the same deterministic lab configuration (seed, policies, budgets):
- they produce the same terminal Outcome (including CancelReason / severity lattice position)
- they satisfy the same safety invariants (no obligation leaks, region close => quiescence, losers drained)
- their executions are equivalent up to allowed commutations of independent events (Mazurkiewicz / trace-monoid equivalence)

We do NOT require identical step-by-step schedules.

Operationally, the lab equivalence oracle will compare:
- canonicalized trace fingerprints (Foata / independence-normalized)
- plus explicit observable state projections (obligation ledger summaries, region tree quiescence)

## Allowed law families (rewrite preconditions)

Every rewrite rule must declare which laws it relies on, in machine-checkable form.

- algebraic laws for combinators (examples):
  - monoid: associativity of join, identity elements
  - semiring-like: distributivity or absorption, if applicable

- concurrency / trace laws:
  - commutation only when independence is proven
  - loser-drain laws for race

- cancellation protocol laws:
  - request -> drain -> finalize (idempotent)
  - masking rules (where cancellation can/cannot be observed)

- obligation laws:
  - linearity: permits/acks/leases must be resolved
  - no implicit drops

- budget laws:
  - meet/propagation laws for Budget semiring
  - deadline safety: rewrites must not weaken deadlines or increase required poll quota beyond declared bound

## Side-condition schema (what the analysis must prove)

Each rewrite step must carry a side-condition object that can be checked by a small verifier:
- independence conditions for commutations
- obligation-flow safety conditions (no new leak paths)
- cancellation safety conditions (loser drain preserved, cancel responsiveness not worsened beyond bound)
- budget monotonicity conditions
- determinism conditions (no iteration-order dependence introduced)

## Certificate/verifier contract (ties into bd-2jck)

A certificate is a sequence of rewrite steps plus their side conditions, with stable hashing.

The verifier must:
- validate each step matches a known rule schema
- validate all referenced side conditions (via analysis summaries or explicit witnesses)
- validate deterministic hashing / ordering constraints

## Acceptance criteria

- Provides an unambiguous equivalence target for tests and certificates.
- Enumerates law families and side-condition schema explicitly.
- Defines what data the verifier needs and what the lab oracle must compare.
close_reason: Added trace-equivalence + side-condition schema to formal semantics docs

title: Phase 0: Cx Capability Boundary & Scope API
description:
# Phase 0: Cx Capability Boundary & Scope API

## Purpose
Expose a user-facing API that makes “incorrect code hard to express” by construction:
- **No ambient authority**: effects flow through `Cx` and explicit capabilities.
- **Structured concurrency**: tasks are owned by regions; regions close to quiescence.

This is the user’s *primary* interface to Asupersync.

## Scope
### 1) `Cx` surface (capability/effect boundary)
Phase 0 must define and implement at least:
- identity: `region_id()`, `task_id()`
- budgets/time: `budget()`, `now()`
- cancellation: `is_cancel_requested()`, `checkpoint()`, `with_cancel_mask()`
- scheduling: `yield_now()`
- timers: `sleep_until()` / `sleep_for()`
- tracing: `trace(event)` / `trace_user(name,data)`

### 2) `Scope` / region API
- `Scope::spawn` (Phase 0: single-thread “fiber” tier is sufficient; later phases add `Send` tasks)
- `Scope::region` (subregion creation) with close-to-quiescence semantics
- finalizers registration APIs
- join handles (await completion; cancel requests)

### 3) Soundness frontier (tiers)
The design distinguishes fibers/tasks/actors/remote. Phase 0 should implement the minimal tier that preserves correctness without pretending “Send across threads” is safe before Phase 1.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Users can express:
  - nested region structure
  - safe spawning
  - safe cancellation and cleanup
  - deterministic tests in lab runtime
- It is impossible (or at least detectable in lab) to perform effects without going through `Cx`.

## Testing Strategy
- Compile-time “doesn’t typecheck” tests for lifetime escape (as feasible).
- Runtime lab tests verifying no ambient authority via trace/oracle.

title: Implement TaskState enum and state machine
description:
# TaskState Enum and State Machine

## Purpose
TaskState represents the lifecycle of a task from creation to completion. The state machine is carefully designed to support the cancellation protocol with explicit drain and finalize phases.

## The Task States
```rust
enum TaskState {
    // Initial state after spawn
    Created,
    
    // Actively being polled
    Running,
    
    // Cancel requested but not yet acknowledged
    CancelRequested {
        reason: CancelReason,
        cleanup_budget: Budget,
    },
    
    // Task has acknowledged cancel, running cleanup code
    Cancelling {
        cleanup_budget: Budget,
    },
    
    // Cleanup done, running finalizers
    Finalizing {
        cleanup_budget: Budget,
    },
    
    // Terminal state
    Completed(Outcome),
}
```

## State Transitions

```
                    ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │                                      │
Created ──────────► Running ──────────────────────────────►│
    │                 │                                    │
    │                 │ cancel_request()                   │
    │                 ▼                                    │
    │           CancelRequested ─────────────────────────►│
    │                 │                                    │
    │                 │ checkpoint (mask=0)                │
    │                 ▼                                    │ Completed
    │              Cancelling ───────────────────────────►│
    │                 │                                    │
    │                 │ cleanup done                       │
    │                 ▼                                    │
    │              Finalizing ───────────────────────────►│
    │                 │                                    │
    │                 │ finalizers done                    │
    │                 ▼                                    │
    └────────────────►  Completed(Outcome)  ◄──────────────┘
```

## Valid Transitions

| From | To | Trigger | Label |
|------|-----|---------|-------|
| Created | Running | Scheduler selects | τ (silent) |
| Created | CancelRequested | Cancel before first poll | cancel(r,reason) |
| Running | Completed(Ok/Err) | Task body returns | complete(t,outcome) |
| Running | CancelRequested | Cancel request arrives | cancel(r,reason) |
| CancelRequested | Cancelling | Checkpoint with mask=0 | τ |
| CancelRequested | CancelRequested | Checkpoint with mask>0 (defer) | τ |
| Cancelling | Finalizing | Cleanup code completes | τ |
| Cancelling | Completed(Cancelled) | No cleanup needed | complete(t,Cancelled) |
| Finalizing | Completed(Cancelled) | All finalizers run | complete(t,Cancelled) |

## Why These States?

### Created vs Running
Separates "spawned but not yet scheduled" from "actively executing." This allows:
- Batch spawning before any execution
- Cancel before first poll (task never runs)
- Clear scheduling semantics

### CancelRequested
The task hasn't observed the cancel yet. This is important because:
- Task may be in the middle of a computation
- Task should reach a checkpoint to observe cancel
- Masking allows bounded deferral

### Cancelling
Task has acknowledged cancel and is running cleanup code. The cleanup_budget ensures bounded cleanup time.

### Finalizing
Cleanup code done, now running registered finalizers (defer_async, defer_sync). Finalizers run under cancel mask.

### Completed
Terminal and absorbing. Once Completed, the state never changes. This supports INV-OBLIGATION-LINEAR.

## Mask Budget

When in CancelRequested, the task has a `mask` count (in TaskRecord, not TaskState):
- Each checkpoint where mask>0 decrements mask and returns Ok
- When mask=0, checkpoint returns Cancelled
- This ensures bounded cancellation deferral (INV-MASK-BOUNDED)

## Implementation Requirements

1. **TaskState must be Clone, Debug**
2. **Completed(Outcome) stores the full outcome**
3. **is_terminal() method**: Returns true only for Completed
4. **is_cancelling() method**: Returns true for CancelRequested/Cancelling/Finalizing
5. **can_be_polled() method**: Returns true for Running/CancelRequested/Cancelling/Finalizing

## Invariant Support

### INV-TASK-OWNED
```rust
∀t: T[t].state ≠ Completed(_) ⟹ t ∈ R[T[t].region].children
```
Non-completed tasks are owned by their region.

### INV-MASK-BOUNDED  
```rust
∀t: T[t].mask ∈ ℕ and only decreases at CHECKPOINT-MASKED
```
Masking is finite.

### INV-OBLIGATION-BOUNDED
```rust
∀o: O[o].state = Reserved ⟹ T[O[o].holder].state ∈ {Running, CancelRequested, Cancelling, Finalizing}
```
Reserved obligations have live holders.

## Testing Requirements

1. Only valid transitions are possible
2. Completed is absorbing (can't transition out)
3. State machine handles all cancel timing scenarios
4. Mask budget decrements correctly

## Example Scenarios

### Normal Completion
```
Created → Running → Completed(Ok(value))
```

### Cancelled at Checkpoint
```
Created → Running → CancelRequested → Cancelling → Finalizing → Completed(Cancelled)
```

### Cancelled Before First Poll
```
Created → CancelRequested → Cancelling → Finalizing → Completed(Cancelled)
```

### Error During Cancellation
```
Created → Running → CancelRequested → Cancelling → Completed(Err(e))
// Error during cleanup is still an error, not Cancelled
```

## References
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §1.5 (Task States)
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §3.1-3.2 (Task lifecycle, Cancellation protocol)
- asupersync_plan_v4.md §7.1 (Task cancellation state machine)

## Acceptance Criteria
- Task lifecycle states match the spec: Created → Running → (CancelRequested → Cancelling → Finalizing) → Completed(outcome).
- Cancellation-related states carry the necessary metadata (reason, budgets/quotas) and strengthen idempotently.
- Completed is terminal/absorbing.
- Unit tests cover legal/illegal transitions and trace-level representation.
notes:
Implemented TaskState + core transitions aligned to formal semantics.

- `src/record/task.rs`: TaskState now `Created | Running | CancelRequested{reason, cleanup_budget} | Cancelling{cleanup_budget} | Finalizing{cleanup_budget} | Completed(TaskOutcome)` where `TaskOutcome = Outcome<(), crate::error::Error>` (Phase 0 concrete outcome storage). Added helpers `is_terminal`, `is_cancelling`, `can_be_polled`, plus TaskRecord transition helpers `start_running` + `complete`.
- Cancellation request handling is idempotent: repeated `request_cancel` strengthens `CancelReason` and tightens `cleanup_budget` via `Budget::combine`.
- Updated affected call sites/tests (notably `src/runtime/state.rs` live-task accounting + policy sibling-cancel tests).
- Added unit tests in `src/record/task.rs` covering cancel-before-first-poll, strengthening, Completed absorbing, and pollability predicate.

Gates: cargo fmt --check, cargo check --all-targets, cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings, cargo test all pass.

# Actor Core Abstraction

## Goal

Implement the foundational actor types that all other actor functionality builds upon.

## Types to Implement

### ActorId
- Unique identifier for an actor within the runtime
- Must be deterministic in lab runtime (arena-based allocation like TaskId/RegionId)
- Includes generation counter for safe reuse after actor termination

### ActorRef<M>
- Typed handle for sending messages to an actor
- Generic over message type M for compile-time type safety
- Cheap to clone (Arc-based or index-based)
- Methods: send(), try_send(), is_alive()

### ActorCell
- Internal runtime state for an actor:
  - actor_id: ActorId

  - mailbox: Receiver<M> (bounded channel)
  - state: ActorState (Created, Running, Stopping, Stopped)
  - parent: Option<ActorId> (supervisor)
  - children: Vec<ActorId> (supervised children)
  - restart_count: u32 (for backoff)
  - created_at: Time

## Integration Points

- ActorId stored in RuntimeState arena (like TaskId)
- ActorCell linked to owning Region (region close terminates actor)
- ActorRef uses same two-phase send as channels (reserve→commit)

description:
# Sub-Epic: Message Queue Clients

## Overview
Implements first-party clients for major message queue systems (NATS, Redis Pub/Sub,
Kafka) with full Cx integration, structured concurrency, and cancel-correct semantics.

## Background & Motivation
Anyone using Tokio will say 'I can use async-nats, rdkafka, redis-rs for message queues.'
We need first-party, cancel-correct alternatives that integrate seamlessly with
Asupersync's structured concurrency model.

## Key Differentiators from Tokio Ecosystem

### Cancel-Correct Consumption
In Tokio, if a task consuming messages is cancelled, messages may be lost.
In Asupersync:
- Message delivery is an obligation
- Consumption must be ack/nack/committed/aborted
- Cancellation drains in-flight handlers gracefully
- No 'message lost because task dropped'

### Backpressure as First-Class Protocol
- Explicit credit windows
- Bounded queues with budget integration
- Producer slowdown when consumers lag

### Structured Lifecycle
- Connection owned by region
- Region close gracefully disconnects
- Child tasks for message handlers scoped to region

## Message Queue Clients

### 1. NATS Client
- Pure Rust implementation (no C dependencies)
- Subject-based pub/sub
- Request-reply pattern
- JetStream support (durable streams)

### 2. Redis Client
- Redis protocol (RESP)
- GET/SET/HGET/etc. operations
- Pub/Sub subscriptions
- Streams (XREAD, XADD, XACK)

### 3. Kafka Client
- Producer with exactly-once semantics
- Consumer groups with commit offsets
- Transactional support
- (May wrap librdkafka for protocol complexity)

## Integration Points
- All clients use Asupersync TCP/TLS stack
- Cx checkpoints for cancellation
- Budget integration for rate limiting
- Tracing for observability

## Tasks in This Sub-Epic
1. NATS client core (connect, pub/sub)
2. NATS JetStream integration
3. Redis client core (commands, connection)
4. Redis Pub/Sub and Streams
5. Kafka producer
6. Kafka consumer
7. Message queue E2E tests

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] NATS client with pub/sub and request-reply
- [ ] Redis client with commands and pub/sub
- [ ] Kafka producer/consumer with commit semantics
- [ ] All clients cancel-correct
- [ ] Backpressure handling
- [ ] E2E tests with real services (Docker)
- [ ] Performance comparable to Tokio alternatives

comments.text:
## Scope

Define the **public** application-facing types:

- `AppSpec` (pure data / builder): describes topology and required capabilities.
- `AppHandle`: handle returned from start.
- `AppStartError` / `AppStopError`: explicit error taxonomy.

## Semantics (must be explicit, testable)

- `start(cx)`:
  - allocates (or is given) a root region
  - compiles `AppSpec` into supervisor/child specs
  - starts children deterministically
  - returns `AppHandle` that owns the root region

- `stop(cx)`:
  - requests cancel on root
  - drains + finalizes
  - returns only when region close implies quiescence

- `join(cx)`:
  - waits for terminal outcome of the root region (including crashes/cancel)

## Invariants

- close => quiescence (no live tasks, no pending obligations, finalizers empty)
- all stop paths are cancel-correct (request -> drain -> finalize)
- no ambient authority: an AppSpec cannot "secretly" reach globals

## Acceptance

- Minimal API compiles and can start a toy app under lab runtime.
- `AppHandle` drop semantics are explicit (either auto-stop or leak-preventing panic; pick and document).
- Doc tests show the recommended usage pattern.

comments.text:
# Agent-First Ergonomics (Why this is explicitly separate)

Jose's claim about Elixir being great for AI is largely about *agent ergonomics*:

- low ambiguity operational model
- consistent conventions
- documentation that doesn't rot
- tooling that makes debugging cheap

Spork can beat that if we design the workflow around deterministic artifacts.

## Agent UX Requirements

A coding agent should be able to:

- run a scenario and get a single `report.json` with:
  - trace fingerprint
  - invariant/oracle outcomes
  - structured failure summary

- when failing, automatically get:
  - crashpack manifest
  - minimal divergent prefix
  - replay command
  - evidence ledger cards (why the supervisor restarted / why the oracle fired)

- search and diff these artifacts deterministically across runs

## No "LLM-specific magic"

This isn't about calling LLM APIs from the runtime.
It's about producing the *kind of deterministic, explainable state* that lets humans and agents collaborate.

## Dependencies

This epic intentionally layers atop:

- Crash artifacts (`bd-qbcnu`)
- Observability / evidence (`bd-iu07v`)
- Lab harness (`bd-1vk6c`)
- Docs + examples (`bd-2rm8l`)

title: Implement IoOp obligation lifecycle (submit/complete/cancel)
description:
# IoOp Obligation Lifecycle

## Purpose
Model every in-flight I/O operation as an obligation:
- created/reserved on submission
- resolved as committed on completion
- resolved as aborted on cancellation (if possible) or on policy escalation

## Semantics
- `submit` creates `ObligationKind::IoOp` in `Reserved` state.
- `complete` transitions to `Committed` and returns result.
- `cancel` attempts to abort; if kernel cannot cancel, policy decides whether to wait or escalate.

## Region Close Interaction
- Region close must not become `Closed(_)` while any `IoOp` remains `Reserved`.

## Acceptance Criteria
- IoOp obligations are registered in the registry.
- Trace captures submit/complete/cancel.

comments.author: GentleMountain
comments.text:
## Profiling Results (GentleMountain)

Created comprehensive benchmark suite: benches/raptorq_benchmark.rs

### GF(256) Primitives Baseline
| Operation | 64B | 256B | 1KB | 4KB | 16KB |
|-----------|-----|------|-----|-----|------|
| add_slice (XOR) | 10.9 GiB/s | 19.3 GiB/s | 22.8 GiB/s | 23.4 GiB/s | 21.8 GiB/s |
| mul_slice | 1.1 GiB/s | 1.1 GiB/s | 0.9 GiB/s | 1.2 GiB/s | 1.1 GiB/s |
| addmul_slice | 1.0 GiB/s | 1.0 GiB/s | 1.1 GiB/s | 1.0 GiB/s | 1.1 GiB/s |

### Key Findings
1. XOR (add_slice) is memory-bound at ~20-24 GiB/s - SIMD autovectorized by LLVM
2. addmul_slice is THE hot path at ~1 GiB/s (20x slower than XOR due to table lookups)
3. Branchless optimization tested but reverted - showed mixed results:
   - +7% at 4KB but -8% to -16% at smaller sizes
   - Branch predictor performs well when data is mostly non-zero (typical case)

### End-to-End Throughput
- Encode (k=32, 1KB symbols): ~36 MiB/s
- Decode (source only): ~70 MiB/s
- Decode (repair only): ~13 MiB/s (Gaussian elimination is O(n^3))

### Next Steps
- bd-35lp: Safe SIMD XOR acceleration (potential 2-4x for addmul with gather)
- bd-1l7k: Buffer reuse to reduce allocations

HOW TO APPLY COMPREHENSIVE LEAN PROOF COVERAGE TO IMPROVE PERFORMANCE, RELIABILITY, AND CORRECTNESS

Performance application model:
- Use proven invariants as optimization envelopes (what can change vs what must stay invariant).
- For each hot-path optimization candidate, attach proof references and required preserved invariants.
- Ship only when benchmark delta + proof obligations + conformance checks all pass.

Reliability application model:
- Translate formal assumptions into production guardrails (assertions, alarms, fail-fast checks, runbooks).
- Map each historical/known failure mode to related theorem/invariant and verify coverage gaps are closed.
- Require proof-referenced incident triage templates so postmortems directly improve formal model coverage.

Correctness application model:
- Make proof impact a mandatory dimension of PR review (what theorem/invariant does this change affect?).
- Classify every runtime change by proof impact (none/local/cross-cutting) and gate accordingly.
- Keep executable Rust↔Lean conformance suites in CI so regressions are detected as semantic divergence, not just test breakage.

Impact loop:
1) Proof insight identifies safe change space.
2) Change lands with benchmark + conformance evidence.
3) Reliability/correctness metrics are measured and archived.
4) Results feed back into coverage matrix and next proof priorities.

title: Instrument cancellation flow with tracing
description:
# Task

Add comprehensive tracing for cancellation propagation through the region tree.

## Why This Is Critical

Cancellation is THE core feature of asupersync. Understanding how cancellation flows
through a region tree is essential for debugging. Users need to see:
- Where cancellation originated
- How it propagated through regions
- Which tasks were affected
- How cleanup proceeded

## What to Instrument

1. **Cancel request**: Initial cancellation trigger
   - Fields: target (task_id or region_id), reason, source_task, budget_for_cleanup
   
2. **Cancel propagation**: As cancellation flows to children
   - Fields: from_region, to_region, to_task, propagation_depth
   - Use follows_from to link propagation chain
   
3. **Cancel observation**: When task observes via checkpoint()
   - Fields: task_id, reason, remaining_budget, mask_depth
   
4. **Drain phase**: Task draining to terminal state
   - Fields: task_id, drain_start, operations_pending
   
5. **Finalize phase**: Finalizer execution
   - Fields: task_id, finalizer_count, finalizer_budget

## Propagation Visualization

The tracing should enable reconstruction of:

```
cancel_request[target=Region(1), reason=Timeout]
  └─> propagate[to=Region(2)]
      ├─> propagate[to=Task(100)] 
      │   └─> observed[at=checkpoint, mask_depth=0]
      │       └─> draining[ops_pending=1]
      │           └─> finalizing[finalizers=2]
      └─> propagate[to=Task(101)]
          └─> observed[at=checkpoint, mask_depth=1] // masked!
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Cancel origin is always traceable
- [ ] Propagation path is fully recorded
- [ ] Observation points are recorded
- [ ] Drain and finalize phases are visible
- [ ] Masked cancellation is distinguishable

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
[2026-02-15 IndigoHawk] Deep-audit finding + fix in HTTP/2 idle-stream enforcement.

Finding (correctness/protocol):
- `Connection::process_window_update` only treated WINDOW_UPDATE as idle-stream protocol error when the stream object already existed in `StreamStore`.
- For not-yet-opened stream IDs (true idle streams absent from map), the frame was silently ignored instead of returning connection-level PROTOCOL_ERROR (RFC 7540/9113 §5.1 behavior expected by local regression test).

Fix implemented:

title: Implement test oracle: deadline_monotone invariant checker
description:
## Purpose
Implement a test oracle that verifies the INV-DEADLINE-MONOTONE invariant: children can never have longer deadlines than their parents.

## The Invariant
From asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §5:
```
∀r ∈ dom(R), ∀r' ∈ R[r].subregions:
  deadline(R[r']) ≤ deadline(R[r])    // Tighter or equal
```

This ensures budget propagation is correct - a child region cannot escape its parent's deadline.

## Why This Matters
- Prevents orphan work that outlives its parent
- Ensures cancellation can always complete within parent's budget
- Critical for bounded cleanup guarantees

## Oracle Design
```rust
pub struct DeadlineMonotoneOracle {
    region_deadlines: HashMap<RegionId, Option<Time>>,
    parent_map: HashMap<RegionId, RegionId>,
}

impl DeadlineMonotoneOracle {
    pub fn on_region_create(
        &mut self,
        region: RegionId,
        parent: Option<RegionId>,
        budget: &Budget
    );
    
    pub fn on_budget_update(
        &mut self,
        region: RegionId,
        new_budget: &Budget
    );
    
    pub fn check(&self) -> Result<(), DeadlineMonotoneViolation>;
}
```

## Violation Detection
```rust
pub struct DeadlineMonotoneViolation {
    pub child: RegionId,
    pub child_deadline: Option<Time>,
    pub parent: RegionId,
    pub parent_deadline: Option<Time>,
}
```

A violation occurs when:
- Child region has deadline D_c
- Parent region has deadline D_p
- D_c > D_p (child deadline is LATER than parent)

## Integration
- Check on region creation
- Check on budget tightening (should always be valid by construction)
- Lab runtime validates after each step

## Testing
1. Valid: child deadline ≤ parent deadline
2. Invalid: manually construct violation → oracle catches
3. None deadline: unbounded is ≤ bounded (None ≤ Some(T)) - actually None means unbounded which is ≥ any bounded

Actually, the semantics here is:
- None = unbounded = infinity
- Some(T) = bounded to T
- So the check is: child_deadline ≤ parent_deadline where None = ∞

## References
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §5: INV-DEADLINE-MONOTONE
- asupersync_plan_v4.md §3.3: Budget product semiring

## Acceptance Criteria
- Oracle verifies deadline monotonicity: children deadlines are ≤ parent deadlines (or None semantics handled explicitly).
- Produces clear diagnostic output pointing to offending parent/child and their budgets.
- Deterministic and usable in both unit and E2E tests.
close_reason: DeadlineMonotoneOracle fully implemented with 350+ lines, 18 unit tests passing. Verifies INV-DEADLINE-MONOTONE: child deadlines must not exceed parent deadlines. Integrated into OracleSuite.

title: Sub-Epic: WebSocket Protocol Implementation
description:
# Sub-Epic: WebSocket Protocol Implementation

## Overview

Implement complete WebSocket (RFC 6455) support for both client and server roles, with proper integration into Asupersync's structured concurrency model.

## Why WebSocket Matters

WebSocket is essential for:
- Real-time applications (chat, notifications, live updates)
- Streaming APIs (financial data, IoT sensors)
- Bidirectional communication (gaming, collaboration tools)
- Long-lived connections (dashboards, monitoring)

**This is THE critical gap** - no WebSocket means no real-time apps.

## Design Principles

### 1. Cancel-Correct Close Handshake

WebSocket has a specific close handshake (close frame exchange). Unlike Tokio where dropping a WebSocket may leak the close, we ensure:
- Close frame sent on region close
- Wait for close acknowledgment (with timeout)
- Proper drain of pending messages

### 2. Region-Owned Connections

```rust
// WebSocket connection belongs to spawning region
let ws = WebSocket::connect(cx, "wss://example.com/ws").await?;

// When region closes, connection closes cleanly
cx.spawn(async move {
    while let Some(msg) = ws.recv(cx).await? {
        // Process messages
    }
});
// Region close -> ws.close() called automatically
```

### 3. Split Read/Write

Like TcpStream, WebSocket supports splitting:
```rust
let (rx, tx) = ws.split();
// rx and tx can be used in separate tasks
// Both owned by same region
```

### 4. Backpressure

Sending respects backpressure:
```rust
// Returns Pending if send buffer full
ws.send(cx, Message::Text("hello")).await?;
```

## Protocol Coverage

RFC 6455 requirements:
- [ ] HTTP upgrade handshake (client and server)
- [ ] Frame parsing (text, binary, ping, pong, close)
- [ ] XOR masking (client->server must mask)
- [ ] Fragmentation (large messages split into frames)
- [ ] Close handshake (bidirectional close frame exchange)
- [ ] Ping/pong keepalive

Extensions (optional):
- [ ] Per-message deflate (compression)
- [ ] Subprotocol negotiation

## Architecture

```
src/ws/
├── mod.rs           # Public API: WebSocket, Message, CloseCode
├── handshake.rs     # HTTP upgrade negotiation
├── frame.rs         # Frame codec (RFC 6455 wire format)
├── mask.rs          # XOR masking implementation
├── close.rs         # Close handshake state machine
├── message.rs       # Message types (Text, Binary, Ping, Pong, Close)
├── split.rs         # ReadHalf, WriteHalf
├── client.rs        # WebSocket::connect()
├── server.rs        # WebSocket::accept()
└── tests/
    ├── handshake_test.rs
    ├── frame_test.rs
    └── integration_test.rs
```

## Integration Points

- Uses existing TcpStream/TlsStream
- Uses existing HTTP/1.1 parser for upgrade
- Integrates with Cx for cancellation checkpoints
- Uses codec framework for framing

## Lab Runtime Considerations

- Virtual time for ping/pong intervals
- Deterministic frame ordering
- Simulated connection drops for close testing

## Dependencies

- Depends on: HTTP/1.1 (for upgrade handshake), TLS (for wss://)
- Blocked by: None (core infrastructure exists)

## Success Criteria

- [ ] Client can connect to standard WebSocket servers
- [ ] Server can accept WebSocket upgrades
- [ ] All frame types handled correctly
- [ ] Close handshake completes cleanly
- [ ] Cancellation triggers proper close
- [ ] Lab runtime tests deterministic
- [ ] Passes Autobahn test suite (industry standard)

## References

- RFC 6455: https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6455
- Autobahn test suite: https://github.com/crossbario/autobahn-testsuite
- tokio-tungstenite (reference): https://github.com/snapview/tokio-tungstenite

title: [ALIEN][SCHED][LYAP] Efficient RuntimeSnapshot extraction (no hot-path allocs)
description:
## Purpose

The governor needs a snapshot of Σ (runtime state) to compute V(Σ).

We must compute this cheaply:
- no per-poll allocations
- stable deterministic counts

## Snapshot contents (candidate)

- outstanding obligations by kind
- pending cancel requests / acks
- deadline slack summary
- IO in-flight counts
- ready queue depth signals

## Acceptance criteria

- Snapshot can be computed with bounded work.
- Snapshot values are deterministic under lab runtime.
design:
### Implementation plan

Add a deterministic, allocation-free constructor for the Lyapunov governor snapshot.

**Location:** `src/obligation/lyapunov.rs` (`impl StateSnapshot`), because the type's docs already claim it can be constructed from `RuntimeState`.

### Snapshot extraction semantics (exact)

Given a `RuntimeState` with logical time `now = state.now`:

- `time`: `now`
- `live_tasks`: count of `state.tasks` whose `TaskState` is *not* terminal (`!task.state.is_terminal()`).
- `pending_obligations`: count of `state.obligations` where `obligation.is_pending()` (i.e. `ObligationState::Reserved`).
- `obligation_age_sum_ns`: `sum now.duration_since(obligation.reserved_at)` over pending obligations.
- `draining_regions`: count of `state.regions` with `RegionState` in `{Draining, Finalizing}`.
- `deadline_pressure`: for each **live** task with a deadline in its `CxInner` budget:
  - `slack_ns = deadline.duration_since(now)` (saturating at 0 when overdue)
  - `term = max(0, 1 - slack_ns / D0)`
  - `deadline_pressure = sum term`

`D0` is a fixed normalization constant (chosen as 1s) to make the signal represent "tasks due soon or overdue" rather than far-future deadlines.

### Determinism + performance constraints

- **No allocations on the hot path:** no `Vec`, no `HashMap`, no `collect`.
- **Deterministic iteration:** only scan arenas in their natural order; no hash iteration.
- **Graceful degradation:** if a task's `CxInner` lock is poisoned, skip its deadline contribution (do not panic).

### Follow-ups (if needed)

If scanning overhead becomes noticeable in profiling, add incremental counters (updated on task/obligation/region transitions) so snapshots become O(1).
acceptance_criteria:
- `StateSnapshot::from_runtime_state(&RuntimeState)` exists and is `#[must_use]`.

title: Task inspector: detailed task state, await points, and waker info
description:
# Task Inspector

## Overview
Deep-dive diagnostic view for individual tasks, showing detailed state, await points,
waker information, and execution history.

## Design

### Task Details View
```rust
pub struct TaskInspector {
    state: Arc<RuntimeState>,
    console: Console,
}

impl TaskInspector {
    /// Inspect a specific task.
    pub fn inspect(&self, task_id: TaskId) -> TaskDetails {
        let task = self.state.get_task(task_id);
        
        TaskDetails {
            id: task_id,
            state: task.state(),
            region: task.region_id(),
            spawn_location: task.spawn_location(),
            last_poll_time: task.last_poll_time(),
            poll_count: task.poll_count(),
            await_point: task.current_await_point(),
            waker_info: task.waker_info(),
            budget_consumed: task.budget_consumed(),
        }
    }
    
    /// List all tasks with summary info.
    pub fn list_tasks(&self) -> Vec<TaskSummary> {
        self.state.all_tasks()
            .map(|t| TaskSummary {
                id: t.id(),
                name: t.name(),
                state: t.state(),
                region: t.region_id(),
            })
            .collect()
    }
}
```

### Output Format
```
Task Inspector: TaskId(42)
╭────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ State:         Polling                         │
│ Region:        Region-2 (HttpHandler)          │
│ Spawned at:    src/http/handler.rs:142         │
│ Last poll:     2.3ms ago                       │
│ Poll count:    17                              │
│ Budget used:   1,234 ops                       │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Current Await Point:                           │
│   -> TcpStream::read() at src/net/tcp.rs:89    │
│   -> IoDriver::poll_ready()                    │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Waker Info:                                    │
│   Type: WorkStealingWaker                      │
│   Registered: yes                              │
│   Wake count: 3                                │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

### Interactive Features (TUI)
- Navigate task list with keyboard
- Click to inspect task
- Filter by state (pending, polling, completed)
- Sort by poll count, age, budget

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Task list view with sorting/filtering
- [ ] Detailed task inspection
- [ ] Await point identification
- [ ] Waker state display
- [ ] Budget tracking per task
- [ ] TUI navigation
- [ ] Unit tests

## Testing Requirements

### Unit Tests
- `inspector::tests::list_all_tasks` - List tasks correctly
- `inspector::tests::inspect_running_task` - Running task details
- `inspector::tests::inspect_pending_task` - Pending task details
- `inspector::tests::await_point_detection` - Current await point
- `inspector::tests::waker_info_display` - Waker state

### Integration Tests

- `inspector::integration::concurrent_updates` - Handle state changes

### Logging Requirements
- TRACE: Individual field lookups
- DEBUG: Task inspection events

## Goal

Provide an end-to-end harness that proves geodesic normalization is useful *in practice* and stays deterministic.

This is not a micro-unit test: it exercises the full surface area that users care about:
- trace capture -> poset build -> normalization (exact/heuristic) -> replay
- stable artifacts (goldens) + explainable decision ledger (when enabled)

## Scenario corpus

Create a small but high-leverage corpus of deterministic lab scenarios + captured traces that exhibit:
- many commutations (low structure)
- structured "two lanes" patterns
- cancellation / obligation-heavy traces
- known DPOR counterexamples where canonicalization makes the trace smaller/cleaner

Each scenario must have:
- fixed seed + fixed config
- an oracle: (a) quiescence, (b) no obligation leaks, (c) loser drain where relevant

## Report + logging requirements

- Core runtime code must not write to stdout/stderr.
- The harness should emit a deterministic JSON report (or trace-backed text report) that includes:
  - original trace length, normalized trace length
  - switch cost before/after

  - optional galaxy-brain ledger excerpt (bounded size)

- Running the harness twice yields byte-identical reports (given same seed/config).
- For at least one scenario, switch cost strictly decreases vs baseline replay, without changing observable outcomes.

title: Implement ObligationRecord structure and registry
description:
# ObligationRecord Structure and Registry

## Purpose
Obligations are the operational enforcement mechanism for the “linear resource” discipline:
- reserve introduces a linear token
- commit/abort resolve it
- leaking a reserved token is a semantic error (caught in lab)

The registry tracks all obligations and ties them to:
- holder task
- owning region

## ObligationRecord (Plan-of-Record)
```rust
pub struct ObligationRecord {
    pub id: ObligationId,
    pub kind: ObligationKind,
    pub holder: TaskId,
    pub region: RegionId,
    pub state: ObligationState,
    pub created_at: Time,
    pub name: Option<String>,
}
```

## ObligationRegistry
Use internal arenas/indices (no slab crate required):

```rust
pub struct ObligationRegistry {
    pub obligations: Arena<ObligationRecord>,
    pub by_region: HashMap<RegionId, HashSet<ObligationId>>,
    pub by_holder: HashMap<TaskId, HashSet<ObligationId>>,
}
```

## Core Operations
- `reserve(kind, holder, region) -> ObligationId`
- `commit(id)` / `abort(id)`
- `on_task_complete(holder)` marks remaining reserved obligations as leaked (lab panic configurable)
- `pending_count(region)` gates region close

## Futurelock Detection (Lab)
A futurelock is “task holds obligations but stops being polled.”
- detect via `created_at` age + task progress counters
- surface as deterministic error in lab runs

## Acceptance Criteria
- Any task completion with outstanding reserved obligations is detected.
- Region close cannot complete with pending obligations.

title: Implement algebraic law property tests for combinators
description:
## Purpose
Implement property-based tests that verify the algebraic laws from asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §7. These laws enable optimizations, compositional reasoning, and are core semantic guarantees.

## The Laws

### LAW-JOIN-ASSOC
```
join(join(a, b), c) ≃ join(a, join(b, c))
```

### LAW-JOIN-COMM (when policy allows)
```
join(a, b) ≃ join(b, a)   // Outcomes may be reordered
```

### LAW-RACE-COMM
```
race(a, b) ≃ race(b, a)   // Winner depends on schedule
```

### LAW-TIMEOUT-MIN
```
timeout(d1, timeout(d2, f)) ≃ timeout(min(d1, d2), f)
```

### LAW-RACE-NEVER
```
race(f, never) ≃ f
```

### LAW-RACE-JOIN-DIST (speculative execution)
```
race(join(a, b), join(a, c)) ≃ join(a, race(b, c))
// Don't run 'a' twice
```

## What ≃ Means (from §7.0)
Observational equivalence up to:
1. Eliding silent steps (τ)
2. Quotienting traces by swaps of independent actions
3. Renaming fresh ids consistently

## Implementation Strategy

Use `proptest` to generate:
- Random task durations
- Random success/failure outcomes
- Random cancellation timing

For each law, verify that the LHS and RHS produce equivalent results.

### Equivalence Checking
```rust
fn outcomes_equivalent(a: Outcome, b: Outcome) -> bool {
    // Same variant and value (up to permutation for join)
}

fn traces_equivalent(a: &Trace, b: &Trace) -> bool {
    // Normalize both traces, compare
}
```

## Test Categories

### 1) Lattice Laws (Outcome)
- Associativity of combine
- Commutativity of combine
- Idempotence of combine
- Identity element (Ok is identity for combine)

### 2) Semiring Laws (Budget)
- Associativity of meet
- Commutativity of meet
- Idempotence of meet (min is idempotent)

### 3) Strengthen Laws (CancelReason)
- Idempotence
- Associativity
- Monotonicity

### 4) Combinator Laws
- All laws listed above

## Acceptance Criteria
- Property tests run deterministically with fixed seeds
- Coverage of all listed laws
- Failures include counterexample and trace

## References
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §7: Algebraic Laws
- asupersync_plan_v4.md §3.2: Near-semiring structure

title: Implement benchmark suite for Phase 0 baseline performance
description:
# Benchmark Suite (Phase 0 Baselines)

## Purpose
Establish baseline performance metrics for Phase 0 primitives so we can:
- detect regressions early
- validate “hot path” expectations (avoid unnecessary allocations)
- measure cancellation/drain latency (latency-sensitive)

Benchmarks should be deterministic in the sense that they:
- run fixed workloads under fixed lab configs
- do not rely on wall-clock randomness

## What to Benchmark (Core)
### Task/Region
- spawn + complete latency (noop tasks)
- region open/close latency (empty region)
- nested region overhead (depth N)

### Scheduler/Waker/Timers
- wake cost under dedup (many wakes => one enqueue)
- timer heap insert/pop costs

### Cancellation
- time from cancel request to terminal state for:
  - single task
  - tree of tasks
- overhead per checkpoint

### Combinators
- join (2-way) overhead
- race (2-way) overhead including loser drain
- timeout happy path vs timeout-trigger path

### Two-phase primitives
- MPSC reserve+commit cost per message
- reserve+drop (abort) cost per message

## Instrumentation
To validate “zero allocations on hot path”:
- use a test allocator or allocation counters in `cfg(test)` / bench cfg
- at minimum, assert checkpoint path does not allocate

## Harness Choice
- If we want statistical rigor: use `criterion` (dev-dependency)
- If we want zero deps initially: use `cargo bench` + `test::Bencher` (nightly) is not acceptable unless toolchain is nightly

Plan-of-record: start with `criterion` only once Phase 0 kernel is working, because toolchain/CI constraints may evolve.

## Determinism
- Bench inputs use fixed seeds/configs.
- Bench output is compared by trend, not by exact nanosecond equality.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Benchmarks exist for the categories above.
- Bench failures/regressions are actionable (identify which benchmark regressed).
- Bench suite does not compromise library purity (no stdout in core; benchmarks may print summaries).

comments.text:
## Scope

Define the **public** application-facing types:

- `AppSpec` (pure data / builder): describes topology and required capabilities.
- `AppHandle`: handle returned from start.
- `AppStartError` / `AppStopError`: explicit error taxonomy.

## Semantics (must be explicit, testable)

- `start(cx)`:
  - allocates (or is given) a root region
  - compiles `AppSpec` into supervisor/child specs
  - starts children deterministically
  - returns `AppHandle` that owns the root region

- `stop(cx)`:
  - requests cancel on root
  - drains + finalizes
  - returns only when region close implies quiescence

- `join(cx)`:
  - waits for terminal outcome of the root region (including crashes/cancel)

## Invariants

- close => quiescence (no live tasks, no pending obligations, finalizers empty)
- all stop paths are cancel-correct (request -> drain -> finalize)
- no ambient authority: an AppSpec cannot "secretly" reach globals

## Acceptance

- Minimal API compiles and can start a toy app under lab runtime.
- `AppHandle` drop semantics are explicit (either auto-stop or leak-preventing panic; pick and document).
- Doc tests show the recommended usage pattern.
