title: Add E2E validation and CI script for property testing
description:
## Overview

Add E2E validation and CI integration for the property-based testing epic, ensuring proper configuration and reproducible test runs.

## Test Configuration

### Proptest Configuration
```rust
/// Standard configuration for property tests
fn proptest_config() -> ProptestConfig {
    ProptestConfig {
        // Run more cases for thorough testing
        cases: 10_000,
        
        // Larger seeds for broader coverage
        max_shrink_iters: 100_000,
        
        // Deterministic for CI
        source_file: Some("proptest-regressions"),
        
        // Better error reporting
        result_cache: proptest::test_runner::basic_result_cache,
        
        ..ProptestConfig::default()
    }
}

/// Quick configuration for development
fn proptest_quick_config() -> ProptestConfig {
    ProptestConfig {
        cases: 100,
        max_shrink_iters: 1000,
        ..ProptestConfig::default()
    }
}
```

## E2E Validation Tests

### Regression Test Collection
```rust
#[test]
fn e2e_run_regression_tests() {
    init_property_test_logging();
    
    tracing::info\!("═══════════════════════════════════════════");
    tracing::info\!("E2E: Property Test Regression Collection");
    tracing::info\!("═══════════════════════════════════════════");
    
    // Run any regression tests from proptest-regressions file
    let regression_path = Path::new("proptest-regressions");
    
    if regression_path.exists() {
        let regressions = std::fs::read_to_string(regression_path).unwrap();
        let count = regressions.lines().filter(|l| \!l.is_empty() && \!l.starts_with('#')).count();
        
        tracing::info\!(regression_count = %count, "Running regression tests");
        
        // Proptest automatically runs these
    } else {
        tracing::info\!("No regression tests found (good\!)");
    }
}
```

### Invariant Summary Report
```rust
#[test]
fn e2e_invariant_summary_report() {
    init_property_test_logging();
    
    tracing::info\!("═══════════════════════════════════════════");
    tracing::info\!("E2E: Property Test Invariant Summary");
    tracing::info\!("═══════════════════════════════════════════");
    
    let invariants = vec\![
        ("No orphan tasks", "Every task has a valid parent region"),
        ("Tree structure", "No cycles, single root, proper parent pointers"),
        ("Child tracking", "Parent's children list matches children's parent pointers"),
        ("ID uniqueness", "No duplicate RegionId or TaskId"),
        ("Cancel propagation", "If parent cancelled, all descendants cancelled"),
        ("Close ordering", "Region cannot close until all children closed"),
        ("Outcome collection", "All child outcomes collected before parent completes"),
        ("No leaks", "After full close, all resources freed"),
        ("Budget inheritance", "Child budgets never exceed parent budgets"),
    ];
    
    tracing::info\!("Invariants tested by property tests:");
    for (name, description) in &invariants {
        tracing::info\!("  ✓ {}: {}", name, description);
    }
    
    tracing::info\!(
        invariant_count = %invariants.len(),
        "Property tests verify {} invariants",
        invariants.len()
    );
}
```

## CI Integration Script

Create `scripts/run_property_tests.sh`:

```bash
#\!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

echo "═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════"
echo "          Property-Based Testing Suite                         "
echo "═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════"

export RUST_LOG=info
export RUST_BACKTRACE=1

# Configuration
CASES=${PROPTEST_CASES:-10000}
SEED=${PROPTEST_SEED:-$(date +%s)}

echo ""
echo "Configuration:"
echo "  Test cases: $CASES"
echo "  Random seed: $SEED"
echo ""

# Create output directory
OUTPUT_DIR="target/proptest-results"
mkdir -p "$OUTPUT_DIR"

TIMESTAMP=$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)
LOG_FILE="$OUTPUT_DIR/proptest_$TIMESTAMP.log"

echo "▶ Running property tests..."
echo "  Log file: $LOG_FILE"
echo ""

# Set proptest environment
export PROPTEST_CASES=$CASES
export PROPTEST_SEED=$SEED

# Run property tests
cargo test property_test     --features test-internals     -- --nocapture     2>&1 | tee "$LOG_FILE"

echo ""
echo "═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════"
echo "                    PROPERTY TEST SUMMARY                       "
echo "═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════"

# Check for failures
if grep -q "FAILED" "$LOG_FILE"; then
    echo "❌ Property tests found failures\!"
    echo ""
    echo "Failures are recorded in proptest-regressions/"
    echo "Run again to reproduce the minimal failing case."
    exit 1
fi

PASSED=$(grep -c "ok" "$LOG_FILE" || echo 0)
echo "✓ All property tests passed"
echo "  Total test functions: $PASSED"
echo "  Cases per test: $CASES"
echo "  Seed: $SEED"
echo ""
echo "To reproduce this exact run:"
echo "  PROPTEST_SEED=$SEED ./scripts/run_property_tests.sh"
```

## GitHub Actions Integration

Create `.github/workflows/property-tests.yml`:

```yaml
name: Property Tests

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
  schedule:
    # Run nightly with more cases
    - cron: '0 3 * * *'

jobs:
  property-tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    
    strategy:
      matrix:
        cases: [1000, 10000]
        
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Install Rust
        uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
      
      - name: Cache cargo
        uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2
      
      - name: Run property tests
        env:
          PROPTEST_CASES: ${{ matrix.cases }}
          PROPTEST_SEED: ${{ github.run_id }}
        run: ./scripts/run_property_tests.sh
      
      - name: Upload regressions
        if: failure()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: proptest-regressions
          path: proptest-regressions/
      
      - name: Upload logs
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: proptest-logs-${{ matrix.cases }}
          path: target/proptest-results/
```

- Exhaustive brute-force tests for n<=10 for (4).
- At least 3 targeted regression fixtures for (5).

title: [EPIC-INFRA] Symbol-Native Distributed Regions
description:
# EPIC: Symbol-Native Distributed Regions

**Bead ID:** asupersync-y1p
**Type:** EPIC
**Priority:** P1
**Status:** OPEN
**Owner:** Dicklesworthstone

---

## Vision

Symbol-Native Distributed Regions extend asupersync's structured concurrency model across machine boundaries using RaptorQ erasure coding for fault-tolerant state replication. This EPIC transforms local regions - with their guarantees of task containment, cancellation propagation, and orderly shutdown - into distributed regions that maintain these same guarantees despite network partitions, node failures, and Byzantine conditions.

The core insight is that region state (task trees, pending obligations, finalizers) can be serialized into RaptorQ symbols and distributed to replica nodes. When quorum is maintained, the distributed region operates normally. When failures occur, the region can recover from any subset of replicas that collectively hold enough symbols to reconstruct the state. This is erasure coding applied to structured concurrency itself.

The distributed region model preserves the local programming model: developers spawn tasks into regions, regions nest hierarchically, cancellation flows from parent to child. The difference is that the region's state is durably replicated, making the structured concurrency tree resilient to infrastructure failures without requiring developers to think about replication.

---

## Goals

- **Define distributed region state model** with clear state machine for initialization, active operation, degradation, and recovery
- **Implement state encoding** that serializes region snapshots into RaptorQ symbols with configurable redundancy
- **Implement symbol distribution** that replicates encoded state to replicas using quorum-based writes
- **Implement recovery protocol** that reconstructs region state from surviving replicas when quorum is lost
- **Integrate with local regions** providing transparent upgrade path from local to distributed operation
- **Preserve structured concurrency guarantees** across the distributed boundary

---

## Non-Goals

- **Distributed consensus**: This layer uses RaptorQ for data redundancy, not Raft/Paxos for agreement
- **Distributed transactions**: ACID transactions across regions are a higher-level concern
- **Automatic sharding**: Horizontal partitioning of regions is not addressed
- **Cross-datacenter replication**: WAN-optimized replication strategies are future work
- **Persistent storage**: Durable storage backends (disk, S3) are external to this layer

---

## Child Beads

| ID | Title | Status | Priority | Description |
|----|-------|--------|----------|-------------|
| asupersync-qqw | Define DistributedRegion State Model | OPEN | P1 | State machine for distributed region lifecycle |
| asupersync-h10 | Implement Region Symbol Encoding/Distribution | OPEN | P1 | Serialize region state to symbols, distribute to replicas |
| asupersync-tjd | Implement Region Recovery Protocol | OPEN | P1 | Reconstruct region state from surviving replicas |
| asupersync-p0u | Integrate with Local Region Types | OPEN | P1 | Bridge between local and distributed regions |
| asupersync-o78 | Comprehensive Distributed Region Tests | OPEN | P2 | Integration tests for distributed operation |

---

## Phases

### Phase 1: State Model and Encoding
**Duration:** 2 sprints
**Deliverables:**
- `DistributedRegionState` enum with all lifecycle states
- `RegionSnapshot` serialization format
- `StateEncoder` converting snapshots to RaptorQ symbols
- Deterministic encoding for testability

**Exit Criteria:**
- State machine transitions are well-defined and tested
- Region state can be encoded and decoded correctly
- Encoding is deterministic (same state = same symbols)

### Phase 2: Distribution and Replication
**Duration:** 2 sprints
**Deliverables:**
- `SymbolDistributor` for routing symbols to replicas
- Quorum-based write acknowledgment
- Incremental/delta state updates
- Epoch-bounded state versions

**Exit Criteria:**
- Writes succeed when quorum acknowledges
- Delta updates reduce bandwidth for incremental changes
- State versions are properly ordered by epoch

### Phase 3: Recovery and Integration
**Duration:** 2 sprints
**Deliverables:**
- `RecoveryCollector` gathering symbols from replicas
- `StateDecoder` reconstructing region state
- `RegionBridge` connecting local and distributed APIs
- Comprehensive test suite

**Exit Criteria:**
- Recovery succeeds from any quorum of replicas
- Local regions can be upgraded to distributed
- All integration tests pass

---

## Success Criteria

1. **Recovery Correctness**: Region state recovers correctly from any K' >= threshold symbols across replicas
2. **Quorum Semantics**: Writes succeed with quorum (N/2+1), reads succeed with quorum
3. **State Consistency**: Recovered state is identical to last committed state
4. **Latency Overhead**: Distributed operation adds <50ms overhead to local region operations
5. **Partition Tolerance**: System continues operating in degraded mode during partitions
6. **Cancel Propagation**: Cancellation flows correctly across distributed region boundaries
7. **Lifecycle Synchronization**: Local and distributed region states remain consistent

---

## Dependencies

### Depends On
- **asupersync-0vx** (Foundation Layer) - RaptorQ encoding/decoding infrastructure
- **asupersync-7gm** (Transport Layer) - Symbol transport to replicas
- **asupersync-bsx** (Epoch Concurrency) - Epoch boundaries for state versioning
- `src/record/region.rs` - Local region infrastructure

### Blocks
- **asupersync-zfn** (Symbolic Obligations) - Uses distributed regions for obligation tracking
- **asupersync-9mq** (Integration) - Distributed regions in unified API

---

## Acceptance Criteria Checklist

### DistributedRegion State Model (asupersync-qqw)
- [ ] `DistributedRegionState` enum: Initializing, Active, Degraded, Recovering, Closing, Closed
- [ ] State transition rules with clear triggers and guards
- [ ] `RegionSnapshot` capturing full region state (tasks, children, finalizers, metadata)
- [ ] Version tracking with epoch bounds
- [ ] Metrics for state transitions

### Region Symbol Encoding/Distribution (asupersync-h10)
- [ ] `StateEncoder` serializing `RegionSnapshot` to bytes
- [ ] RaptorQ encoding of serialized state into symbols
- [ ] `SymbolDistributor` routing symbols to configured replicas
- [ ] Quorum write acknowledgment with configurable consistency level
- [ ] Delta encoding for incremental state updates
- [ ] Symbol tagging with region ID, epoch, and version

### Region Recovery Protocol (asupersync-tjd)
- [ ] Recovery trigger detection (quorum loss, node restart, admin command)
- [ ] `RecoveryCollector` querying replicas for symbols
- [ ] Progress tracking during symbol collection
- [ ] RaptorQ decoding when threshold reached
- [ ] State reconstruction from decoded snapshot
- [ ] Partial recovery for large regions
- [ ] Cancellation-aware recovery (interruptible)

### Integration with Local Region Types (asupersync-p0u)
- [ ] `RegionBridge` connecting local Region API to distributed backend
- [ ] Transparent promotion of local regions to distributed
- [ ] Lifecycle synchronization between local and distributed states
- [ ] Type conversions preserving structured concurrency guarantees
- [ ] API compatibility (spawn, cancel, close work identically)
- [ ] Mixed region trees (local and distributed in same hierarchy)

### Test Suite (asupersync-o78)
- [ ] State machine transition tests
- [ ] Encoding/decoding roundtrip tests
- [ ] Quorum write tests
- [ ] Recovery from various failure scenarios
- [ ] Integration with local regions
- [ ] Performance benchmarks

---

## State Machine Overview

```
                    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │                                         │
                    ▼                                         │
  ┌──────────────────────┐                                    │
  │     Initializing     │────────────────┐                   │
  │  (gathering quorum)  │                │                   │
  └──────────┬───────────┘                │                   │
             │ quorum_reached             │ timeout           │
             ▼                            ▼                   │
  ┌──────────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────────┐      │
  │       Active         │      │       Failed         │      │
  │  (normal operation)  │      │  (initialization     │      │
  └──────────┬───────────┘      │   failed)            │      │
             │                  └──────────────────────┘      │
             │ quorum_lost                                    │
             ▼                                                │
  ┌──────────────────────┐                                    │
  │      Degraded        │◀───────────────────────────────────┤
  │  (partial quorum)    │                                    │
  └──────────┬───────────┘                                    │
             │ recovery_triggered                             │
             ▼                                                │
  ┌──────────────────────┐      recovery_complete             │
  │     Recovering       │────────────────────────────────────┘
  │  (rebuilding state)  │
  └──────────┬───────────┘
             │ close_requested
             ▼
  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │       Closing        │
  │  (draining tasks)    │
  └──────────┬───────────┘
             │ drained
             ▼
  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │       Closed         │
  │  (terminal state)    │
  └──────────────────────┘
```

---

## Risk Assessment

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation |
|------|------------|--------|------------|
| State serialization bloat | Medium | Medium | Delta encoding, compression, lazy serialization |
| Recovery takes too long for large regions | Medium | High | Incremental recovery, parallel collection |
| Split-brain during network partition | Medium | High | Epoch fencing, quorum validation |
| Local/distributed state divergence | Low | High | Strong lifecycle synchronization, invariant checking |
| Recovery loop (constant re-recovery) | Low | High | Backoff, circuit breaker on recovery attempts |

# Phase 1: Work-Stealing Scheduler

## Purpose
Extend Phase 0’s single-thread scheduler to a parallel work-stealing scheduler while preserving all invariants and retaining deterministic lab behavior.

## Core Requirements
- Per-worker local queues (fast path)
- Steal protocol for load balancing
- Global injection queue for external wakes/spawns
- Wake dedup across threads
- Cancel lane priority must remain semantically dominant

## Determinism Constraint
Even if production scheduling is nondeterministic, the lab runtime must be able to:
- simulate multi-worker scheduling deterministically
- replay schedules

This implies the scheduler must expose a “virtual schedule” control surface in lab mode.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Parallel execution preserves:
  - region close ⇒ quiescence
  - cancellation protocol drains
  - losers drained
  - no obligation leaks
- No task can be orphaned due to migration.

## Testing
- Parallel stress tests with deterministic seed.
- Schedule replay tests.
- Work-stealing invariants tests (no lost tasks, no duplicate polls, no starvation).

title: Implement test oracle: no_task_leaks invariant checker
description:
## Purpose
Implement a test oracle that verifies the "no task leaks" invariant: after any region closes, no tasks spawned within that region remain running. This is one of the 6 non-negotiable invariants.

## The Invariant
From asupersync_plan_v4.md:
> Every spawned task is owned by a region; region close waits for all children

Formally: `∀r ∈ closed_regions: tasks_in_region(r) = ∅`

After `scope.region(...).await` returns, the region's `TaskSet` must be empty (all tasks in Completed state).

## Oracle Design

```rust
pub struct TaskLeakOracle {
    // Tracks all task spawns and completions
    spawns: Vec<(TaskId, RegionId, Time)>,
    completions: Vec<(TaskId, Time)>,
    region_closes: Vec<(RegionId, Time)>,
}

impl TaskLeakOracle {
    /// Called by scheduler on each spawn
    pub fn on_spawn(&mut self, task: TaskId, region: RegionId, time: Time);
    
    /// Called when task reaches Completed
    pub fn on_complete(&mut self, task: TaskId, time: Time);
    
    /// Called when region reaches Closed
    pub fn on_region_close(&mut self, region: RegionId, time: Time);
    
    /// Verify invariant holds
    pub fn check(&self) -> Result<(), TaskLeakViolation>;
}
```

## Violation Detection
```rust
pub struct TaskLeakViolation {
    pub region: RegionId,
    pub leaked_tasks: Vec<TaskId>,
    pub region_close_time: Time,
}
```

A violation occurs when:
1. Region R closes at time T
2. ∃ task spawned in R with no completion record at time ≤ T

## Integration Points
The oracle hooks into:
1. `Cx::spawn()` - records spawn event
2. Task state transition to `Completed` - records completion
3. Region state transition to `Closed` - records close and triggers check

## Lab Runtime Integration
In lab runtime, oracle checks run automatically:
- After each region close
- At end of test execution
- Before schedule replay verification

## Invariant Mapping

| Invariant | Oracle |
|-----------|--------|
| 1. Structured concurrency | **no_task_leaks** |
| 2. Region close = quiescence | quiescence_on_close |
| 3. Cancellation is protocol | (verified by state machine tests) |
| 4. Losers are drained | losers_always_drained |
| 5. No obligation leaks | no_obligation_leaks |
| 6. No ambient authority | no_ambient_authority |

This oracle verifies invariant #1.

## Testing the Oracle Itself
1. **Correct case**: Region with tasks that all complete → check passes
2. **Leak case**: Deliberately break invariant → check catches it
3. **Nested regions**: Parent close requires all descendant tasks done
4. **Cancellation**: Cancelled tasks still count as completed

## Performance Considerations
- Oracle overhead acceptable in lab runtime
- Production runtime: oracle disabled or sampled
- Data structures: consider append-only log vs indexed sets

## References
- asupersync_plan_v4.md: §1.1 Non-negotiable invariants
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md: Invariant I1 (task_leak_free)
- AGENTS.md: 6 non-negotiable invariants

## Acceptance Criteria
- Oracle verifies task ownership/leak invariant: every spawned task is eventually completed (no orphans) within a closed region.
- Diagnostics include the set of missing completions and their owning region(s).
- Deterministic and integrated into E2E harness.

title: EPIC: Asupersync ↔ fastapi_rust Integration
description:
# EPIC: Asupersync ↔ fastapi_rust Integration

## Executive Summary

This epic tracks the co-development coordination between Asupersync (spec-first async runtime) and fastapi_rust (Rust web framework). fastapi_rust will use Asupersync as its async runtime foundation, requiring close API alignment and coordinated development.

## Background

**Asupersync** provides:
- Structured concurrency with region-based task ownership
- Cancel-correct operations with bounded cleanup
- Two-phase effects (reserve/commit) preventing data loss
- Capability-secured effects through explicit `Cx` tokens
- Deterministic lab runtime for testing

**fastapi_rust** needs:
- Async runtime for HTTP request handling
- Request context (similar to Cx) for per-request state
- Error handling compatible with HTTP semantics
- TCP I/O for network operations
- Graceful shutdown for zero-downtime deployments
- Deterministic testing for request handlers

## Integration Architecture

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      fastapi_rust Application                     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                   │
│  ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐          │
│  │   Router    │ →  │  Middleware │ →  │   Handler   │          │
│  └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └──────┬──────┘          │
│                                               │                   │
│                                               ▼                   │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │                    RequestContext (Cx)                     │  │
│  │  • Request metadata    • Response builder                  │  │
│  │  • Budget (timeout)    • Cancellation token                │  │
│  │  • Trace/span context  • Capability tokens                 │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                              │                                    │
└──────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┘
                               │
                               ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      Asupersync Runtime                           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                   │
│  ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐          │
│  │   Regions   │    │    Tasks    │    │ Obligations │          │
│  │  (per-req)  │    │  (handlers) │    │  (2-phase)  │          │
│  └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘          │
│                                                                   │
│  ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐          │
│  │  Scheduler  │    │   TCP I/O   │    │ Lab Runtime │          │
│  └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘          │
│                                                                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Development Phases

### Phase 0 (Immediate) - Foundation
- Cx capability token integration for RequestContext
- Outcome type exposure for HTTP error handling  
- Public API surface documentation
- Cross-crate compilation verification

### Phase 1 (Core HTTP) - Networking
- TCP I/O traits (TcpListener, TcpStream)
- Budget integration for request timeouts
- Connection lifecycle management
- Accept loop with backpressure

### Phase 2+ (Advanced) - Full Integration
- Request handlers as regions (structured concurrency)
- Lab runtime for deterministic HTTP testing
- Graceful shutdown coordination
- Distributed tracing integration

## Key Design Decisions

### 1. RequestContext as Cx Extension
fastapi_rust's RequestContext will WRAP Asupersync's Cx, not replace it:
```rust
pub struct RequestContext<'a> {
    cx: Cx<'a>,              // Asupersync capability
    request: &'a Request,     // HTTP request
    response: ResponseBuilder, // HTTP response
    // ... fastapi-specific fields
}
```

### 2. Outcome ↔ HTTP Status Mapping
```
Outcome::Ok(T)        → 200 OK / custom success status
Outcome::Err(E)       → 4xx/5xx based on error kind
Outcome::Cancelled    → 499 Client Closed Request
Outcome::Panicked     → 500 Internal Server Error
```

### 3. Request Budget = Request Timeout
HTTP request timeouts map directly to Asupersync Budget:
- deadline_ns: request timeout
- poll_quota: optional compute limit
- cost_quota: optional memory limit

### 4. Connection as Region
Each HTTP connection spawns a region; each request spawns a sub-region:
```
Server Region
├── Connection Region (long-lived)
│   ├── Request Region (short-lived)
│   ├── Request Region
│   └── ...
└── Connection Region
    └── ...
```

## Success Criteria

1. fastapi_rust can depend on asupersync as sole async runtime
2. RequestContext provides full Cx capability access
3. HTTP errors map cleanly to Outcome semantics
4. Request timeouts use Budget system
5. Graceful shutdown cancels all in-flight requests correctly
6. Lab runtime can test HTTP handlers deterministically
7. No orphaned connections or leaked resources

## Cross-Project Coordination

### Communication
- Use thread_id prefix: `fastapi-asupersync-integration`
- Beads reference each other via ID
- Agent Mail for async coordination

### Dependency Management
- fastapi_rust depends on asupersync (Cargo.toml)
- API breaking changes require coordination
- Shared types may need `asupersync-api` crate

## References
- Asupersync README.md: Architecture and design philosophy
- asupersync_plan_v4.md: Detailed specification
- AGENTS.md: Non-negotiable invariants (fastapi must not violate)

## Owner
Joint: Asupersync team + IvoryWolf (fastapi_rust)
close_reason: EPIC completed. Phase 0 Foundation and Cross-Project Coordination Protocol are both done. fastapi_rust integration architecture established with: (1) path dependency in Cargo.toml, (2) API stability documented, (3) thread naming conventions defined, (4) Cx integration patterns documented in README.

title: [ALIEN][TRACE][HOMO] Fix persistence_pairs() panic on non-square matrices
description: ReducedMatrix::persistence_pairs() in src/trace/gf2.rs:442 creates is_birth vector sized by cols but indexes it with pivot row indices (birth) that can be >= cols when rows > cols. For example, boundary_1() on a 4x4 grid produces a 16x24 matrix (16 rows=vertices, 24 cols=edges). After reduction, pivot rows can reach index 15 — but is_birth is only sized 24... wait, that's fine for this case. The real issue is boundary_2() which produces a 24x9 matrix (24 rows=edges, 9 cols=squares). Pivots can be up to row 23, but is_birth is only 9 elements. Fix: size is_birth to max(rows, cols) or rows.

title: [ALIEN-GRAVEYARD] Prove SendPermit no-aliasing invariant
description:
Prove using Separation Logic that the SendPermit obligation satisfies the no-aliasing invariant: at any program point, exactly one task owns any given SendPermit.

BACKGROUND (Separation Logic, Graveyard section 5.8): Separation logic extends Hoare logic with the separating conjunction (P * Q), meaning P and Q hold on disjoint portions of the heap. This makes it possible to reason about ownership: if SendPermit(p) * Frame, then the frame (rest of the heap) does not contain p. Transfer of ownership is modeled by consuming the resource predicate from the caller and giving it to the callee. This is the formal foundation for Rust's ownership model.

PROOF STRUCTURE: (1) Allocation proof: show that SendPermit::new() creates a fresh resource predicate SendPermit(p) that is not aliased. Formally: { emp } let p = SendPermit::new() { SendPermit(p) }. The emp (empty heap) precondition ensures no prior alias exists. (2) Transfer proof: show that SendPermit::transfer(from, to) consumes the caller's predicate and gives it to the callee. Formally: { SendPermit(p) @ from } transfer(p, to) { SendPermit(p) @ to }. The separating conjunction ensures no duplication -- the predicate moves, it is not copied. (3) Release proof: show that SendPermit::release() consumes the predicate, returning to empty heap. Formally: { SendPermit(p) } release(p) { emp }. After release, no reference to p exists.

RUST IMPLEMENTATION GUIDANCE: (1) Use Creusot (preferred) or Verus for Rust-native deductive verification. Creusot provides a Rust-embedded proof language compatible with separation logic. (2) Annotate the actual SendPermit implementation with pre/post conditions using #[requires] and #[ensures] attributes. (3) Ghost state: define a ghost map of permit ownership: ghost_permits: GhostMap<PermitId, TaskId>. Invariant: for any permit p, ghost_permits.get(p) returns exactly one task. (4) Handle concurrent creation: different permits are independent (separating conjunction of distinct SendPermit(p1) * SendPermit(p2)). (5) Handle task cancellation: the Drop impl for SendPermit must consume the predicate (release on drop). (6) Integration with channel state machine: the channel's internal state must be consistent with the outstanding permits.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: (1) Creusot or Verus verifier accepts the proof without admits/sorry/trusted blocks. (2) Proof covers all public API methods of SendPermit (new, transfer, release, drop). (3) Proof handles concurrent creation of independent permits. (4) Proof handles the cancellation path (Drop impl). (5) Proof assumptions are documented and justified (no hidden axioms). (6) Proof can be re-verified by CI (automated verification as part of build).

LOGGING REQUIREMENTS: Proof verification results logged to CI: proof_name, verifier (creusot|verus), verification_time_ms, result (verified|failed|timeout), admitted_count (must be 0), axiom_count, lemma_count. EvidenceLedger entry: component=separation_logic_proof, action=sendpermit_no_aliasing_verified, includes proof_size_loc, assumption_count.

TESTING APPROACH: (1) The proof itself is the test -- verification by the tool is the acceptance criterion. (2) Additionally, write runtime tests that exercise the same API paths and verify the invariants dynamically (defense in depth). (3) Mutation testing: introduce known bugs in SendPermit (e.g., allow cloning), verify the proof fails. (4) If using Creusot: cargo creusot in CI as a required check.

title: [ALIEN-GRAVEYARD] Implement Session Types for Obligation Protocols
description: Asupersync's obligation system (SendPermit, Ack, Lease) currently enforces linearity at runtime via dynamic checking. Session types (§5.2 in Alien CS Graveyard) can make this statically checkable at compile time, eliminating an entire class of bugs. This is the #1 highest-impact alien concept for Asupersync because it makes linearity a compile-time guarantee rather than a runtime assertion. Key papers: Honda 1993 (binary session types), Honda-Yoshida-Carbone 2008 (multiparty). Implementation approach: Use Rust's typestate pattern with PhantomData to encode protocol states. Channel<Send<M, Cont>> transitions to Channel<Cont> after send. The key challenge is encoding multiparty sessions where multiple participants must follow a global protocol. Acceptance criteria: (1) Obligation protocols are statically checkable — protocol violations are compile errors, (2) Zero runtime overhead for session type checking, (3) Backward compatibility with existing dynamic checking as fallback, (4) At least 3 obligation protocols converted to session types.

title: [EPIC-INFRA] Symbolic Obligations
description:
# EPIC: Symbolic Obligations

**Bead ID:** asupersync-zfn
**Type:** EPIC
**Priority:** P1
**Status:** OPEN
**Owner:** Dicklesworthstone

---

## Vision

Symbolic Obligations bring linear type semantics to distributed symbol operations, ensuring that every symbol that must be delivered is tracked, every acknowledgment that must be sent is recorded, and any leaked obligation is detected and reported. This EPIC extends asupersync's existing obligation tracking system to the RaptorQ distributed layer.

The core insight is that symbol delivery is not just data transfer - it's a responsibility. When a task takes ownership of symbols to transmit, it acquires an obligation that must be resolved: either the symbols are successfully delivered (committed) or the transmission is explicitly abandoned (aborted). Silently dropping symbols without resolution is a programming error that the obligation system will detect and report.

This model directly supports asupersync's cancel-correctness guarantee: cancellation is a protocol, not silent data loss. When a symbol transmission is cancelled, the obligation is aborted cleanly, and cleanup handlers run to notify relevant parties. The two-phase pattern (reserve/commit) prevents data loss during cancellation by ensuring obligations are tracked before any work begins.

Symbolic obligations also enable partial fulfillment tracking. When transmitting an object that requires 100 symbols, the obligation tracks how many have been acknowledged. Progress is observable, and the system knows exactly when delivery is complete.

---

## Goals

- **Define SymbolicObligation type** that wraps core obligations with symbol-specific metadata
- **Track partial fulfillment** for multi-symbol object deliveries
- **Detect leaked obligations** when tasks complete without resolving their symbol responsibilities
- **Integrate with epoch windows** so obligations have bounded validity
- **Integrate with existing obligation system** preserving the two-phase (Reserved/Committed/Aborted) protocol
- **Provide RAII guards** for automatic obligation resolution on scope exit

---

## Non-Goals

- **Exactly-once delivery**: Delivery guarantees are a system property, not a type guarantee
- **Distributed obligation tracking**: This is local tracking; distributed coordination is separate
- **Persistent obligation storage**: Obligations are runtime state, persistence is external
- **Automatic retry**: Retry logic is application-level, not obligation-level
- **Transaction semantics**: ACID across multiple obligations is not addressed

---

## Child Beads

| ID | Title | Status | Priority | Description |
|----|-------|--------|----------|-------------|
| asupersync-fxd | Implement SymbolicObligation Type and Partial Fulfillment | OPEN | P1 | Core obligation type with progress tracking |
| asupersync-t3v | Integrate with Existing Obligation Tracking | OPEN | P1 | Bridge to ObligationRecord system |

---

## Phases

### Phase 1: SymbolicObligation Type
**Duration:** 1 sprint
**Deliverables:**
- `SymbolicObligation` type wrapping `ObligationRecord`
- `SymbolObligationKind` enum (Transmit, Ack, Decoding, EncodingSession, Lease)
- Epoch window validity checking
- Deadline expiry detection
- Commit/abort/mark_leaked methods

**Exit Criteria:**
- All obligation kinds can be created and resolved
- Epoch and deadline validity correctly enforced
- Double-resolution panics with clear message

### Phase 2: Tracking and Integration
**Duration:** 1 sprint
**Deliverables:**
- `SymbolicObligationTracker` for managing obligations within a region
- Indices by symbol ID and object ID for fast lookup
- `ObligationGuard` RAII wrapper for automatic resolution
- Integration with region close (leak detection)
- Epoch-based and deadline-based automatic abort

**Exit Criteria:**
- Tracker correctly maintains obligations
- Guards resolve obligations on drop
- Leaks detected during region close
- Automatic abort on epoch/deadline expiry

### Phase 3: Testing and Documentation
**Duration:** 0.5 sprint
**Deliverables:**
- Comprehensive unit tests (12+ scenarios)
- Integration with region lifecycle tests
- API documentation with usage examples

**Exit Criteria:**
- All acceptance criteria met
- Full test coverage
- Clear documentation

---

## Success Criteria

1. **Leak Detection**: 100% of unresolved obligations are detected during region close
2. **Type Safety**: Impossible to silently drop a symbolic obligation without resolution
3. **Partial Progress**: Object delivery progress is trackable at symbol granularity
4. **Epoch Enforcement**: Obligations outside their epoch window are automatically aborted
5. **Deadline Enforcement**: Obligations past their deadline are automatically aborted
6. **Double-Resolution Prevention**: Resolving an already-resolved obligation panics
7. **RAII Semantics**: ObligationGuard correctly resolves on drop

---

## Dependencies

### Depends On
- **asupersync-0vx** (Foundation Layer) - `SymbolId`, `ObjectId` types
- **asupersync-bsx** (Epoch Concurrency) - `EpochId`, `EpochWindow` types
- `src/record/obligation.rs` - Base `ObligationRecord` and `ObligationState`
- `src/types/id.rs` - `ObligationId`, `TaskId`, `RegionId`, `Time`

### Blocks
- **asupersync-9mq** (Integration) - Obligation tracking in unified API

---

## Acceptance Criteria Checklist

### SymbolicObligation Type and Partial Fulfillment (asupersync-fxd)
- [ ] `SymbolicObligation` wraps `ObligationRecord` with symbol metadata
- [ ] `SymbolObligationKind` enum with all five kinds:
  - [ ] `SymbolTransmit { symbol_id, destination }`
  - [ ] `SymbolAck { symbol_id, source }`
  - [ ] `DecodingInProgress { object_id, symbols_received, symbols_needed }`
  - [ ] `EncodingSession { object_id, symbols_encoded }`
  - [ ] `SymbolLease { object_id, lease_expires }`
- [ ] `EpochWindow` with start/end epochs and validity checking
- [ ] Factory methods: `transmit()`, `ack()`, `decoding()`, `lease()`
- [ ] `is_pending()` returns true until resolved
- [ ] `is_epoch_valid(current_epoch)` checks epoch window
- [ ] `is_expired(now)` checks deadline
- [ ] `commit()` for successful resolution
- [ ] `abort()` for clean cancellation
- [ ] `mark_leaked()` for runtime-detected leaks
- [ ] `update_decoding_progress()` for partial fulfillment
- [ ] Double resolution panics

### Integrate with Existing Obligation Tracking (asupersync-t3v)
- [ ] `SymbolicObligationTracker` managing obligations per region
- [ ] HashMap storage indexed by `ObligationId`
- [ ] Secondary index by `SymbolId` for fast symbol-based lookup
- [ ] Secondary index by `ObjectId` for decoding/encoding obligations
- [ ] `register()` adds obligation and returns ID
- [ ] `resolve(id, commit)` removes and sets final state
- [ ] `pending()` iterator over unresolved obligations
- [ ] `by_symbol(symbol_id)` returns obligations for a symbol
- [ ] `pending_count()` returns count
- [ ] `check_leaks()` marks all pending as leaked, returns list
- [ ] `abort_expired_epoch(current_epoch)` aborts out-of-window
- [ ] `abort_expired_deadlines(now)` aborts past-deadline
- [ ] `ObligationGuard<'a>` with `commit()` and `abort()` methods
- [ ] Guard resolves (abort) on drop if not explicitly resolved
- [ ] Logging for register, resolve, leak, abort events

---

## Obligation Lifecycle

```
     ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │                     RESERVED                                    │
     │                                                                 │
     │  SymbolicObligation created via factory method                 │
     │  Registered in SymbolicObligationTracker                       │
     │  Work begins (symbol transmission, decoding, etc.)             │
     │                                                                 │
     └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                │                    │                    │
                │ success            │ failure            │ dropped
                │                    │                    │
                ▼                    ▼                    ▼
     ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐
     │   COMMITTED     │  │    ABORTED      │  │     LEAKED      │
     │                 │  │                 │  │                 │
     │  Symbols        │  │  Operation      │  │  Task ended     │
     │  delivered      │  │  cancelled      │  │  without        │
     │  successfully   │  │  cleanly        │  │  resolution     │
     │                 │  │                 │  │  (BUG!)         │
     └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘
```

---

## Integration Patterns

### Pattern 1: Symbol Transmission with Tracking
```rust
async fn send_symbol(
    cx: &Cx,
    tracker: &mut SymbolicObligationTracker,
    symbol: Symbol,
    destination: RegionId,
) -> Result<(), Error> {
    // Create and register obligation
    let ob = SymbolicObligation::transmit(
        generate_id(), cx.task_id(), cx.region_id(),
        symbol.id(), destination, Some(cx.deadline()), None,
    );
    let ob_id = tracker.register(ob);

    // Perform work
    match transport.send(symbol).await {
        Ok(()) => {
            tracker.resolve(ob_id, true); // Commit
            Ok(())
        }
        Err(e) => {
            tracker.resolve(ob_id, false); // Abort
            Err(e)
        }
    }
}
```

### Pattern 2: RAII Guard for Automatic Resolution
```rust
async fn with_lease<T>(
    tracker: &mut SymbolicObligationTracker,
    object_id: ObjectId,
    f: impl FnOnce() -> Result<T, Error>,
) -> Result<T, Error> {
    let ob = SymbolicObligation::lease(/* ... */);
    let ob_id = tracker.register(ob);
    let guard = ObligationGuard::new(tracker, ob_id);

    let result = f();

    if result.is_ok() {
        guard.commit(); // Explicit success
    }
    // If result is Err, guard drops and aborts automatically

    result
}
```

---

## Risk Assessment

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation |
|------|------------|--------|------------|
| Too many obligations cause memory pressure | Medium | Medium | Per-region limits, TTL-based cleanup |
| Leak detection floods logs in failure scenarios | Medium | Low | Rate limiting, aggregation |
| Epoch window misconfiguration causes false aborts | Low | Medium | Validation, sensible defaults |
| Guard drop order causes surprising behavior | Medium | Medium | Clear documentation, explicit API preference |
| Integration with existing obligations fragile | Low | High | Careful wrapping, exhaustive tests |

title: Implement Scope API (user-facing region handle)
description:
# Scope API (User-Facing Region Handle)

## Purpose
`Scope<'r>` is the user-facing handle to a region. It is the API surface that enforces structured concurrency:
- every spawned task is owned by exactly one region
- region close implies quiescence (no live children, finalizers done, obligations resolved)

The lifetime `'r` prevents handles from escaping their region.

## Core Responsibilities
- spawn work (Phase 0: single-thread fiber tier; Phase 1: Send task tier)
- create subregions
- register finalizers
- surface `Cx` capabilities and tracing

## Policy Integration (must exist)
`Scope::region_with_policy` (or equivalent) requires a `Policy` type that defines:
- how to aggregate child outcomes
- how to react to child failures (e.g., fail-fast cancels siblings)

## Key APIs (Sketch)
### spawn
```rust
pub fn spawn<F, T>(&self, f: F) -> JoinHandle<'r, T>
where
    F: Future<Output = T> + 'r,
```

### region
```rust
pub async fn region<F, Fut>(&self, f: F) -> Outcome<()>
where
    F: FnOnce(Scope<'_>) -> Fut,
    Fut: Future<Output = ()>,
```

### finalizers
- `defer_sync` / `defer_async`

### handles
`JoinHandle` supports:
- `join().await -> Outcome<T>`
- `cancel(reason)` (request cancellation; must still drain)

## “Dropping a JoinHandle” Rule
Dropping a handle **does not detach work**. The region still owns the task and will cancel/drain it on region close.

## Example (No stdout/stderr in core)
```rust
root.region(|sub| async move {
    sub.defer_sync(|cx| cx.trace_user("cleanup", TraceData::None));

    let h1 = sub.spawn(async move { 1 });
    let h2 = sub.spawn(async move { 2 });

    let _ = h1.join().await;
    let _ = h2.join().await;
}).await;
```

## Acceptance Criteria
- Lifetimes prevent escaping scopes.
- Region close waits for children/finalizers/obligations.
- Policy hooks exist for fail-fast semantics.

## Testing
- Compile-time tests where feasible (no escape).
- Lab E2E scenarios validate nested regions and quiescence.

title: [ALIEN][SCHED][LYAP] Efficient RuntimeSnapshot extraction (no hot-path allocs)
description:
## Purpose

The governor needs a snapshot of Σ (runtime state) to compute V(Σ).

We must compute this cheaply:
- no per-poll allocations
- stable deterministic counts

## Snapshot contents (candidate)

- outstanding obligations by kind
- pending cancel requests / acks
- deadline slack summary
- IO in-flight counts
- ready queue depth signals

## Acceptance criteria

- Snapshot can be computed with bounded work.
- Snapshot values are deterministic under lab runtime.
design:
### Implementation plan

Add a deterministic, allocation-free constructor for the Lyapunov governor snapshot.

**Location:** `src/obligation/lyapunov.rs` (`impl StateSnapshot`), because the type's docs already claim it can be constructed from `RuntimeState`.

### Snapshot extraction semantics (exact)

Given a `RuntimeState` with logical time `now = state.now`:

- `time`: `now`
- `live_tasks`: count of `state.tasks` whose `TaskState` is *not* terminal (`!task.state.is_terminal()`).
- `pending_obligations`: count of `state.obligations` where `obligation.is_pending()` (i.e. `ObligationState::Reserved`).
- `obligation_age_sum_ns`: `sum now.duration_since(obligation.reserved_at)` over pending obligations.
- `draining_regions`: count of `state.regions` with `RegionState` in `{Draining, Finalizing}`.
- `deadline_pressure`: for each **live** task with a deadline in its `CxInner` budget:
  - `slack_ns = deadline.duration_since(now)` (saturating at 0 when overdue)
  - `term = max(0, 1 - slack_ns / D0)`
  - `deadline_pressure = sum term`

`D0` is a fixed normalization constant (chosen as 1s) to make the signal represent "tasks due soon or overdue" rather than far-future deadlines.

### Determinism + performance constraints

- **No allocations on the hot path:** no `Vec`, no `HashMap`, no `collect`.
- **Deterministic iteration:** only scan arenas in their natural order; no hash iteration.
- **Graceful degradation:** if a task's `CxInner` lock is poisoned, skip its deadline contribution (do not panic).

### Follow-ups (if needed)

If scanning overhead becomes noticeable in profiling, add incremental counters (updated on task/obligation/region transitions) so snapshots become O(1).
acceptance_criteria:
- `StateSnapshot::from_runtime_state(&RuntimeState)` exists and is `#[must_use]`.
- Snapshot extraction is deterministic and allocation-free.
- Unit tests cover:
  - live task counting
  - pending obligation counting + age sum
  - draining/finalizing region counting
  - deadline pressure for both "due soon" and "overdue" cases
- `cargo test -p asupersync snapshot_from_runtime` passes (once repo-wide compile blockers are cleared).
notes:
### Progress

- Implemented `StateSnapshot::from_runtime_state` + unit tests in `src/obligation/lyapunov.rs`.

title: [EPIC-PHASE] Phase 0 - Single-Thread Deterministic Kernel
description:
# Phase 0: Single-Thread Deterministic Kernel

## Overview
This is the foundational phase of Asupersync. It establishes the core runtime semantics on a single thread with deterministic execution, enabling rigorous testing and validation of the fundamental invariants before adding complexity.

## Why Single-Thread First?
1. **Correctness Before Performance**: Multi-threading adds non-determinism and complexity. By starting single-threaded, we can prove our semantic model is correct.
2. **Deterministic Testing**: Single-thread execution with virtual time enables perfect reproducibility - the same test always produces the same behavior.
3. **Simpler Debugging**: When something goes wrong, there's only one execution path to analyze.
4. **Foundation for Parallelism**: Everything built here transfers directly to Phase 1's parallel scheduler.

## Core Components
- **Outcome Type**: The four-valued severity lattice (Ok < Err < Cancelled < Panicked)
- **Budget System**: Product semiring for deadline/quota propagation
- **Region Tree**: Structured concurrency ownership hierarchy
- **Task System**: Task lifecycle and state machine
- **Cancellation Protocol**: Request → Drain → Finalize with bounded cleanup
- **Obligation System**: Two-phase effects with linear resource tracking
- **Cx Capability Boundary**: All effects through explicit capabilities
- **Scheduler**: Cancel > Timed > Ready lane priority
- **Lab Runtime**: Virtual time and deterministic scheduling

## Success Criteria
- All 6 non-negotiable invariants hold in all reachable states
- All progress properties verified under fair scheduling
- Test oracles verify: no task leaks, no obligation leaks, quiescence on close, losers drained, all finalizers ran, no ambient authority
- Trace capture/replay works perfectly
- Derived combinators (join, race, timeout) behave according to algebraic laws

## Mathematical Foundations Implemented
- Severity lattice for outcome aggregation
- Near-semiring operations for join/race
- Product semiring for budget combination
- Linear resource discipline for obligations
- Mazurkiewicz trace equivalence (foundation for Phase 5 DPOR)

## The 6 Non-Negotiable Invariants (from AGENTS.md)

| # | Invariant | Oracle |
|---|-----------|--------|
| 1 | **Structured concurrency** – every task is owned by exactly one region | no_task_leaks |
| 2 | **Region close = quiescence** – no live children + all finalizers done | quiescence_on_close |
| 3 | **Cancellation is a protocol** – request → drain → finalize | (state machine tests) |
| 4 | **Losers are drained** – races must cancel AND fully drain losers | losers_always_drained |
| 5 | **No obligation leaks** – permits/acks/leases must be committed or aborted | no_obligation_leaks |
| 6 | **No ambient authority** – effects flow through Cx and explicit capabilities | no_ambient_authority |

Additionally, **Determinism** is a first-class property of the lab runtime that enables testing.

## Key Implementation Beads (Phase 0)

### Core Types
- Outcome type with severity lattice
- CancelReason with severity ordering
- Budget with product semiring semantics
- Core identifiers (RegionId, TaskId, ObligationId, Time)

### State Machines
- TaskState: Pending → Running → CancelRequested → Cancelling → Finalizing → Completed
- RegionState: Open → Closing → Draining → Finalizing → Closed
- ObligationState: Reserved → Committed/Aborted/Leaked

### Records
- TaskRecord, RegionRecord, ObligationRecord and registries

### Runtime
- Global RuntimeState (Σ)
- Scheduler with 3-lane priority
- Waker (std::task::Wake) and wake deduplication (no unsafe)
- Timer heap for sleep operations

### Cx/Scope
- Scope API for user-facing region handles
- Cx capability boundary

### Cancellation/Finalization
- Cancellation protocol transitions
- Finalization system (defer_async, defer_sync, bracket)

### Combinators
- join (parallel composition)
- race (alternative composition with loser draining)
- timeout (race with deadline)

### Lab Runtime
- Virtual time
- Deterministic scheduling
- Trace capture/replay

### Test Oracles
- 6 oracles matching the 6 invariants

## References
- asupersync_plan_v4.md §21 (Phase-0 kernel reference implementation plan)
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md (complete operational semantics)
- AGENTS.md (non-negotiable invariants)

All 10 sub-beads closed: Scaffolding (akx.1), Semantics Types (akx.2), Records & State Machines (akx.3), Scheduler & Waker (akx.4), Cancellation & Finalization (akx.5), Cx Capability (akx.6), Trace & Lab Runtime (akx.7), Combinators (akx.8), Verification (akx.9), Two-Phase Primitives (akx.10). 2145+ lib tests, 23 E2E tests, all invariants verified.

title: [ALIEN-CS] Epic: High-EV Runtime Enhancements (Conformal Hedging & Power of 2 Choices)
description:
Comprehensive program to inject high-EV, mathematically grounded alien-CS primitives into the core runtime to bound tail latency and reduce lock contention under load.

Background and rationale:
- Hardcoded timeouts in Hedge combinators are fragile, causing either tail latency spikes or thundering herd problems.
- Standard work-stealing sequentially probes queues, causing O(N) lock contention and suboptimal tail latency under heavy burst workloads.

Program intent:
1) Implement AdaptiveHedgePolicy using Distribution-Free Marginal Conformal Prediction to target exact empirical coverage bounds (e.g. true P95).
2) Implement Power of Two Choices (Mitzenmacher) for work-stealing, bounding maximum queue length variance to O(log log N) and drastically reducing average lock contention.

This epic organizes the operationalization of these concepts into self-contained, formally guaranteed runtime artifacts.

2. Power of Two Choices stealing is implemented with O(1) len oracle and verified via deterministic unit tests.

4. Both enhancements implement detailed structured logging providing a verifiable 'evidence ledger' for debugging and performance tuning.

title: [ALIEN][TRACE] Persistent-Homology Schedule Prioritization (Topological Coverage)
description:
## Goal

Use topology-derived novelty signals to prioritize which schedules (equivalence classes / backtracks) to explore next in the deterministic lab runtime.

The core idea: the "space of executions" is not a list of interleavings; it is a cubical complex induced by commutations of independent actions. Some bugs (deadlocks, obligation-lifetime shapes) correspond to essential cycles/holes.

We want a *deterministic scoring function* that prefers schedules exposing new topological features early.

## Practical scope (what we will actually build)

We start with a pragmatic proxy:
- build a 2D cell complex where 2-cells represent commuting squares (adjacent swaps of independent events)
- compute H1 persistence over GF(2) under a filtration (prefix length / commutation depth)
- use persistence + novelty to prioritize exploration nodes

This is engineered to be:
- deterministic
- dependency-free (bitset algebra)
- explainable (evidence ledger)

## Deliverables

- Complex builder: from trace poset + independence to a square-complex proxy.
- Persistent homology (start with H1) implementation over GF(2).
- Scoring function producing stable, explainable ranks.
- Integration with lab explorer / DPOR work queue (priority scheduling of exploration nodes).
- Deterministic benchmark demonstrating fewer explored schedules to surface a known bug shape.

title: Implement RRef<'r, T> (region-owned Send reference)
description:
# RRef<'r, T> (Region-Owned Reference)

## Purpose
Provide a way for migrating (`Send`) tasks to reference data allocated in the region heap safely.

## Requirements
- `RRef<'r, T>` ties to region lifetime `'r`.
- `RRef<'r, T>` can be `Send`/`Sync` when `T` is.
- No unsafe code in core (if possible). If unavoidable, redesign.

## Design Sketch
- Internally represent as:
  - `Arc<RegionHeap>` + offset/index into heap
  - OR `Arc<T>` allocated via region heap wrapper (but `Arc` implies refcount overhead)

Given performance goals, prefer region heap + offset, but we must reconcile with `unsafe` prohibition.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Users can spawn Send tasks that capture `RRef`s without lifetime violations.
- Region close guarantees memory validity until tasks are done.

## Testing
- Compile-time tests for trait bounds (`Send`/`Sync` conditions).
- Runtime tests: create `RRef`, spawn tasks across workers, validate reads.
close_reason: RRef implemented in src/types/rref.rs with Send/Sync bounds + tests

title: [EPIC-PHASE] Phase 1 - Parallel Scheduler and Region Heap
description:
## Overview
Phase 1 extends the single-threaded deterministic kernel (Phase 0) to support parallel execution with work-stealing, region-isolated heaps, and multi-threaded scheduling while preserving all invariants.

## Goals
1. Enable true parallelism for throughput
2. Maintain determinism in lab runtime (parallel simulation)
3. Implement region heap for memory isolation
4. Work-stealing scheduler for load balancing
5. All Phase 0 invariants MUST be preserved

## Key Components

### 1. Work-Stealing Scheduler
- Per-worker local queues
- Global steal queue for overflow
- Lock-free deque implementation
- Maintain scheduling determinism via virtual schedule in lab mode

### 2. Region Heap
- Each region owns its allocations
- Mass deallocation on region close
- Thread-safe allocation within region
- Region-local bump allocator (fast path)
- Fallback to global allocator

### 3. Parallel Task Model
- `Task<T>` is `Send` - can migrate between workers
- Wake deduplication across threads
- Atomic task state transitions
- Thread-safe RegionRecord access

### 4. Synchronization Primitives (Parallel Versions)
- Lock-free MPSC queue
- Sharded counters for obligations
- Atomic region state machine

## Dependencies
- Requires complete Phase 0 kernel
- Requires all Phase 0 invariants proven/tested
- Requires two-phase primitives from Phase 0

## Constraints
- No additional invariants beyond Phase 0
- Must support lab runtime schedule replay
- Must support deterministic parallel simulation
- Cannot break cancel-correctness

## Non-Goals for Phase 1
- I/O integration (Phase 2)
- Actor model (Phase 3)
- Distributed execution (Phase 4)
- DPOR/TLA+ tooling (Phase 5)

## Mathematical Foundation
From the spec:
- Work-stealing preserves eventual quiescence
- Region heap uses arena allocation semantics
- Parallel near-semiring: join/race laws still hold under parallelism

## Testing Strategy
- All Phase 0 tests must pass
- Add parallel stress tests
- Add work-stealing correctness tests
- Verify determinism under parallel lab runtime

## References
- asupersync_plan_v4.md: §7 Phase 1 (Parallel)
- Chase-Lev work-stealing deque
- Region-based memory management (Tofte-Talpin)

## Success Criteria
- Parallel scheduler executes `Send` tasks across multiple workers while preserving Phase 0 invariants.
- Region heap enables safe region-owned allocation and quiescent reclamation on close.
- Lab runtime can deterministically *simulate* multi-worker schedules (repeatable traces).
- Stress/E2E tests cover work stealing, cancellation drain, and quiescence under contention.

title: [ALIEN-GRAVEYARD] Convert SendPermit/Ack obligation to session types
description:
Convert the SendPermit->Ack protocol to use session types. This is the simplest obligation protocol (binary, no branching) and serves as the proof-of-concept for the session type system.

BACKGROUND (Session Types, Graveyard section 5.2): Session types encode communication protocols in the type system. A session-typed channel Channel<S> can only perform the operation specified by state S. After performing that operation, the channel transitions to the next state. Protocol violations become compile errors. Key paper: Honda 1993 (binary session types).

CURRENT STATE: SendPermit and Ack are runtime-checked tokens. A task acquires a SendPermit, sends a message, and receives an Ack. Protocol violations (e.g., sending without a permit, acking without receiving) are caught at runtime via panics or Result errors.

TARGET STATE: Channel<SendState> can only call send() which returns Channel<AckState>, which can only call ack() which returns Channel<Done>. Attempting to call ack() before send() is a compile error. The session-typed API wraps the existing runtime-checked API so both can coexist during migration.

RUST IMPLEMENTATION GUIDANCE: (1) Define state types: struct SendReady; struct WaitingAck; struct Done;. (2) Define typed channel: struct ObligationChannel<S> { inner: RawChannel, _state: PhantomData<S> }. (3) Implement transitions: impl ObligationChannel<SendReady> { fn send(self, msg: M) -> ObligationChannel<WaitingAck> { ... } } -- note self is consumed (moved), preventing reuse. (4) Use the typestate macros from bd-3u5d3.2 to generate these types from a protocol spec rather than hand-coding. (5) Integrate with Cx: the send() method requires Cx<SendCapability> proving the caller has permission. (6) Backward compat: impl From<ObligationChannel<SendReady>> for LegacySendPermit for gradual migration.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: (1) Calling send() on a Channel<SendReady> compiles and returns Channel<WaitingAck>. (2) Calling ack() on a Channel<SendReady> fails to compile with a clear error message. (3) Calling send() twice on the same channel fails to compile (moved value). (4) Zero runtime overhead vs current implementation (verified by criterion.rs benchmark). (5) Legacy API still works and interoperates with session-typed API. (6) All protocol transitions logged to EvidenceLedger.

LOGGING REQUIREMENTS: Each state transition emits a structured log via tracing: obligation_channel_id, from_state, to_state, transition (send|ack), trace_id, task_id. EvidenceLedger entry on channel creation and completion: component=obligation_channel, action=send_permit_ack_complete, includes total_transition_count and latency_us. On protocol error (legacy API path): ERROR log with channel_id, expected_state, actual_state.

TESTING APPROACH: (1) Use trybuild crate for compile-fail tests verifying invalid protocol sequences produce errors. (2) Unit tests for happy path: create channel, send, ack, verify Done state. (3) Integration test: run SendPermit/Ack protocol under FrankenLab with 100 concurrent channels. (4) Backward compat test: legacy API and session-typed API produce identical observable behavior. (5) Benchmark: criterion.rs comparing session-typed vs legacy performance.

[EPIC] Cancel-Aware Synchronization Primitives (tokio-sync equivalent)
description:
# Cancel-Aware Synchronization Primitives

## Overview
Synchronization primitives that integrate with cancellation protocol and support two-phase patterns where needed.

## Components

### 1. Mutex
- lock() returns LockGuard (obligation)
- try_lock() for non-blocking
- Cancel-aware: waiting for lock respects cancellation
- Unlock is automatic via Drop

### 2. RwLock
- read() returns ReadGuard
- write() returns WriteGuard
- Upgradable read locks
- Cancel-aware waiting

### 3. Semaphore
- Two-phase: acquire_permit() returns Permit obligation
- Permit must be released or explicitly dropped
- Bounded and unbounded variants
- OwnedPermit for 'static lifetime

### 4. Barrier
- wait() blocks until N waiters
- Returns BarrierWaitResult (is_leader)
- Cancel-aware: if cancelled, barrier may never complete

### 5. Notify
- notify_one(), notify_waiters()
- notified() returns future
- Cancel-aware waiting

### 6. OnceCell
- get_or_init() with async initializer
- get_or_try_init() for fallible init
- Cancel-aware: racing initializers handled correctly

### 7. Watch Channel
- Single-producer, multi-consumer
- Receivers get latest value
- Cancel-aware subscription

## Invariants
- No deadlocks in well-formed programs
- Cancel-safe acquisition
- Obligations properly tracked
- Deterministic behavior in lab runtime

## Testing
- Concurrent access patterns
- Cancellation during wait
- Deadlock detection (debug builds)
- Deterministic scheduling in lab

title: [TLS] Implement TlsAcceptor and Certificate Types
[EPIC-INFRA] Hierarchical Timer Wheel
description:
## Overview

Implement a hierarchical timer wheel for O(1) timer operations, replacing naive linear timer storage. This is a performance-critical optimization for workloads with many concurrent timers.

## Strategic Value

**Problem Solved**: Current timer implementations (if using Vec or BTreeMap) have O(n) or O(log n) cost for timer operations. Servers handling thousands of connections each with timeouts need O(1) operations.

**Why Hierarchical**: Simple timer wheels have limited range. Hierarchical wheels (like Linux kernel) provide O(1) insert/cancel/expire across wide time ranges (milliseconds to hours).

**Production Necessity**: Any serious async runtime needs efficient timer management. This is foundational for production use.

## Algorithm Overview

### Timer Wheel Structure
```
Level 0: 256 slots, 1ms resolution (covers 256ms)
Level 1: 64 slots, 256ms resolution (covers 16.4 seconds)  
Level 2: 64 slots, 16.4s resolution (covers 17.5 minutes)
Level 3: 64 slots, 17.5min resolution (covers 18.6 hours)
```

### Operations
- **Insert**: Hash deadline to appropriate level/slot, O(1)
- **Cancel**: Remove from linked list at slot, O(1) with handle
- **Tick**: Process Level 0, cascade higher levels periodically

### Cascading
When Level 0 wraps, cascade Level 1 slot into Level 0. This amortizes the cost of long-duration timers.

## Design Considerations

### Memory Layout
- Intrusive linked lists for zero-allocation in steady state
- Timer handles store list pointers for O(1) cancel
- Cache-friendly slot arrays

### Precision Trade-offs
- 1ms base resolution is sufficient for network timeouts
- Sub-millisecond needs separate approach (spin loops, etc.)
- Configuration allows tuning resolution vs. memory

### Integration
- Replace current timer storage in time module
- Maintain same API (sleep, timeout, Delay)
- Lab runtime gets separate virtual time wheel

## Acceptance Criteria

1. O(1) insert, cancel, and per-tick expire operations
2. Supports at least 24-hour timer range
3. Memory overhead < 1KB for wheel structure
4. Benchmark shows 10x improvement over BTreeMap for 10K timers
5. No changes to public timer API

## Dependencies

- Standalone module, no major dependencies
- Benefits from good integration test coverage

## Priority Rationale

Ranked #7 because while important for production performance, it is primarily an internal optimization. Users benefit indirectly through better performance, but it does not add new capabilities.
close_reason: All 4 sub-tasks closed: gt1c (Lab virtual time wheel), jrrw (overflow and coalescing), h7as (comprehensive test suite), uyqb (benchmarks). HierarchicalTimerWheel in src/time/intrusive_wheel.rs, VirtualTimerWheel in src/lab/virtual_time_wheel.rs, TimerWheel in src/time/wheel.rs. O(1) operations, hierarchical 4-level design, tests passing, benchmarks complete.

title: [EPIC-PHASE] Phase 3 - Actors and Session Types
description:
## Overview
Phase 3 introduces the actor model with supervision trees, region-owned actors, and optional session types for protocol-safe communication.

## Goals
1. Long-lived actors owned by regions
2. Supervision policies (restart, escalate, ignore)
3. Cancel-correct actor shutdown
4. Optional session types for protocol verification

## Key Components

### 1. Actor Model
```rust
pub trait Actor: Send + 'static {
    type Message: Send;
    
    async fn handle(&mut self, cx: &mut Cx<'_>, msg: Self::Message);
    
    /// Called before first message
    async fn on_start(&mut self, cx: &mut Cx<'_>) {}
    
    /// Called on actor shutdown
    async fn on_stop(&mut self, cx: &mut Cx<'_>) {}
}
```

### 2. Actor Handle
```rust
pub struct ActorHandle<A: Actor> {
    tx: Sender<A::Message>,
    // Two-phase send via tx.reserve().send()
}

impl<A: Actor> ActorHandle<A> {
    pub async fn send(&self, cx: &mut Cx<'_>, msg: A::Message) -> Result<(), SendError>;
    pub async fn ask<R>(&self, cx: &mut Cx<'_>, f: impl FnOnce(oneshot::Sender<R>) -> A::Message) -> R;
}
```

### 3. Supervision
```rust
pub enum SupervisionPolicy {
    /// Restart actor on panic/error
    Restart { max_restarts: u32, within: Duration },
    /// Escalate failure to parent region
    Escalate,
    /// Ignore failure, actor stops
    Ignore,
    /// Stop entire region on failure
    StopAll,
}
```

### 4. Region-Owned Actors
- Actors are spawned into regions like tasks
- Region close shuts down all actors
- Actor shutdown respects cancellation protocol:
  1. Stop accepting new messages
  2. Drain mailbox with budget
  3. Run on_stop finalizer
  4. Complete

### 5. Session Types (Optional, Advanced)
```rust
// Example: ATM protocol
type AtmSession = Send<Card, Recv<Pin, Choose<
    Send<Amount, Recv<Cash, End>>,  // Withdraw
    Recv<Balance, End>              // Check balance
>>>;
```

Session types encode protocol states at compile time. Violations become type errors.

## Dependencies
- Requires Phase 0 complete (core runtime)
- Requires Phase 1 complete (parallel scheduler)
- Requires Phase 2 complete (I/O for network actors)
- Requires two-phase channels

## Actor Lifecycle
```
Created → Running → ShutdownRequested → Draining → Finalizing → Stopped
```

Mirrors task lifecycle but with message-based trigger.

## Testing Strategy
- Actor spawn and message handling
- Supervision restart policies
- Graceful shutdown under cancellation
- Session type protocol compliance (if implemented)

## References
- asupersync_plan_v4.md: §7 Phase 3 (Actors)
- Erlang/OTP supervision trees
- Actix (Rust actor framework)
- Session types (Gay & Hole, Honda et al.)

## Success Criteria
- Actors run as region-owned long-lived tasks; no detached-by-default behavior.
- Supervision policies are explicit, monotone, and trace-visible.
- Optional session types provide protocol conformance checks without changing runtime semantics.
- E2E tests cover actor lifecycle, supervision escalation, and structured shutdown/quiescence.

title: Implement test oracle: no_obligation_leaks invariant checker
description:
## Purpose
Implement a test oracle that verifies the "no obligation leaks" invariant: all obligations (SendPermit, Ack, Lease, IoOp) are either committed or aborted before their owning region closes.

## The Invariant
From asupersync_plan_v4.md:
> Permits/acks/leases must be committed or aborted; no silent drops

Formally: `∀o ∈ obligations: state(o) ∈ {Committed, Aborted}` at region close

## Obligation Lifecycle
```
Created → [Committed | Aborted]
```

An obligation leak occurs when an obligation exists in Created state when its region closes.

## Oracle Design

```rust
pub struct ObligationLeakOracle {
    // Tracks all obligation lifecycle events
    creates: Vec<(ObligationId, ObligationKind, RegionId, Time)>,
    resolutions: Vec<(ObligationId, ObligationState, Time)>,  // Committed or Aborted
    region_closes: Vec<(RegionId, Time)>,
}

impl ObligationLeakOracle {
    /// Called when reserve() creates obligation
    pub fn on_create(&mut self, id: ObligationId, kind: ObligationKind, region: RegionId, time: Time);
    
    /// Called when commit() or abort() resolves obligation
    pub fn on_resolve(&mut self, id: ObligationId, state: ObligationState, time: Time);
    
    /// Called when region closes
    pub fn on_region_close(&mut self, region: RegionId, time: Time);
    
    /// Verify invariant holds
    pub fn check(&self) -> Result<(), ObligationLeakViolation>;
}
```

## Violation Detection
```rust
pub struct ObligationLeakViolation {
    pub region: RegionId,
    pub leaked_obligations: Vec<ObligationId>,
    pub kinds: Vec<ObligationKind>,  // SendPermit, Ack, Lease, IoOp
    pub region_close_time: Time,
}
```

A violation occurs when:
1. Region R closes at time T
2. ∃ obligation O in R with state ∉ {Committed, Aborted} at time T

## Obligation Kinds and Their Semantics
| Kind | Created By | Committed By | Aborted By |
|------|-----------|--------------|------------|
| SendPermit | tx.reserve() | permit.send() | permit.abort() or Drop |
| Ack | receive message | ack.commit() | ack.nack() |
| Lease | acquire_lease() | lease.release() | lease.expire() |
| IoOp | io.start() | io.complete() | io.cancel() |

## Linear Type Enforcement
The oracle complements Rust's ownership model:
- In ideal code, obligations are `#[must_use]` and consumed exactly once
- Oracle catches runtime violations that slip through static checks
- Particularly important for dynamic scenarios (vec of obligations, etc.)

## Testing the Oracle
1. **Correct case**: All obligations resolved → check passes
2. **Leak cases by kind**: Each obligation type can leak → check catches
3. **Nested regions**: Inner region obligations must resolve before inner closes
4. **Cancellation**: Cancelled tasks must still resolve their obligations (via abort)

## References
- asupersync_plan_v4.md: §4.4 Obligation Registry, §6.5 Two-Phase Operations
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md: Invariant I2 (obligation_resolved)

## Acceptance Criteria
- Oracle flags any leaked obligation (task completes with unresolved reserved obligations).
- Supports per-kind accounting (permits/acks/leases/ioops) and region-scoped checks.
- Diagnostics include obligation id, kind, holder task, and owning region.
- Deterministic; usable on both trace events and direct registry snapshots.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## Deep Audit: src/http/h2/frame.rs (1948 lines)

**Verdict: 1 MEDIUM bug found**

### BUG: Unknown frame types rejected instead of ignored (MEDIUM)

**Location**: `parse_frame()` line 1058
**Impact**: RFC 7540 compliance violation; interop failure with HTTP/2 extensions

`parse_frame()` returns `H2Error::protocol("unknown frame type: ...")` for unrecognized frame type bytes. However, RFC 7540 §4.1 explicitly mandates:

> Implementations MUST ignore and discard any frame that has a type that is unknown.

This means any peer sending extension frames (which is permitted by the spec) will trigger a connection error and tear down the session. The function should return something like `Ok(None)` or a dedicated `Frame::Unknown` variant to let the caller skip the frame.

### Analysis

HTTP/2 binary frame parser implementing all 10 frame types from RFC 7540 §4-§6.

**FrameHeader parse/write (lines 122-157):**
- Correct 24-bit length, 8-bit type, 8-bit flags, 31-bit stream ID (reserved bit masked with & 0x7f) in both directions
- Roundtrip-tested with high-bit stream IDs

**Per-frame validation (all correct):**
- DATA: stream_id != 0, PADDED handling (pad_length byte + overflow check + strip) ✓
- HEADERS: stream_id != 0, padding → priority → strip order correct per §6.2, self-dependency rejection ✓
- PRIORITY: stream_id != 0, exact 5 bytes → stream-level FrameSizeError (correct per §6.3), self-dependency check ✓
- RST_STREAM: stream_id != 0, exact 4 bytes ✓
- SETTINGS: stream_id == 0, ACK+payload rejected, length%6 check, ENABLE_PUSH 0/1 validation ✓
- PUSH_PROMISE: stream_id != 0, PADDED handling, min 4 bytes for promised_stream_id ✓
- PING: stream_id == 0, exact 8 bytes ✓
- GOAWAY: stream_id == 0, min 8 bytes, debug_data as remainder ✓
- WINDOW_UPDATE: exact 4 bytes, zero increment → connection error on stream 0, stream error on stream != 0 (correctly differentiated per §6.9) ✓
- CONTINUATION: stream_id != 0 ✓

**Encoders:** All 10 encode methods correct. Reserved bits properly masked on stream_id, last_stream_id, promised_stream_id, and increment. Priority exclusive bit correctly OR'd into dependency field.

**Design note (not a bug):** SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE (must be <= 2^31-1, §6.5.2 FLOW_CONTROL_ERROR) and SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE (must be in [16384, 16777215], §6.5.2 PROTOCOL_ERROR) are not range-validated at parse time, while ENABLE_PUSH is. This validation may be deferred to the connection layer when applying settings, but the inconsistency is notable.

**Tests:** 47 tests covering roundtrips for all 10 types, invalid inputs (zero stream IDs, wrong sizes, bad padding, self-dependency), size limits, flag validation, setting variants. Good coverage.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
**CORRECTION**: The unknown frame type error in parse_frame (line 1058) is unreachable from production code. connection.rs line 105-107 already filters unknown frame types with FrameType::from_u8().is_none() + continue BEFORE calling parse_frame. The implementation IS RFC-compliant at the connection layer.

Downgrading to DESIGN NOTE: parse_frame's API is defensive-only here. The error path exists as a safety net for any direct callers but is never hit in production.

**Revised verdict: SOUND — no bugs.**

# Admission Control / Backpressure (Per Region)

The design calls out admission control and backpressure as core scheduling features:

  - max outstanding obligations
- Define backpressure signals surfaced to users:
  - reserve waits
  - spawn returns error or waits depending on policy

## Acceptance Criteria
- Admission control does not break invariants.
- Backpressure is deterministic in lab mode.

## pool.rs Full Audit (2515 lines) - SapphireHill

### Finding 1: TOCTOU in can_create() - pool can exceed max_size (NEW BUG)
Severity: Medium | Lines 1128-1131, 1243-1257

can_create() checks total_count() < max_size under lock, releases lock, then create_resource().await runs without lock, then record_acquisition() re-acquires lock. Under concurrent load, N tasks can all pass the check simultaneously, all create resources, and all call record_acquisition(), causing active to exceed max_size.

Impact: Pool over-provisions beyond configured max_size. Self-correcting (subsequent can_create() calls see the inflated count), but violates the active + idle <= max_size invariant temporarily.

Fix: Speculatively increment active (or a creating counter) inside can_create() before releasing the lock. On factory failure, decrement. This is the standard async pool pattern.

### Finding 2: total_acquisitions decrement (KNOWN - previously reported)
Severity: Low | Line 1221

When health check fails on an idle resource, total_acquisitions is decremented via saturating_sub(1). The field is documented as Total acquisitions since pool creation (line 337) - a monotone counter. Decrementing breaks monotonicity for external observers doing periodic sampling.

### Finding 3: Redundant unsafe impl Send (STYLE)
Severity: None (correctness ok) | Lines 516-517

PooledResource has unsafe impl Send. All fields (Option R, ReturnObligation bool, mpsc Sender, Instant) auto-derive Send when R: Send. The manual impl is unnecessary but harmless.

### Finding 4: Crate uses deny not forbid
lib.rs line 50: deny(unsafe_code) - MEMORY.md previously stated forbid. The allow(unsafe_code) on pool.rs line 516 is valid because deny can be overridden by allow (forbid cannot).

### Verdict: 1 new bug (TOCTOU), 1 known issue, 2 informational. Tests (lines 1800-2515) are thorough.
