title: Sync primitives: comprehensive test suite and stress tests
description:
# Task: Comprehensive Test Suite for Sync Primitives

## Overview

After fixing the sync primitive bugs, we need comprehensive testing to:
1. Verify the fixes work correctly
2. Prevent regression
3. Stress test under load
4. Systematic concurrency testing with Loom

## Test Categories

### Unit Tests (per primitive)

#### Mutex Tests
- [ ] `test_mutex_basic_lock_unlock` - Basic acquire/release
- [ ] `test_mutex_try_lock_success` - Non-blocking acquire when unlocked
- [ ] `test_mutex_try_lock_fail` - Non-blocking returns Err when locked
- [ ] `test_mutex_contention_fifo` - Multiple waiters, verify FIFO ordering
- [ ] `test_mutex_cancel_waiting` - Cancel while waiting, verify cleanup
- [ ] `test_mutex_poison_on_panic` - Panic in guard, verify poisoned
- [ ] `test_mutex_wake_outside_lock` - Verify waker called after lock released
- [ ] `test_mutex_no_queue_growth` - Repeated poll doesn't grow waiter queue
- [ ] `test_mutex_get_mut` - Exclusive access via &mut self
- [ ] `test_mutex_into_inner` - Consume mutex and extract value

#### OwnedMutexGuard Tests
- [ ] `test_owned_guard_lock` - Arc<Mutex<T>> lock returns OwnedMutexGuard
- [ ] `test_owned_guard_try_lock` - Non-blocking owned acquire
- [ ] `test_owned_guard_deref` - Deref/DerefMut work correctly
- [ ] `test_owned_guard_drop_unlocks` - Dropping releases lock
- [ ] `test_owned_guard_poison_on_panic` - Panic poisons mutex
- [ ] `test_owned_guard_send` - OwnedMutexGuard is Send

#### Semaphore Tests
- [ ] `test_semaphore_basic_acquire_release` - Basic permit flow
- [ ] `test_semaphore_try_acquire_success` - Non-blocking when permits available
- [ ] `test_semaphore_try_acquire_fail` - Non-blocking returns Err when exhausted
- [ ] `test_semaphore_fairness_fifo` - Earlier waiters served first
- [ ] `test_semaphore_no_queue_jumping` - New arrivals don't bypass waiters
- [ ] `test_semaphore_partial_acquire` - Request more permits than available
- [ ] `test_semaphore_cancel_partial` - Cancel while waiting for permits
- [ ] `test_semaphore_add_permits` - Dynamic permit addition
- [ ] `test_semaphore_close` - Closing wakes all waiters with error
- [ ] `test_semaphore_available_permits` - Accurate permit count

#### Barrier Tests
- [ ] `test_barrier_all_arrive` - All tasks arrive and proceed
- [ ] `test_barrier_cancel_race` - Cancel right as barrier trips
- [ ] `test_barrier_leader_election` - One leader per generation
- [ ] `test_barrier_reuse` - Barrier can be used multiple times
- [ ] `test_barrier_notification_not_lost` - Woken tasks always proceed
- [ ] `test_barrier_wait_result` - BarrierWaitResult correct for leader
- [ ] `test_barrier_zero_parties` - Edge case: zero parties

#### RwLock Tests
- [ ] `test_rwlock_readers_concurrent` - Multiple readers simultaneously
- [ ] `test_rwlock_writer_exclusive` - Writer has exclusive access
- [ ] `test_rwlock_writer_preference` - Writers block new readers
- [ ] `test_rwlock_downgrade` - Write -> Read downgrade
- [ ] `test_rwlock_cancel_waiting_writer` - Cancel waiting write lock
- [ ] `test_rwlock_try_read` - Non-blocking read acquire
- [ ] `test_rwlock_try_write` - Non-blocking write acquire
- [ ] `test_rwlock_poison_on_writer_panic` - Writer panic poisons lock
- [ ] `test_rwlock_read_guard_clone` - Multiple read guards if supported

#### Notify Tests
- [ ] `test_notify_one_wakes_single` - notify_one wakes exactly one waiter
- [ ] `test_notify_all_wakes_all` - notify_all wakes all waiters
- [ ] `test_notify_before_wait` - Notify before wait is remembered (permit)
- [ ] `test_notify_no_waiters` - Notify with no waiters doesn't block
- [ ] `test_notify_cancel_waiting` - Cancel while waiting
- [ ] `test_notify_spurious_safe` - Handles spurious wakeups correctly
- [ ] `test_notify_fifo_ordering` - Waiters woken in FIFO order

#### OnceCell Tests
- [ ] `test_once_cell_get_or_init` - Initialize on first access
- [ ] `test_once_cell_get_or_try_init` - Fallible initialization
- [ ] `test_once_cell_double_init` - Second init returns existing value
- [ ] `test_once_cell_concurrent_init` - Race to initialize
- [ ] `test_once_cell_get_before_init` - Returns None before init
- [ ] `test_once_cell_get_after_init` - Returns Some after init
- [ ] `test_once_cell_into_inner` - Consume and extract value
- [ ] `test_once_cell_init_panic` - Panic during init doesn't poison

### Stress Tests (run with --ignored)

- `stress_test_mutex_high_contention` - 100 tasks x 10,000 iterations, verify exact count
- `stress_test_semaphore_fairness` - 50 tasks, measure wait distribution, no starvation
- `stress_test_barrier_rapid_cycles` - 10 tasks x 1,000 cycles, verify generations
- `stress_test_rwlock_mixed_workload` - 80% readers/20% writers, checksum verification
- `stress_test_notify_broadcast` - Producer/consumer, verify all wake
- `stress_test_once_cell_concurrent_init` - 100 threads race, one winner

### Loom Tests

- `loom_mutex_wake_outside_lock` - Verify no deadlock on waker call
- `loom_semaphore_fairness` - FIFO ordering under all interleavings
- `loom_notify_no_lost_wakeup` - Notify always reaches waiter
- `loom_once_cell_exactly_once` - Exactly one initializer runs
- `loom_barrier_all_proceed` - All waiters released together

### E2E Test Script

scripts/test_sync_primitives_e2e.sh:
1. Unit tests with RUST_LOG=debug
2. Stress tests with --release --ignored
3. Loom tests with RUSTFLAGS="--cfg loom"
4. Miri memory safety checks (if available)
5. Result aggregation and summary
6. Proper exit codes for CI integration

## Logging Requirements

- Timestamp (microseconds), Thread ID, Test name
- Operation type (acquire, release, wake, cancel)
- Duration for timing-sensitive operations
- Primitive state (queue length, permit count, generation)

## Test Infrastructure

1. Test helpers module (src/sync/test_utils.rs)
2. Property-based tests with proptest
3. Coverage tracking >90%

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] All 60+ unit tests implemented and passing
- [ ] Stress tests run 60+ seconds without failure
- [ ] Loom tests cover all critical interleavings
- [ ] Miri checks pass for memory safety
- [ ] E2E script runs in CI with proper exit codes
- [ ] Structured logging for all tests
- [ ] No clippy warnings in test code

title: Implement test oracle: all_finalizers_ran invariant checker
description:
## Purpose
Implement a test oracle that verifies the "all finalizers ran" invariant: every registered finalizer (defer_async, defer_sync, bracket cleanup) executes before its owning region closes.

## The Invariant
From asupersync_plan_v4.md:
> Finalizers run even under cancellation (masked, budgeted)

Finalizers are the cleanup guarantee - they WILL run regardless of success, failure, or cancellation.

## Finalizer Types
1. **defer_async**: Async cleanup registered with `cx.defer_async()`
2. **defer_sync**: Sync cleanup registered with `cx.defer_sync()`
3. **bracket cleanup**: Cleanup registered via `bracket(setup, action, cleanup)`

All must run in LIFO order (last registered, first to run).

## Oracle Design

```rust
pub struct FinalizerOracle {
    // Tracks finalizer registration and execution
    registrations: Vec<FinalizerRegistration>,
    executions: Vec<FinalizerExecution>,
    region_closes: Vec<(RegionId, Time)>,
}

pub struct FinalizerRegistration {
    pub finalizer_id: FinalizerId,
    pub kind: FinalizerKind,  // DeferAsync, DeferSync, BracketCleanup
    pub region: RegionId,
    pub registered_at: Time,
}

pub struct FinalizerExecution {
    pub finalizer_id: FinalizerId,
    pub started_at: Time,
    pub completed_at: Time,
    pub outcome: Outcome<(), FinalizerError>,
}

impl FinalizerOracle {
    /// Called when finalizer registered
    pub fn on_register(&mut self, id: FinalizerId, kind: FinalizerKind, region: RegionId, time: Time);
    
    /// Called when finalizer starts execution
    pub fn on_start(&mut self, id: FinalizerId, time: Time);
    
    /// Called when finalizer completes
    pub fn on_complete(&mut self, id: FinalizerId, outcome: Outcome<(), FinalizerError>, time: Time);
    
    /// Called when region closes
    pub fn on_region_close(&mut self, region: RegionId, time: Time);
    
    /// Verify all finalizers ran
    pub fn check(&self) -> Result<(), FinalizerViolation>;
}
```

## Violation Detection
```rust
pub struct FinalizerViolation {
    pub region: RegionId,
    pub unexecuted_finalizers: Vec<FinalizerId>,
    pub partial_executions: Vec<(FinalizerId, Time)>,  // Started but not completed
    pub region_close_time: Time,
}
```

A violation occurs when:
1. Region R closes at time T
2. ∃ finalizer F in R with no completion record at time ≤ T

## LIFO Order Verification
Additionally verify:
- Finalizers execute in reverse registration order
- Later-registered finalizers complete before earlier ones start

```rust
pub struct OrderViolation {
    pub out_of_order: Vec<(FinalizerId, FinalizerId)>,  // (expected_first, actual_first)
}
```

## Masked Execution Verification
Finalizers run with cancellation masked:
- Incoming cancellation does not interrupt finalizer
- Finalizer budget bounds execution time
- Oracle verifies finalizers complete even under cancellation

## Testing the Oracle
1. **Normal completion**: All finalizers run → passes
2. **Cancelled task**: Finalizers still run
3. **Nested finalizers**: Order preserved across nesting
4. **Finalizer failure**: Failed finalizer still counts as "ran"
5. **Budget exceeded**: Oracle tracks if finalizer exceeded budget
6. **Multiple finalizers**: LIFO order verified

## References
- asupersync_plan_v4.md: §4.6 Finalizers and Cleanup, §5.6 defer_async/defer_sync
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md: FINALIZE rule, masked execution

## Acceptance Criteria
- Oracle verifies every registered finalizer for a region runs exactly once (or is escalated explicitly per policy).
- Verifies LIFO ordering when applicable.
- Diagnostics include finalizer identifiers/order and the region id.
- Deterministic and integrated into E2E harness.

title: Phase 0: Semantics Types & Policy
description:
# Phase 0: Semantics Types & Policy

## Purpose
Codify the core semantic “atoms” that the runtime is built from. These types are *not* incidental—they are the engineering surface that enforces the spec’s reasoning principles:

- Outcomes form a **severity lattice** so aggregation is monotone (“worse wins”).
- Cancellation reasons have an **ordering** so multiple cancels **strengthen** deterministically.
- Budgets form a **product semiring** so limits propagate down the region tree (“stricter wins”).
- Policies define how regions aggregate and respond to child outcomes (fail-fast, supervision-like behavior).

If these are wrong, everything above them becomes confusing or unsound.

## Scope
### Outcome
- 4-valued terminal outcome: `Ok < Err < Cancelled < Panicked`.
- Must support monotone aggregation across join, region close, supervision.

### CancelReason / CancelKind
- Ordered cancel kinds (at minimum): `User < Timeout < FailFast < ParentCancelled < Shutdown`.
- **Strengthening** operation is idempotent + monotone.
- Must carry enough context for trace/debug (optional message, source, timestamp).

### Budget
- Product structure with componentwise meet (min) except priority (max):
  - deadline
  - poll quota
  - cost quota
  - priority
- Combines parent/child budgets so children cannot exceed parents.

### Policy (MISSING TODAY — MUST ADD)
Policy is required by the spec’s region semantics:
- Region close computes its terminal outcome by aggregating:
  - child outcomes
  - finalizer outcomes
  - policy-defined escalation rules

Plan-of-record policy surface:
- Default aggregation: **max severity wins**.
- Optional overrides:
  - fail-fast: error cancels siblings
  - panic handling: propagate vs isolate vs convert to error (explicitly decided)
  - cancellation handling: whether child cancellation cancels siblings

We should explicitly document which policies are part of Phase 0 versus later phases.

## Critical Spec Properties
- Monotonicity: combining information cannot make outcomes “better.”
- Determinism: repeated runs with same seed/config yield same combined results.
- Local reasoning: users can predict what happens on region close, join, and race.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Types are fully specified with:
  - ordering semantics
  - combine/strengthen semantics
  - debug/trace representation
- Property tests cover:
  - lattice laws for Outcome combine
  - idempotence/associativity/monotonicity for CancelReason strengthen
  - associativity/commutativity/idempotence for Budget meet (where applicable)
- Policy is implemented (or at least specified) sufficiently for Phase 0 region close and join/race semantics.

## Testing Strategy
- Unit tests for each type.
- Property tests for algebraic laws.
- Integration tests that validate policy effects (e.g., fail-fast cancels siblings and losers are drained).
close_reason: Implemented: Outcome<T,E> severity lattice, CancelKind/CancelReason, Budget product semiring, Policy. All in src/types/ with passing tests.

title: [EPIC-INFRA] OpenTelemetry Metrics Export
description:
## Overview

Implement OpenTelemetry metrics export for runtime observability, enabling integration with standard monitoring systems like Prometheus, Datadog, and Grafana.

## Strategic Value

**Problem Solved**: Production systems need metrics for monitoring and alerting. Without standard metrics export, operators must build custom solutions.

**Why OpenTelemetry**: OTel is the emerging standard for observability. It supports multiple backends (Prometheus, OTLP, etc.) through a single API.

**Production Requirement**: Any runtime targeting production use needs metrics. This is table stakes for enterprise adoption.

## Metrics Categories

### Runtime Metrics
- `asupersync.tasks.active` - Currently running tasks (gauge)
- `asupersync.tasks.spawned` - Total tasks spawned (counter)
- `asupersync.tasks.completed` - Tasks completed by outcome (counter, labeled)
- `asupersync.regions.active` - Currently open regions (gauge)
- `asupersync.regions.created` - Total regions created (counter)

### Timing Metrics
- `asupersync.task.duration` - Task execution time (histogram)
- `asupersync.region.lifetime` - Region open duration (histogram)
- `asupersync.scheduler.poll_time` - Time spent in poll (histogram)

### Cancellation Metrics
- `asupersync.cancellations` - Cancellation count by reason (counter, labeled)
- `asupersync.drain_duration` - Time spent in drain phase (histogram)

### Budget Metrics
- `asupersync.deadline.remaining` - Time remaining at task start (histogram)
- `asupersync.poll_quota.usage` - Poll quota utilization (histogram)

### Resource Metrics
- `asupersync.obligations.active` - Undischarged obligations (gauge)
- `asupersync.obligations.undischarged` - Obligations dropped undischarged (counter)

## Integration Design

### Feature Flag
```toml
[features]
metrics = ["opentelemetry", "opentelemetry-prometheus"]
```

### Metrics Provider
```rust
pub trait MetricsProvider: Send + Sync {
    fn task_spawned(&self, region_id: RegionId);
    fn task_completed(&self, task_id: TaskId, outcome: &Outcome<()>, duration: Duration);
```

title: Define Send task tier API and soundness rules
description:
# Send Task Tier API + Soundness Rules

## Purpose
Make the “soundness frontier” explicit:
- Phase 0 supports single-thread fibers that can borrow.
- Phase 1 adds Send tasks that may migrate across workers.

This task defines the API and rules for spawning Send tasks.

## Rules to Encode
- A migrating task must be `Send`.
- Captured data must be safe across threads:
  - either `'static`
  - or allocated in region heap and referenced via `RRef<'r, T>`.
- Cancellation and obligations semantics are identical to fibers.

## API Sketch
```rust
impl<'r> Scope<'r> {
    pub fn spawn_task<T: Send + 'r>(...) -> JoinHandle<'r, T>;
}
```

We may also model capabilities:
- `FiberCap` vs `TaskCap`

## Acceptance Criteria
- API prevents accidental unsound captures.
- Lab runtime can simulate this tier deterministically.

## Testing
- Compile-fail tests for borrowing captures in Send tasks.
- Runtime tests for cross-thread execution.

title: [EPIC-INFRA] Task Tree Visualization Dashboard
description:
# Overview

A web-based debugging dashboard that visualizes the runtime's task tree in real-time,
showing region hierarchy, task states, obligation status, cancellation flow, and
budget consumption.

## Why This Is Compelling

This is THE "killer feature" that makes structured concurrency tangible. Users can:
- SEE that their concurrent code forms a proper tree
- SEE cancellation propagate through regions
- SEE obligations being tracked and resolved
- SEE budget consumption in real-time

No other async runtime offers this visibility.

## Visual Design

```
┌─ Task Tree ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                  │
│  ▼ Region[1] root (Open, budget: ∞)                            │
│    ├─ ▼ Region[2] http_server (Open, budget: 10s)              │
│    │   ├─ Task[100] accept_loop (Running)                       │
│    │   ├─ Task[101] handle_request (Cancelling) ⚠️              │
│    │   │   └─ Obligation: SendPermit (Reserved) ⚠️              │
│    │   └─ Task[102] handle_request (Running)                    │
│    │       └─ Obligation: IoOp (Committed) ✓                    │
│    └─ ▼ Region[3] background_jobs (Draining) 🔄                │
│        └─ Task[103] cleanup (Finalizing)                        │
│                                                                  │
├─ Timeline ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  [━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━│━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━]                       │
│  10:00:00.000        now              10:00:00.500              │
│                                                                  │
│  Events:                                                         │
│  • 10:00:00.123 Task[101] CancelRequested (Timeout)             │
│  • 10:00:00.124 Region[3] Draining                              │
│  • 10:00:00.125 Task[103] Finalizing                            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Features

1. **Live Tree View**: Region/task hierarchy with real-time updates
2. **State Indicators**: Visual cues for task/region states
3. **Obligation Tracking**: Show active obligations and their states
4. **Budget Display**: Remaining time/polls for each region
5. **Event Timeline**: Scrollable history of state changes
6. **Cancellation Flow**: Animate cancellation propagation
7. **Filtering**: Filter by state, region, task name
8. **Search**: Find tasks by ID or name

## Architecture

```
┌─────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────┐
│   Runtime       │────▶│   HTTP Server   │────▶│   Web UI        │
│   (snapshots)   │     │   (optional)    │     │   (JS/HTML)     │
└─────────────────┘     └─────────────────┘     └─────────────────┘
        │                       │
        ▼                       ▼
    JSON export          WebSocket for
    for post-mortem      live updates
```

## Implementation Approach

1. **Snapshot API**: `RuntimeState::snapshot() -> RuntimeSnapshot`
2. **HTTP Server**: Optional feature with `/debug` endpoint
3. **WebSocket**: Real-time updates when dashboard is open
4. **Static Assets**: Self-contained HTML/JS/CSS
5. **Lab Export**: Export full trace for post-mortem analysis

## Dependencies

- Requires Tracing Epic (#2) for event history
- Benefits from Cancel Attribution (#10) for provenance

## Success Criteria

- [ ] Tree visualization shows correct hierarchy
- [ ] Task/region states update in real-time
- [ ] Obligations displayed with correct states
- [ ] Budget consumption visible
- [ ] Event timeline shows history
- [ ] Cancellation flow is visible
- [ ] Works in both live and post-mortem modes
- [ ] Responsive and performant

title: Implement trace compression with LZ4
description:
## Overview

Implement optional LZ4 compression for trace files to reduce storage and I/O overhead.

## Requirements

### Compression Integration
```rust
pub struct TraceFileConfig {
    /// Enable compression (default: true for large traces).
    pub compression: CompressionMode,
    
    /// Chunk size for streaming compression (default: 64KB).
    pub chunk_size: usize,
}

pub enum CompressionMode {
    None,
    Lz4 { level: i32 },  // -1 to 16, default 1
    Auto,  // Compress if > 1MB
}
```

### Streaming Compression
- Compress in chunks for memory efficiency
- Decompress on-the-fly during streaming read
- Detect compression from file header (magic bytes)

### File Format Extension
```
Header:
  Magic: "ASUPERTRACE" (11 bytes)
  Version: u16
  Flags: u16 (bit 0 = compressed)
  Compression: u8 (0=none, 1=lz4)
```

### Performance Targets
- Compression ratio: > 5x for typical traces
- Compression speed: > 500MB/s
- Decompression speed: > 1GB/s

## Acceptance Criteria
1. CompressionMode enum with None, Lz4, Auto
2. Streaming compression in TraceWriter
3. Streaming decompression in TraceReader
4. Auto-detect compression during read
5. Benchmark: compression ratio and speed
6. Optional dependency: lz4_flex (feature-gated)

## Test Requirements
- Test roundtrip with compression
- Test reading compressed with uncompressed reader (error)
- Test large trace compression ratio
- Benchmark compression vs raw speed

title: [RANDOM-AUDIT] Deep audit batch 71: bytes/bytes, bytes/bytes_mut, http/compress, http/pool, runtime/obligation_table, runtime/region_heap, types/outcome
[AUDIT] Deep correctness audit: channel/watch.rs + channel/broadcast.rs + channel/oneshot.rs
notes:
VERDICT: SOUND — 0 bugs found

## watch.rs (1,277 lines)

### Concurrency primitives: 5 patterns
- RwLock<(T, u64)>: value + version
- Mutex<usize>: receiver_count
- Mutex<bool>: sender_dropped
- Mutex<SmallVec<[WatchWaiter; 4]>>: waiters
- Arc<AtomicBool>: per-waiter queued dedup flag

### Lock ordering: receiver_count → value → waiters (consistent across all paths)
- send: receiver_count → value(write) → waiters
- poll: value(read) → waiters → value(read) [re-check]
- subscribe: receiver_count → value(read)
- No inversions.

### Lost wakeup protection (ChangedFuture::poll, line 462-545)
Check-register-recheck pattern:
1. Read version (RwLock read)
2. Register/refresh waker (waiters Mutex)
3. Re-check version (RwLock read)

If send() happens between steps 1-2: step 3 catches it.
If send() happens during step 2: wake_all_waiters wakes us (benign spurious wake).
If send() happens after step 3: waker is registered, we'll be woken.

### Waker dedup (Arc<AtomicBool> queued flag)
- First poll: create Arc<AtomicBool>(true), register WatchWaiter
- Re-poll with queued=true: refresh_waker in-place (no clone)
- Re-poll with queued=false (was woken): re-register with queued=true
- Stale pruning: Arc::strong_count(&entry.queued) == 1 → only waiters vec holds it → prune

### Cancel safety
changed() sets self.waiter = None at start (line 397), invalidating stale entries from prior cancelled futures. Version only updated on Ready return.

### Wake-outside-lock
wake_all_waiters: mem::take under lock, wake outside. Correct.

## broadcast.rs (968 lines)

### Concurrency primitives: 1
Single Mutex<Shared<T>> — all operations under one lock. No lock ordering issues.

### Arena<Waker> dedup
Arena gives generation-based ArenaIndex per waiter. Re-poll checks if token still valid (not cleared by retain). No unbounded growth.

### Lost wakeup: not possible
Check and register happen atomically under the single Mutex. Send also modifies buffer and collects wakers under the same lock.

### Waker lifecycle
- SendPermit::send: retain(false) collects all wakers, wake outside lock
- Sender::drop: if last sender, retain(false) collects all, wake outside
- Recv::drop: clear_waiter_registration removes entry. No stale wakers.

### Lag detection correct
earliest = buffer.front().index or total_sent if empty. If next_index < earliest, report Lagged(earliest - next_index), advance cursor to earliest.

## oneshot.rs (804 lines)

### Concurrency primitives: 1
Single Mutex<OneShotInner<T>>. No lock ordering issues.

### State machine: sender_consumed + receiver_dropped + permit_outstanding + value
- is_closed = sender_consumed && !permit_outstanding && value.is_none()
- is_ready = value.is_some()

### Linear type via ownership
- Sender consumed by reserve() (takes self by value)
- SendPermit tracks sent: bool
- SendPermit::drop acts as abort if !sent → obligation always resolved
- Sender::drop only sets sender_consumed if not already consumed (reserve was called)

### RecvFuture::poll order of checks
1. value.take() → Ready(Ok) — delivers available value even if cancelled
2. is_closed() → Ready(Err(Closed))
3. checkpoint → Ready(Err(Cancelled))
4. Register waker

### Wake-outside-lock
All paths: take waker under lock, wake outside. Prevents inline-executor deadlock.

No bugs found in any of the three files.

# HTTP Server/Client Verification Suite

## Purpose
Comprehensive verification for the HTTP layer (if7, hyper equivalent) ensuring protocol compliance, cancel-correctness, and performance.

## Test Categories

### 1. Unit Tests
- Request parsing: methods, headers, body
- Response construction: status, headers, body
- HTTP/1.1: keep-alive, chunked encoding, pipelining
- HTTP/2: streams, flow control, HPACK
- Connection management: pooling, reuse

### 2. E2E Scenarios
| Scenario | Verifies |
|----------|----------|
| GET request/response | Basic HTTP lifecycle |
| POST with body | Request body handling |
| Streaming response | Chunked transfer |
| Keep-alive reuse | Connection pooling |
| HTTP/2 multiplexing | Stream concurrency |
| Cancel mid-request | Client abort handling |
| Server shutdown | Graceful drain |
| Large body transfer | Memory efficiency |

### 3. Protocol Compliance Tests
- RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
- RFC 9112 (HTTP/1.1)
- RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
- Header validation
- Content-Length vs Transfer-Encoding

### 4. Performance Tests
- Requests per second baseline
- Concurrent connection handling
- Memory usage under load
- Latency distribution (p50, p95, p99)

### 5. Security Tests
- Request smuggling prevention
- Header injection prevention
- Timeout enforcement
- Resource exhaustion protection

## Logging Requirements
- HTTP events logged with request IDs
- On failure: dump connection state, pending requests
- Timing breakdown: parsing, processing, serialization

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Protocol compliance tests pass
- [ ] E2E scenarios cover HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2
- [ ] Cancel-safety verified for client and server
- [ ] Performance baselines established
- [ ] `cargo test http` passes deterministically

## Verification Commands
```bash
cargo test --package asupersync --lib http
cargo test --test http_e2e
cargo bench --bench http_perf
```

notes: VERDICT: SOUND. 0 bugs, 1 LOW finding. 1771 lines audited. Multipath symbol aggregation: TransportPath (AtomicU8 state, AtomicU64 counters, RwLock<Time> last_activity), PathSet (RwLock<HashMap>, 5 selection policies), SymbolDeduplicator (RwLock<HashMap<ObjectId, state>>, per-object HashSet seen), SymbolReorderer (RwLock<HashMap<ObjectId, state>>, BTreeMap buffer, u32 sequence tracking). No lock nesting - each component has exactly one RwLock. title: Comprehensive unit test suite for all Phase 0 components
description:
# Comprehensive Unit Test Suite

## Purpose
Provide thorough unit test coverage for all Phase 0 components with deterministic execution and high-quality diagnostics.

Core principle:
- **tests should be reproducible** (lab runtime seed/config)
- **failures should be explainable** (trace dump + invariant evidence)

## Logging / Diagnostics Strategy (No `tracing` dependency)
We avoid relying on global logging infrastructure in core tests.

Plan-of-record:
- Use the runtime’s own `TraceBuffer` + `TraceFormatter`.
- On assertion failure, dump:
  - formatted trace
  - invariant violation evidence
  - first divergence step for replay/determinism checks

This aligns with the “no stdout/stderr in core” rule while still allowing tests to print helpful debug output.

## Test Categories

### 1) Core Type Tests
- Outcome severity ordering and aggregation laws
- CancelReason ordering + strengthen laws
- Budget product semantics laws
- Identifier invariants
- Policy aggregation / fail-fast behavior

### 2) State Machine Tests
- TaskState valid/invalid transitions
- RegionState lifecycle rules
- ObligationState terminal absorption

### 3) Registry/Arena Tests
- Task/Region/Obligation arenas behave correctly
- ObligationRegistry leak detection and marking projection

### 4) Scheduler/Waker/Timer Tests
- Cancel lane priority
- Timer wake behavior
- Wake dedup invariants

### 5) Cancellation/Finalization Tests
- cancel propagation
- bounded masking
- finalizer LIFO ordering

### 6) Combinator Tests
- join/race/timeout semantics
- loser draining

### 7) Two-Phase Primitive Tests
- oneshot reserve/commit/abort
- MPSC reserve/commit + receiver ack/nack (if implemented)

## Property-Based Testing
Use `proptest` to test algebraic laws:
- Outcome lattice laws
- Budget meet laws
- CancelReason strengthen laws

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Deterministic: tests pass under fixed seeds.
2. Diagnostics: failures dump trace and evidence.
3. Coverage: all Phase 0 components have targeted unit tests.

DEPENDS ON
- Lab runtime
- Trace infrastructure

# Task: Comprehensive Test Suite for HTTP/2 Security Hardening

## Overview

After fixing the HTTP/2 security vulnerabilities, we need comprehensive testing to:
1. Verify all security fixes work correctly
2. Prevent regression of security issues
3. Fuzz test with malicious inputs
4. Verify compliance with RFC 7540/7541

## Test Categories

### Unit Tests - HPACK Decoding

#### Integer Decoding Tests
- [ ] `test_decode_integer_basic` - Standard integer values (1, 127, 128, 255)
- [ ] `test_decode_integer_max_prefix` - Values at prefix boundary (5-bit, 6-bit, 7-bit)
- [ ] `test_decode_integer_multi_byte` - Multi-byte continuation sequences
- [ ] `test_decode_integer_overflow_shift` - Shift >28 bits rejected with H2Error
- [ ] `test_decode_integer_overflow_addition` - Addition overflow rejected
- [ ] `test_decode_integer_truncated` - Incomplete input rejected (need more data)
- [ ] `test_decode_integer_max_value` - Maximum valid integer accepted
- [ ] `test_decode_integer_leading_zeros` - Redundant continuation bytes handled

#### Integer Encoding Tests
- [ ] `test_encode_integer_basic` - Standard values round-trip correctly
- [ ] `test_encode_integer_prefix_sizes` - All prefix sizes (5, 6, 7, 8 bits)
- [ ] `test_encode_integer_boundary` - Values at 2^N-1 boundaries

- [ ] `test_huffman_all_symbols` - Full alphabet (0x00-0xFF) coverage

#### Huffman Encoding Tests

### Security Stress Tests

```rust
}

#[test]

    // Verify pending settings queue bounded
```

### E2E Test Script

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# scripts/test_http2_security_e2e.sh

set -euo pipefail

SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
PROJECT_ROOT="$(dirname "$SCRIPT_DIR")"
LOG_DIR="$PROJECT_ROOT/test_logs/http2_$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)"
mkdir -p "$LOG_DIR"

echo "=== HTTP/2 Security E2E Test Suite ==="
echo "Log directory: $LOG_DIR"
echo "Start time: $(date -Iseconds)"

# Run HPACK unit tests
echo ""
echo "[1/7] Running HPACK unit tests..."
RUST_LOG=debug cargo test --lib h2::hpack -- --nocapture 2>&1 | tee "$LOG_DIR/hpack_tests.log"
HPACK_EXIT=${PIPESTATUS[0]}

# Run frame parsing tests
echo ""
echo "[2/7] Running frame parsing tests..."
RUST_LOG=debug cargo test --lib h2::frame -- --nocapture 2>&1 | tee "$LOG_DIR/frame_tests.log"
FRAME_EXIT=${PIPESTATUS[0]}

# Run connection state machine tests
echo ""
echo "[3/7] Running connection tests..."
RUST_LOG=debug cargo test --lib h2::connection -- --nocapture 2>&1 | tee "$LOG_DIR/connection_tests.log"
CONNECTION_EXIT=${PIPESTATUS[0]}

# Run security stress tests
echo ""
echo "[4/7] Running security stress tests (timeout: 300s)..."
timeout 300s cargo test --lib --release h2_security_stress -- --ignored --nocapture 2>&1 | tee "$LOG_DIR/stress_tests.log"
STRESS_EXIT=${PIPESTATUS[0]}

# Run fuzz tests (limited iterations for CI)
echo ""
echo "[5/7] Running fuzz tests (60s each target)..."
if command -v cargo-fuzz &>/dev/null; then
    for target in fuzz_hpack_decode fuzz_frame_parse fuzz_huffman_decode fuzz_settings_frame; do
        echo "Fuzzing $target..."
        timeout 60s cargo +nightly fuzz run "$target" -- -max_total_time=60 2>&1 | tee "$LOG_DIR/fuzz_${target}.log" || true
    done
    FUZZ_EXIT=0
else
    echo "cargo-fuzz not available, skipping fuzz tests"
    FUZZ_EXIT=0
fi

# Check for memory leaks with valgrind
echo ""
echo "[6/7] Checking for memory leaks..."
if command -v valgrind &>/dev/null; then
    cargo test --lib h2::hpack::tests --release --no-run 2>/dev/null
    TEST_BIN=$(find target/release/deps -name "asupersync-*" -type f -executable | head -1)
    if [ -n "$TEST_BIN" ]; then
        valgrind --leak-check=full --error-exitcode=1 "$TEST_BIN" --test hpack 2>&1 | tee "$LOG_DIR/valgrind.log" || true
    fi
else
    echo "Valgrind not available, skipping"
fi

# Generate summary
echo ""
echo "[7/7] Generating summary..."
cat > "$LOG_DIR/summary.md" << EOF
# HTTP/2 Security Test Report

## Date: $(date -Iseconds)

## Test Results

| Suite | Status |
|-------|--------|
| HPACK | $([ $HPACK_EXIT -eq 0 ] && echo "✅ PASS" || echo "❌ FAIL") |
| Frame Parsing | $([ $FRAME_EXIT -eq 0 ] && echo "✅ PASS" || echo "❌ FAIL") |
| Connection | $([ $CONNECTION_EXIT -eq 0 ] && echo "✅ PASS" || echo "❌ FAIL") |
| Stress Tests | $([ $STRESS_EXIT -eq 0 ] && echo "✅ PASS" || echo "❌ FAIL") |
| Fuzz Tests | $([ $FUZZ_EXIT -eq 0 ] && echo "✅ PASS" || echo "⚠️ SKIPPED") |

## Failures

$(grep -hE "(FAILED|panicked|ERROR)" "$LOG_DIR"/*.log 2>/dev/null || echo "None")

## Coverage

$(grep -hE "^test result:" "$LOG_DIR"/*.log 2>/dev/null || echo "N/A")
EOF

cat "$LOG_DIR/summary.md"

echo ""
echo "End time: $(date -Iseconds)"
echo "Logs saved to: $LOG_DIR"
```

title: [ALIEN-CS][Hedge] AdaptiveHedgePolicy via Marginal Conformal Prediction
description:
Design and implement the `AdaptiveHedgePolicy` leveraging Marginal Conformal Prediction to eliminate magic threshold values in latency hedging.

Background and Rationale:
- The `Hedge` combinator is designed to cap P99 tail latency by speculatively firing a backup task when the primary exceeds a deadline.
- Static delays are a critical failure mode: if set too high, the system absorbs tail latency; if set too low, the system suffers from a thundering herd of redundant backup tasks, worsening congestion.
- Conformal Prediction allows us to compute the exact upper prediction bound (1-alpha) from a sliding window of recent primary latencies without assuming any underlying probability distribution (e.g., Gaussian vs heavy-tailed).

Implementation Constraints & Specifications:
1. **State Maintenance**: Maintain a fast, allocation-free (or pre-allocated) sliding window of recent primary execution latencies.
2. **Conformal Algorithm**: Calculate the empirical quantile using the exact conformal rank formula: `Rank = ceiling((n + 1) * (1 - alpha))`.
3. **Safe-mode/Fallback**: Implement hard `min_delay` and `max_delay` clamps. If fewer than 10 samples exist, deterministically fall back to `max_delay` to avoid premature hedging.
4. **Isomorphism Proof**: Ensure the underlying `Hedge` combinator semantics remain unchanged; only the policy determining the `HedgeConfig` delay changes.
5. **Testing Requirements**: Add unit tests verifying the conformal math (e.g., given a uniform 1-100ms distribution and alpha=0.05, the bound is exactly 96ms) and testing the clamp behavior.

Adoption Wedge:
- Shipped as an opt-in policy struct (`AdaptiveHedgePolicy`) alongside the existing `HedgeConfig` to allow progressive adoption and A/B benchmarking.

Proof Artifacts & Reproducibility:
- Unit tests acting as executable math proofs for the conformal ranking logic.
- Documentation inline explaining the assumptions (exchangeability) and the exact derivation.

title: Implement TraceRecorder for Lab runtime
description:
## Overview

Implement the TraceRecorder that instruments the Lab runtime to emit trace events during execution.

## Background

Once we have the TraceEvent schema, we need to hook into Lab runtime's decision points to capture events without adding significant overhead.

## Design Requirements

### Low Overhead
- Recording should not significantly slow down test execution
- Use buffered writes
- Consider memory-mapped file for large traces

### Non-Invasive
- Lab runtime code changes should be minimal
- Use callback/observer pattern
- Recording should be opt-in (disabled by default)

### Thread-Safe
- Handle recording from multiple Lab runtime threads
- Use lock-free structures where possible

## Implementation Approach

```rust
pub struct TraceRecorder {
    events: Vec<TraceEvent>,
    metadata: TraceMetadata,
    enabled: bool,
}

impl TraceRecorder {
    pub fn new(config: RecorderConfig) -> Self;
    pub fn record(&mut self, event: TraceEvent);
    pub fn finish(self) -> RecordedTrace;
}

// In Lab runtime, add hooks:
impl LabRuntime {
    pub fn with_recorder(config, recorder: TraceRecorder) -> Self;
}
```

## Integration Points

1. `Scheduler::pick_next_task()` - record choice
2. `VirtualClock::advance()` - record time changes
3. `SimulatedIo::complete()` - record I/O results
4. `DeterministicRng::next()` - record RNG values

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] TraceRecorder captures all TraceEvent variants
- [ ] Recording adds < 5% overhead to test execution
- [ ] Events are captured in correct causal order
- [ ] Integration with Lab runtime is clean and minimal
- [ ] Unit tests verify recording correctness

title: [ALIEN][TRACE][HOMO] Spec: commutation complex proxy + filtration + scoring
description:
## Purpose

Define a concrete, implementable notion of "topological novelty" for schedule exploration.

We want a deterministic function `score(node)` that ranks which exploration node (seed/backtrack) to run next.

## Mathematical model (practical)

- Start from a trace poset (events + dependency edges) and independence relation.
- Build a 2D square complex proxy:
  - 1-cells represent adjacent swaps of independent events (local commutations)
  - 2-cells (squares) represent commuting squares (swap a then b == swap b then a)

This captures classic concurrency shapes; deadlock-like patterns often create persistent cycles.

## Filtration

Define a filtration parameter `t` (monotone):
- prefix length (steps)
- commutation depth
- or "budget" of swaps

Complex K_t includes cells observable/derivable from a prefix up to t.

## Scoring

We will compute H1 persistence over GF(2) on this filtered complex and derive a score:
- novelty: introduces a new long-lived class
- persistence: birth/death interval length
- stability: deterministic tie-break by fingerprint

## Acceptance criteria

- The spec defines exactly what cells exist, what filtration is used, and what score is computed.
- It states performance bounds and explicit fallback when analysis is too expensive.
close_reason: Completed spec: local commutation proxy, prefix filtration, H1 persistence scoring, deterministic ranking, bounds + fallback.

(6) JSONL rotation — write entries until rotation threshold (100MB or 1 hour), verify new file created with schema version header, old file correctly closed.
(7) Zstd compression — verify that compressed rotated files decompress to identical content as uncompressed originals.
(8) Concurrent writer safety — spawn 10 threads writing simultaneously; verify no interleaved lines, no data corruption, all entries recoverable.
(9) Galaxy-brain Level 0 — verify one-liner format contains action, expected loss, and calibration score.
(10) Galaxy-brain Level 1 — verify paragraph format contains all summary fields in human-readable layout.
(11) Galaxy-brain Level 2 — verify ASCII histogram is generated for posterior distribution with correct bin widths.

**Integration tests:**

# Task

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text: MEDIUM severity. In BufferFuture::poll (src/service/buffer.rs:276), mem::replace sets state to Done before calling inner.poll_ready(cx), inner.call(req), or Pin::new(&mut future).poll(cx). If any of these panic, the Drop impl sees Done and skips the pending-count decrement, permanently leaking a buffer slot. After capacity such panics, the buffer is permanently full. title: Spec reconciliation: budget exhaustion as CancelReason vs Error
description:
# Spec Reconciliation: Budget Exhaustion as CancelReason vs Error

## Purpose
The design introduces budgets with multiple components (deadline, poll quota, cost quota) and relies on budgets for cancellation completeness and bounded cleanup.

We need a clear, user-facing story for what happens when a budget component is exhausted:
- Is it represented as `Outcome::Cancelled(CancelReason::...)`?
- Is it represented as `Outcome::Err(ErrorKind::...)`?
- Does it depend on which component is exhausted?

The current beads mention:
- `ErrorKind::{DeadlineExceeded, PollQuotaExhausted, CostQuotaExhausted}`
- E2E scenarios expecting a “BudgetExhausted” trace marker
- The formal semantics enumerates cancel kinds without an explicit “BudgetExhausted” kind

This task resolves the mismatch and sets the plan-of-record semantics.

## Design Options
### Option A: Budget exhaustion => Cancelled
- Extend `CancelKind` with explicit variants:
  - `BudgetDeadlineExceeded` (or keep `Timeout`)
  - `PollQuotaExhausted`
  - `CostQuotaExhausted`
- Pros: uniform cancellation protocol; easy to reason about “why stopped”.
- Cons: expands cancel-kind surface; needs careful ordering.

### Option B: Budget exhaustion => Err
- Keep `CancelKind` minimal; treat budget exhaustion as an error outcome.
- Pros: cancel kinds remain small.
- Cons: conflates “stopped by runtime limits” with application errors.

### Option C: Mixed
- Deadline => `CancelKind::Timeout`
- Quotas => `ErrorKind::{PollQuotaExhausted, CostQuotaExhausted}`

## Plan-of-Record Recommendation (tentative)
Prefer **Option A** (budget exhaustion as cancellation) because it aligns with:
- cancellation as a protocol
- explicit “reason” for termination
- monotone aggregation (Cancelled is more severe than Err)

If we adopt Option A, update:
- CancelKind ordering
- trace event fields
- tests (unit + e2e)

## Acceptance Criteria
- A single documented decision is recorded in this issue.
- Dependent beads are updated to match (CancelReason, Error strategy, scheduler budget enforcement, E2E scenario expectations).
close_reason: Decision: Option C (Mixed) adopted. Deadline => CancelKind::Timeout (via timeout combinator). Poll/Cost quotas are enforced at scheduler level but surfaced as explicit errors when exceeded in user code, not automatic cancellation. CancelKind enum kept minimal. This aligns with implementation where timeout races against sleep and budget is advisory/propagated.

title: [SUB-EPIC-PHASE] io_uring Reactor (Linux Modern Async I/O)
description:
# Sub-Epic: io_uring Reactor

## Overview

io_uring is Linux's modern async I/O interface (kernel 5.1+), offering significant performance advantages over epoll for certain workloads.

## Why io_uring

1. **True async**: Operations complete in kernel, no syscall per I/O
2. **Batching**: Submit multiple operations with single syscall
3. **Zero-copy**: Can use registered buffers
4. **Lower latency**: Kernel polling mode avoids context switches

## Scope

This sub-epic covers:
- IoUringReactor implementing Reactor trait
- Submission/completion queue management
- Buffer registration for zero-copy
- Polled mode for latency-critical paths

## Design Decisions

### When to Use io_uring vs epoll

| Use Case | Recommended |
|----------|-------------|
| Many idle connections | epoll (lower memory) |
| High throughput file I/O | io_uring |
| Network with many small ops | io_uring (batching) |
| Compatibility (old kernels) | epoll |

### Feature Detection

```rust
fn has_io_uring() -> bool {
    // Check kernel version >= 5.1
    // Try io_uring_setup() and check for features
}
```

## Dependencies

```toml
[target.'cfg(target_os = "linux")'.dependencies]
io-uring = "0.6"  # Safe Rust wrapper
```

## Task Breakdown

1. IoUringReactor core structure
2. Submission queue management
3. Completion queue processing
4. Register/deregister implementation
5. Probing for supported operations
6. Buffer registration API
7. Polled mode option
8. Fallback to epoll on old kernels

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] IoUringReactor implements Reactor trait
- [ ] Passes same tests as EpollReactor
- [ ] Graceful fallback when unavailable
- [ ] Benchmark shows improvement for applicable workloads
close_reason: io_uring Reactor fully implemented in src/runtime/reactor/io_uring.rs. IoUringReactor implements Reactor trait (register/modify/deregister/poll/wake). 25+ integration tests pass. Feature-gated (io-uring). Graceful fallback for non-Linux. All acceptance criteria verified.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text: Initial scan: Reactor trait in src/runtime/reactor/mod.rs expects register/modify/deregister/poll/wake with Token + Interest. EpollReactor (epoll.rs) implements via polling crate with token->fd bookkeeping; kqueue.rs similar. There is an unused linux.rs stub with outdated Reactor signature (returns Registration) — likely ignore/replace. Integration points: runtime/state.rs + io_driver.rs tests currently instantiate EpollReactor on Linux; io_uring should be optional (feature/cfg) and likely selected via builder/explicit choice with fallback to epoll when unavailable.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text: Doc notes (io-uring crate): IoUring::new(entries) requires power-of-two queue size; IoUring::builder() exists for custom params. PollAdd opcode can poll an fd; it is one-shot by default and can be multi-shot via .multi(true) (kernel 5.13+), with CQE flag IORING_CQE_F_MORE indicating more events. PollAdd::new takes flags from poll.h and builds an Entry; user_data can carry Token for completion mapping. (See docs.rs io-uring and PollAdd)

title: Obligation leak detection: runtime enforcement and diagnostics
description:
# Obligation Leak Detection

## Goal

Implement comprehensive runtime detection and diagnostics for obligation leaks, ensuring the 'no obligation leaks' invariant is enforceable.

## Background

Asupersync's obligation system tracks linear resources:
- SendPermit: Reserved channel slot
- Ack: Message acknowledgement
- Lease: Remote resource claim
- IoOp: Pending I/O operation

Obligations MUST be resolved (committed or aborted) before the holder completes. A 'leak' is when a task completes while still holding an obligation.

## Current State

The codebase has:
- ObligationRecord in src/record/obligation.rs
- Various dialect implementations (dialectica, graded, guarded, etc.)
- Placeholder leak detection

Missing:
- Runtime enforcement on task completion
- Diagnostic messages with source locations
- Integration with all obligation types
- Lab oracle for testing

## Detection Points

### 1. Task Completion
When a task reaches terminal state, check for held obligations.

### 2. Region Close
When a region closes, all tasks must have resolved obligations.

### 3. Cancellation Drain
During cancellation, obligations must be resolved in drain phase.

## Diagnostic Information

ObligationLeakError includes:
- task: TaskId that leaked
- obligations: Vec<LeakedObligation>
- completion: CompletionReason

LeakedObligation includes:
- id: ObligationId
- kind: ObligationKind
- acquired_at: SourceLocation (file, line, column)
- acquire_trace: Option<Backtrace> (debug mode)
- held_duration: Duration

## Acquisition Tracking

Use #[track_caller] to capture source locations:
```rust
impl ObligationRegistry {
    #[track_caller]
    pub fn reserve(&mut self, kind: ObligationKind, holder: TaskId) -> ObligationId {
        let location = std::panic::Location::caller();
        // ... create record with location
    }
}
```

## Leak Responses

- Debug Mode: Panic with full diagnostic
- Release Mode: Convert to Outcome::Panicked, log warning
- Lab Mode: Record in trace, available via oracle

## ObligationLeakOracle

```rust
pub struct ObligationLeakOracle {
    leaks: Vec<ObligationLeakError>,
}

impl Oracle for ObligationLeakOracle {
    fn check(&self, runtime: &RuntimeState) -> OracleResult {
        if self.leaks.is_empty() {
            OracleResult::Pass
        } else {
            OracleResult::Fail(format\!(...))
        }
    }
}
```

## Test Directory Structure

```
tests/
├── obligation/
│   ├── mod.rs
│   ├── unit/
│   │   ├── registry.rs           # Reserve/commit/abort
│   │   ├── source_location.rs    # #[track_caller] works
│   │   └── leak_detection.rs     # Detection logic
│   ├── integration/
│   │   ├── task_completion.rs    # Leak on task complete
│   │   ├── region_close.rs       # Leak blocks region close
│   │   ├── cancellation.rs       # Drain resolves obligations
│   │   └── oracle.rs             # Oracle integration
│   └── e2e/
│       ├── channel_permit.rs     # SendPermit scenarios
│       ├── multi_obligation.rs   # Multiple obligations
│       └── nested_regions.rs     # Obligations in nested regions
```

## Logging Requirements

```rust
error\!(
    event = 'obligation_leak',
    task_id = %task_id,
    obligation_id = %ob.id,
    kind = ?ob.kind,
    acquired_at = %ob.acquired_at,
    held_duration_ms = ob.held_duration.as_millis(),
    'Obligation leaked on task completion'
);
```

## Test Cases

### Unit Tests
- reserve() returns ObligationId
- commit() resolves obligation
- abort() resolves obligation
- #[track_caller] captures correct location

### Integration Tests
- Task completes with obligation -> leak detected
- Task aborts obligation correctly -> no leak
- Region close with leaked obligation -> blocked
- Cancellation with obligation -> drain must resolve

### E2E Tests
- SendPermit in channel operations
- Multiple obligations from same task
- Nested regions with obligations

## Test Script

`scripts/test_obligations.sh`:
```bash
#\!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

LOG_DIR='./test_logs/obligations'
mkdir -p "$LOG_DIR"

echo '=== Obligation Unit Tests ==='
RUST_LOG=debug cargo test --test obligation_unit -- --nocapture 2>&1 | tee "$LOG_DIR/unit.log"

echo '=== Obligation Integration Tests ==='
RUST_LOG=info cargo test --test obligation_integration -- --nocapture 2>&1 | tee "$LOG_DIR/integration.log"

echo '=== Obligation E2E Tests ==='
RUST_LOG=info cargo test --test obligation_e2e -- --nocapture 2>&1 | tee "$LOG_DIR/e2e.log"

# Check for any leaked obligations in logs
if grep -q 'obligation_leak' "$LOG_DIR/"*.log; then
    echo 'WARNING: Found obligation leaks in test logs\!'
    grep 'obligation_leak' "$LOG_DIR/"*.log
fi

echo 'All obligation tests passed\!'
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Detection on task completion
- [ ] Detection on region close
- [ ] ObligationLeakError with full diagnostics
- [ ] SourceLocation tracking via #[track_caller]
- [ ] Optional stack trace capture
- [ ] ObligationLeakOracle for testing
- [ ] Configurable leak response (panic/log/silent)
- [ ] Forced abort on budget exhaustion
- [ ] All test files created with structured logging
- [ ] Test script runs with log capture
close_reason: All acceptance criteria met: task/region leak detection, ObligationLeakError diagnostics, SourceLocation+track_caller, backtrace capture, ObligationLeakOracle (3 tests passing), configurable response, forced abort on cancel. 257-line oracle + full state.rs integration.

title: Budget monitor: real-time budget consumption across regions
description:
# Budget Monitor

## Overview
Real-time dashboard for monitoring budget consumption across all regions,
with alerts, trends, and exhaustion prediction.

## Design

### Budget Monitor
```rust
pub struct BudgetMonitor {
    state: Arc<RuntimeState>,
    console: Console,
    history: BudgetHistory,
}

impl BudgetMonitor {
    /// Get current budget status for all regions.
    pub fn status(&self) -> Vec<RegionBudgetStatus> {
        self.state.all_regions()
            .map(|r| RegionBudgetStatus {
                region_id: r.id(),
                region_name: r.name(),
                total: r.budget().total(),
                remaining: r.budget().remaining(),
                consumed: r.budget().consumed(),
                percent_used: r.budget().percent_used(),
                exhaustion_eta: self.predict_exhaustion(&r),
            })
            .collect()
    }
    
    /// Predict when a region will exhaust its budget.
    fn predict_exhaustion(&self, region: &Region) -> Option<Duration> {
        let history = self.history.get(region.id());
        let rate = history.consumption_rate()?;
        let remaining = region.budget().remaining();
        
        if rate > 0.0 {
            Some(Duration::from_secs_f64(remaining as f64 / rate))
        } else {
            None
        }
    }
    
    /// Get budget breakdown by resource type.
    pub fn breakdown(&self, region_id: RegionId) -> BudgetBreakdown {
        let region = self.state.get_region(region_id);
        BudgetBreakdown {
            ops: region.budget().ops_consumed(),
            bytes: region.budget().bytes_consumed(),
            time: region.budget().time_consumed(),
            connections: region.budget().connections_consumed(),
        }
    }
}
```

### Output Format
```
Budget Monitor
╭─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ Region                     Budget          ETA     Rate        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Root (Region-0)           ████████░░  80%   -       -          │
│ ├─ HttpServer (Region-1)  ███████░░░  70%  12m     58 ops/s    │

│ │  └─ Request-2           ██░░░░░░░░  20%   2m    180 ops/s    │

├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ⚠️  ALERTS:                                                     │
│   Request-2 will exhaust budget in ~2m at current rate         │
│   Request-1 consumption rate increasing (+15% last 30s)        │
╰─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

Budget Breakdown: Request-2 (Region-3)
╭────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ Resource          Used    /   Total    │
├────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Operations        8,234   /  10,000    │
│ Bytes            12.3 MB  /  50 MB     │
│ Time              2.1s    /   5s       │

╰────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

### Historical Trends

title: Implement map_reduce combinator (monoid-based aggregation)
description:
# map_reduce (Monoid-Based Parallel Aggregation)

## Purpose
Provide a derived combinator that expresses parallel map followed by reduction under an associative operation (monoid). This is called out explicitly as a derived combinator in the design.

## Semantics
- Spawn N tasks that each compute a partial result.
- Join all.
- Reduce results using an associative combine function.

## Requirements
- Must preserve structured concurrency: no detached work.
- Cancellation:
  - If the parent region cancels, all children cancel/drain.
  - If a child errors and policy is fail-fast, siblings cancel/drain.
- Deterministic lab runtime behavior (for a fixed schedule/seed).

## API Sketch
```rust
pub async fn map_reduce<I, F, T>(
    scope: &Scope<'_>,
    inputs: I,
    map: impl Fn(I::Item) -> F,
    reduce: impl Fn(T, T) -> T,
) -> Outcome<T>
where
    I: IntoIterator,
    F: Future<Output = Outcome<T>>,
{
    // spawn map futures
    // join_all
    // reduce
}
```

## Notes
- Reduction order may affect determinism if `reduce` is not commutative; we must define the reduction order (e.g., input order) and document it.

## Acceptance Criteria
- All tasks complete or are cancelled/drained before return.
- Reduction order is documented and deterministic.

## Testing
- Unit test with associative reduce.
- Negative test demonstrating non-associative reduce yields schedule-dependent results (documented).
close_reason: Implemented MapReduce<T> marker type, MapReduceResult/MapReduceError types, map_reduce_outcomes/make_map_reduce_result/map_reduce_to_result/reduce_successes functions with comprehensive tests. All 23 tests pass.

description: Implement the JSONL exporter for the EvidenceLedger in franken_evidence. The exporter writes one JSON object per line to an append-only file, enabling efficient offline replay and analysis of runtime decisions. Implementation: (1) JsonlExporter struct with buffered file writer, (2) Append-only semantics -- never modify existing lines, (3) Atomic flush -- use write + fsync to prevent partial lines on crash, (4) Rotation -- support file rotation by size (default 100MB) or time (default 1 hour), (5) Compression -- optional zstd streaming compression for rotated files, (6) Schema version header -- first line of each file is a schema version record. Performance targets: <1us per record append, <10MB/hour at 1000 decisions/second. Must handle concurrent writers, disk full, and crash recovery. DEBUG: JSONL entry written: offset={byte_offset}, size={entry_bytes}, flush_latency_us={lat}. INFO: JSONL file rotated: reason={reason}, old_file={path}, old_size={bytes}, entries_written={n}. WARN: JSONL write latency exceeded threshold: latency_us={lat}, threshold_us={thresh} -- indicates I/O contention. WARN: disk space low: available_bytes={avail}, threshold_bytes={thresh}. ERROR: JSONL write failed: error={err}, dropping entry (no blocking). ERROR: crash recovery: partial last line detected at offset={offset}, skipping {bytes} bytes. Metrics: jsonl_write_latency_us (histogram), jsonl_entries_written_total (counter), jsonl_bytes_written_total (counter), jsonl_rotation_total (counter by reason), jsonl_write_errors_total (counter), jsonl_crash_recovery_skipped_bytes (counter).

title: Implement internal Arena<T> utilities for runtime records
description:
# Internal Arena<T> Utilities

## Purpose
Phase 0 needs stable, compact IDs and fast lookup for runtime records:
- regions
- tasks
- obligations

We want the benefits of a slab/arena without bringing in external crates unless necessary.

## Design Requirements
- Deterministic behavior (no hash-randomized iteration relied on for semantics)
- O(1) insert/get/get_mut by ID
- Clear policy about ID reuse (reuse allowed only after safe removal; documented)
- Ergonomic newtype IDs (e.g., `TaskId(u32)`) with explicit conversion

## Plan-of-Record Design
### Arena storage
Use a `Vec<Option<T>>` plus a free list:
- `slots: Vec<Option<T>>`
- `free: Vec<u32>`

Insert:
- if `free` non-empty, pop index and fill
- else push new slot

Remove:
- set slot to None
- push index to free list

### ID types
- `RegionId`, `TaskId`, `ObligationId` are newtypes around `u32`.
- Reserve `0` as root region if desired (explicit constant).

### Safety / invariants
- All public APIs that accept an ID must validate existence (in debug/lab) or be carefully audited.
- Removal rules must be documented:
  - Phase 0 may keep records forever (no removal) to simplify.
  - If we do remove, it must only happen after quiescence/closure.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `Arena<T>` supports:
  - `insert -> Id`
  - `get/get_mut`
  - `contains`
  - `iter` for debugging
- Unit tests validate:
  - no accidental reuse while still live
  - removed IDs become invalid
  - insertion after removals reuses indices (if we choose reuse)

## Notes
We should avoid depending on iteration order of arenas for semantics. If order matters for determinism, we must explicitly sort by IDs or use ordered structures.

title: [ALIEN-CS][Scheduler] Power of Two Choices Work Stealing
description:
Replace linear-probe work stealing with the Power of Two Choices randomized load-balancing algorithm.

Background and Rationale:
- The current `steal_task` implementation uses a random starting index and sequentially probes all `Stealer` instances.
- Under high load, linear probing heavily contends on locks (even short-lived ones) and isn't optimal at finding the most congested queue quickly.
- Michael Mitzenmacher's 'Power of Two Choices' (2001) proves that selecting exactly *two* random queues and choosing the lesser-loaded (or in our case, stealing from the *more* loaded) exponentially reduces maximum queue length variance from O(log n / log log n) to O(log log n).

Implementation Constraints & Specifications:
1. **O(1) Length Oracle**: Add an `inline` `len()` method to `Stealer` that briefly locks the queue to read its length without executing a full steal protocol.
2. **Stochastic Control Logic**: In `steal_task`, pick two random, distinct stealers. Query both lengths. Attempt to steal from the one with the larger `len`. 
3. **Fallback Policy**: If the primary choice yields no task (e.g., lock contended or tasks are strictly local/unstealable), immediately attempt the secondary choice. If both fail, gracefully fall back to a linear scan to ensure no work is orphaned.
4. **Isomorphism Proof**: The fundamental invariants of work-stealing (no lost tasks, strict adherence to `is_local` locality flags) must remain intact.

Adoption Wedge:
- In-place replacement of the `steal_task` function since it strictly improves the runtime's internal load-balancing without altering public APIs.

Proof Artifacts & Reproducibility:
- Deterministic test scenarios must demonstrate that with a fixed RNG seed, the correct larger queue is chosen.
- Linear fallback must be proven to engage if both choices fail.
close_reason: Implemented already (power-of-two steal policy + tests in place); no additional code delta required in this slice.

description:
# Cross-Project Coordination Protocol

## Objective
Establish communication and dependency management protocols between the Asupersync and fastapi_rust projects.

## Background

### Why Cross-Project Coordination?
- fastapi_rust depends on Asupersync APIs
- API changes in Asupersync can break fastapi_rust
- Shared development benefits from synchronized planning
- Bug reports may span both projects

## Requirements

### 1. Communication Channels

#### Beads Thread Prefix
All integration-related beads use thread_id prefix:
- `fastapi-asupersync-integration`

Example:
```
bd create --title="[fastapi-integration] ..." --thread=fastapi-asupersync-integration
```

#### Agent Mail Threads
For async agent coordination:
- Thread: `fastapi-asupersync-sync`
- Subject format: `[fastapi-asupersync] <topic>`

### 2. Dependency Management

#### Cargo.toml Pattern
```toml
# In fastapi_rust/Cargo.toml

[dependencies]
# During development: path dependency
asupersync = { path = "../asupersync" }

# For release: crates.io with version
# asupersync = "0.1"
```

#### Version Pinning Strategy
- fastapi_rust pins Asupersync to minor version: `"0.1"`
- Breaking changes require coordination before release
- Pre-release testing with git dependency

### 3. API Stability Contract

#### Stable APIs (semver guaranteed)
- `Cx` capability token
- `Outcome` type and variants
- `Budget` type and methods
- Core combinators (join, race, timeout)

#### Unstable APIs (may change)
- Internal scheduler details
- Lab runtime internals
- Platform-specific I/O backends

### 4. Shared Type Considerations

#### Option A: Re-export
fastapi_rust re-exports Asupersync types:
```rust
// In fastapi_rust
pub use asupersync::{Outcome, Budget, Cx};
```

#### Option B: Thin API Crate
Create `asupersync-api` crate with just types:
```
asupersync-api/
├── Outcome
├── Budget
├── CancelReason
└── Error types
```

Both asupersync and fastapi_rust depend on asupersync-api.

#### Recommendation
Start with Option A (re-export), consider Option B if:
- Multiple downstream projects need shared types
- Compile times become an issue
- Need to decouple version cycles

### 5. Breaking Change Protocol

When Asupersync makes a breaking change:
1. Open bead in both projects
2. Document migration path
3. fastapi_rust tests against branch BEFORE merge
4. Coordinate release timing

### 6. Bug Report Protocol

Cross-project bugs:
1. Determine root cause location
2. File bead in appropriate project
3. Link beads if fix spans both projects
4. Coordinate testing

### 7. Sync Meetings (if needed)

For complex coordination:
- Ad-hoc via Agent Mail thread
- Decision log in bead comments

## Deliverables
1. [ ] Thread naming convention documented
2. [ ] Cargo.toml pattern documented
3. [ ] API stability classification documented
4. [ ] Breaking change protocol documented
5. [ ] Bug report protocol documented

## References
- AGENTS.md: Agent coordination via beads and Agent Mail
- Cargo documentation: dependency specifications

title: Implement test oracle: quiescence_on_close invariant checker
description:
## Purpose
Implement a test oracle that verifies the "quiescence on close" invariant: when a region closes, it has achieved complete quiescence - no live children, all finalizers run, all obligations resolved.

## The Invariant
From asupersync_plan_v4.md:
> Region close = quiescence: no live children + all finalizers done

This is the foundational guarantee of structured concurrency. A region close is a HARD synchronization point.

## Quiescence Components
Quiescence requires ALL of:
1. **No live tasks**: All tasks in Completed state
2. **No live subregions**: All subregions Closed
3. **All finalizers run**: defer_async and defer_sync complete
4. **All obligations resolved**: No pending SendPermit, Ack, Lease, IoOp

## Oracle Design

```rust
pub struct QuiescenceOracle {
    // Tracks region state
    region_states: HashMap<RegionId, RegionSnapshot>,
}

pub struct RegionSnapshot {
    pub tasks: Vec<(TaskId, TaskState)>,
    pub subregions: Vec<(RegionId, RegionState)>,
    pub finalizers: Vec<(FinalizerId, FinalizerState)>,
    pub obligations: Vec<(ObligationId, ObligationState)>,
}

impl QuiescenceOracle {
    /// Take snapshot of region state
    pub fn snapshot(&mut self, region: RegionId, snapshot: RegionSnapshot);
    
    /// Called when region transitions to Closed
    pub fn on_close(&mut self, region: RegionId, time: Time);
    
    /// Verify quiescence at close
    pub fn check_quiescence(&self, region: RegionId) -> Result<(), QuiescenceViolation>;
}
```

## Violation Types
```rust
pub enum QuiescenceViolation {
    LiveTasks { region: RegionId, tasks: Vec<TaskId> },
    OpenSubregions { region: RegionId, subregions: Vec<RegionId> },
    PendingFinalizers { region: RegionId, finalizers: Vec<FinalizerId> },
    UnresolvedObligations { region: RegionId, obligations: Vec<ObligationId> },
}
```

## Close Protocol Verification
The oracle verifies the close protocol from the spec:
```
CLOSE-PEND:   Live(r) = ∅ ⟹ r.state := ClosePending
CLOSE-FINAL:  r.state = ClosePending ∧ FinalizersRan(r) ⟹ r.state := FinalDone  
CLOSE-DONE:   r.state = FinalDone ∧ Quiescent(r) ⟹ r.state := Closed
```

Each transition has preconditions; oracle verifies they hold.

## Recursive Verification
For nested regions:
1. Inner regions must close before outer can close
2. Oracle tracks region tree
3. Close of region R implies close of all descendants first

## Testing the Oracle
1. **Clean close**: All components quiescent → passes
2. **Live task violation**: Task still running at close attempt
3. **Open subregion violation**: Subregion not closed
4. **Pending finalizer violation**: Finalizer not run
5. **Unresolved obligation violation**: Obligation in Created state
6. **Nested regions**: Verify recursive quiescence

## Integration with Scheduler
Oracle hooks:
- Region state transitions (Open → ClosePending → FinalDone → Closed)
- Task state transitions
- Finalizer execution events
- Obligation resolution events

## References
- asupersync_plan_v4.md: §4.2 Region Lifecycle, §1.1 Non-negotiable invariants
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md: CLOSE-* rules, Quiescent predicate

## Acceptance Criteria
- Oracle verifies region close implies quiescence: no live tasks, all subregions closed, all obligations resolved, all finalizers done.
- Diagnostics identify the exact remaining live items (tasks/regions/obligations/finalizers).
- Deterministic and usable both on Σ snapshots and trace projections.

RUST IMPLEMENTATION GUIDANCE: (1) Use FrankenLab's deterministic scheduler with random seed generation: let seed = rand::thread_rng().gen::<u64>(); (2) Test program: a realistic workload with multiple concurrent tasks, channels, obligations, cancellation, and budget propagation. At minimum: 10 tasks, 5 channels, 3 obligation types, 1 cancellation event, budget propagation through 3 levels. (3) For each of 1000 iterations: (a) Generate random seed, (b) Run workload under Lab scheduler with recording, (c) Capture output hash (SHA-256 of all observable side effects: task return values, channel message order, obligation lifecycle events), (d) Replay from recorded trace, (e) Capture replay output hash, (f) Assert record_hash == replay_hash. (4) Use rayon::par_iter for parallel execution of the 1000 iterations. (5) Store all seeds and hashes in a results CSV for analysis.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: (1) 100% replay determinism: all 1000 iterations produce identical record/replay hashes. (2) Test completes in < 10 minutes on CI (parallelized). (3) Any replay divergence produces a detailed diff showing the first diverging event with full context. (4) Test is itself deterministic: running the test with the same meta-seed produces the same 1000 sub-seeds. (5) Cross-platform: hashes are identical on x86_64 and aarch64 (floating-point determinism verified).

LOGGING REQUIREMENTS: Per-iteration structured JSON log: iteration_index, seed, record_hash, replay_hash, match (bool), record_time_ms, replay_time_ms, event_count. Summary log at completion: total_iterations, match_count, mismatch_count, determinism_rate (target 1.0), total_wall_time_ms, avg_replay_overhead_percent. On divergence: full event-level diff with timestamps, task IDs, and event types for both record and replay traces. All logs emitted to both stdout (CI visible) and JSONL file for offline analysis.

TESTING APPROACH: (1) Smoke test: single iteration with known seed, verify manually computed expected hash. (2) Regression: if any iteration ever fails, add its seed to a pinned regression set that runs on every CI build. (3) Statistical: track determinism rate over time in a dashboard -- any rate below 1.0 is a P0 bug.

title: Local Task Safety & spawn_local Completion
description:
Goal: make spawn_local safe and fully scheduled under ThreeLane without !Send tasks ever leaving their origin worker. Resolve correctness gaps: no scheduling, illegal moves in is_local, cross-worker stealing, cancel promotion parity, and local waiter wakeups. Add tests and docs to lock the invariant.

Background: spawn_local currently stores tasks in TLS without enqueueing; LocalQueue::schedule_local exists. Local tasks can be stolen from ready lanes, violating !Send. Local cancel path does not promote already-queued tasks unlike global cancel. Completion currently wakes waiters via global queue, risking wrong-worker wakeups for local waiters.

Definition of done:
- spawn_local schedules onto a non-stealable local lane.
- !Send local tasks never cross worker boundaries.
- Cancellation promotion for local tasks matches global behavior.
- Local waiters are awakened on their owner worker.
- All tests/linters pass; regression tests added.
- Unit/regression tests explicitly assert local-task invariants (non-steal, cancel parity, waiter routing).
- E2E test script with structured logging (seed, worker id, queue sizes, local task count) proves no cross-worker leakage; run with --nocapture.
acceptance_criteria:
1. spawn_local schedules onto a non-stealable local lane; no cross-worker execution for !Send tasks.
2. Cancellation promotion for local tasks matches global behavior; local waiter routing uses owner worker.
3. Unit/regression tests assert local-task invariants (non-steal, cancel parity, waiter routing, and progress under local scheduling only).
4. E2E lab test script with structured logs (seed, worker id, queue sizes, local task count) proves no cross-worker leakage; run with --nocapture.
5. All gates pass: cargo fmt --check, cargo check --all-targets, cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings, cargo test (and --nocapture for new E2E).

## Random Module Audit Complete (IvoryPrairie)

### Bugs Fixed

1. **Modulo bias in `DetRng::next_usize`** (`det_rng.rs:56`)
   - Was: `(self.next_u64() as usize) % bound` — introduces statistical bias
   - Fix: Rejection sampling (matching the correct implementation in `Cx::random_usize`)

2. **`DetHasher::write_u64` violated Hasher contract** (`det_hash.rs:41-43`)
   - Was: Single-step `mul ^ value` — differs from `write(&val.to_ne_bytes())` which does 8 separate steps
   - Fix: Removed specializations; all writes go through the correct `write` path
   - Added regression test: `det_hasher_write_u64_consistent_with_write`

3. **`ThreadLocalEntropy::for_thread` produced correlated seeds when global_seed=0** (`entropy.rs:152`)
   - Was: `0.wrapping_mul(constant) = 0`, so thread seeds became `0, 1, 2, ...`
   - Fix: Use additive golden ratio constant + `mix_seed()` for proper avalanche
   - Added regression test: `thread_local_entropy_zero_seed_not_correlated`

4. **Misleading `DetHashMap` doc comment** (`det_hash.rs:69`)
   - Was: "reproducible iteration order across runs" — false for HashMap
   - Fix: Corrected to "deterministic hashing" with note to use BTreeMap for ordered iteration

- All 40 util tests pass (including 2 new regression tests)
- Full lib suite: 4781 passed, 0 failed

# Phase 4: Distributed Trace (Causal Ordering + Convergent State)

## Purpose
Make distributed traces honest:
- represent time as a partial order (causal ordering), not a fake total order
- ensure obligation/lease state converges across replicas via join-semilattice rules

This is required for replay/debugging and for making distributed structured concurrency coherent.

## Core Elements
- Vector clocks (or equivalent causal metadata)
- Trace events that include node identity and causal metadata
- Obligation/lease state lattice with explicit conflict states

## Acceptance Criteria
- Trace metadata supports causal ordering (vector clocks or equivalent) so concurrent remote events remain unordered.
- Obligation/lease state converges via a join-semilattice (CRDT-style) with explicit conflict detection.
- Lab simulation can replay distributed traces deterministically up to the causal model.

description:
# Task: Benchmark Suite for Scheduler Performance

## Overview

After performance improvements, we need comprehensive benchmarks to:
1. Measure baseline performance metrics
2. Track performance regression on every PR
3. Compare against alternatives (Tokio, async-std, smol)
4. Validate fairness guarantees statistically
5. Profile for optimization opportunities

## Benchmark Categories

### Micro-benchmarks

#### Queue Operations
- [ ] `bench_priority_scheduler_push_empty` - Insert into empty queue
- [ ] `bench_priority_scheduler_push_100` - Insert into 100-item queue
- [ ] `bench_priority_scheduler_push_10000` - Insert into 10000-item queue
- [ ] `bench_priority_scheduler_pop` - Dequeue from queue
- [ ] `bench_local_queue_push_pop` - Worker-local queue cycle
- [ ] `bench_global_queue_push` - Global queue insertion
- [ ] `bench_global_queue_drain` - Drain batch from global
- [ ] `bench_work_stealing_solo` - Steal with no contention
- [ ] `bench_work_stealing_contended` - Multiple stealers

#### Synchronization Operations
- [ ] `bench_parker_park_unpark_solo` - No contention park/unpark
- [ ] `bench_parker_park_unpark_contended` - High contention scenario
- [ ] `bench_condvar_signal` - Signaling overhead
- [ ] `bench_wake_state_transition` - Atomic state changes
- [ ] `bench_try_lock_success` - Uncontended try_lock
- [ ] `bench_try_lock_failure` - Contended try_lock

#### Task Operations
- [ ] `bench_task_create` - Task allocation cost
- [ ] `bench_task_schedule` - Push to scheduler
- [ ] `bench_task_poll_noop` - Poll empty future
- [ ] `bench_task_poll_yield` - Poll future that yields
- [ ] `bench_waker_wake` - Waker invocation cost
- [ ] `bench_waker_clone` - Waker cloning cost

### Macro-benchmarks

#### Throughput Benchmarks
- [ ] `bench_throughput_empty_10k` - 10K empty tasks, measure tasks/sec
- [ ] `bench_throughput_empty_100k` - 100K empty tasks
- [ ] `bench_throughput_yielding_1k` - 1K tasks, 10 yields each
- [ ] `bench_throughput_yielding_10k` - 10K tasks, 10 yields each
- [ ] `bench_throughput_cpu_bound` - CPU-intensive tasks
- [ ] `bench_throughput_mixed` - 70% yield, 30% CPU-bound
- [ ] `bench_throughput_chained` - Tasks spawn subtasks

#### Latency Benchmarks
- [ ] `bench_latency_spawn_to_poll` - Time from spawn() to first poll
- [ ] `bench_latency_wake_to_poll` - Time from wake() to re-poll
- [ ] `bench_latency_idle_to_run` - Task on idle worker start time
- [ ] `bench_latency_steal_to_run` - Task stolen, time to run
- [ ] `bench_latency_p50_p99_p999` - Full latency distribution

#### Fairness Benchmarks
- [ ] `bench_fairness_equal_priority` - Variance in execution count
- [ ] `bench_fairness_priority_ratio` - Higher priority gets more CPU
- [ ] `bench_fairness_starvation_max_wait` - Max wait time < 10x average
- [ ] `bench_fairness_worker_balance` - Work distributed evenly

#### Concurrency Scaling Benchmarks
- [ ] `bench_scale_workers_1` - Single worker baseline
- [ ] `bench_scale_workers_4` - 4 workers
- [ ] `bench_scale_workers_8` - 8 workers
- [ ] `bench_scale_workers_16` - 16 workers
- [ ] `bench_scale_workers_ncpu` - Number of CPUs
- [ ] `bench_scale_efficiency` - Throughput per worker

#### Memory Benchmarks
- [ ] `bench_memory_task_overhead` - Bytes per task
- [ ] `bench_memory_scheduler_idle` - Idle scheduler footprint
- [ ] `bench_memory_scheduler_loaded` - 10K pending tasks
- [ ] `bench_memory_worker_overhead` - Per-worker memory
- [ ] `bench_memory_allocation_rate` - Allocations/sec under load

### Comparative Benchmarks

```rust
// Compare against Tokio
#[bench]
fn bench_vs_tokio_spawn_throughput() {
    // Same workload, measure relative performance
    // Report: asupersync_ops/sec, tokio_ops/sec, ratio
}

#[bench]
fn bench_vs_tokio_latency_p99() {
    // Same workload, compare p99 latency
}

#[bench]
fn bench_vs_async_std_spawn_throughput() {
    // Compare against async-std
}

#[bench]
fn bench_vs_smol_spawn_throughput() {
    // Compare against smol
}
```

### Regression Test Suite

```rust
// Run on every PR to catch regression
#[test]
fn regression_throughput_baseline() {
    warm_up();
    let ops = measure_throughput_10k_empty();
    let baseline = BASELINE_THROUGHPUT;
    let threshold = baseline * 0.9; // Allow 10% regression
    
    assert!(ops >= threshold,
        "Throughput regression: {} ops/sec < {} (baseline {} * 0.9)\n\
         This PR reduces throughput by {:.1}%",
        ops, threshold, baseline,
        (1.0 - ops as f64 / baseline as f64) * 100.0
    );
}

#[test]
fn regression_latency_p99() {
    warm_up();
    let p99 = measure_p99_latency_us();
    let baseline = BASELINE_P99_LATENCY_US;
    let threshold = baseline * 1.2; // Allow 20% regression
    
    assert!(p99 <= threshold,
        "P99 latency regression: {}us > {} (baseline {} * 1.2)\n\
         This PR increases p99 latency by {:.1}%",
```
