comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# Spork "Application" Layer (OTP-style, region-compiled)

OTP's killer feature is not only supervisors; it's that *applications* are the unit of deployment/ops.

Spork needs an explicit application layer so users (and coding agents) can:

- define a top-level tree of supervised services
- start/stop it with deterministic semantics
- get a single handle for shutdown (close => quiescence)
- integrate with lab harness + crash artifacts without extra wiring

## Design: Compile an AppSpec to a Root Region

An application is a *region-owned* tree.

- `AppSpec` defines the topology: supervisors + child specs + registry wiring.
- `App::start(cx)` allocates a root region (or uses an existing one) and boots the tree.
- `AppHandle::stop(cx)` requests cancel on the root region and waits for quiescence.

Key property vs OTP:
- In OTP, a supervision tree can outlive the call site if you're sloppy.
- In Spork, the tree is *owned* by a region and must close to quiescence.

## Deterministic Start/Stop Contracts

We need explicit ordering contracts so that lab replay and DPOR exploration are meaningful:

- deterministic child start order (stable sort key)
- deterministic stop ordering (reverse-topo or spec-defined)
- deterministic DOWN/EXIT delivery ordering during shutdown

## Observability + Agent Workflow

App start/stop must automatically attach:

- trace collection
- crashpack builder hooks
- evidence ledger root (so supervisors can explain restarts)

The goal: a coding agent can run a single scenario and get:
- a stable report fingerprint
- minimal repro artifacts

## Acceptance Criteria

- API supports a minimal `AppSpec` + `AppHandle` path for real apps.
- Integration tests prove:
  - close => quiescence
  - no task leaks / obligation leaks
  - deterministic ordering of start/stop side effects
- Lab harness can run an app spec as a scenario.

title: Message queue E2E test suite: NATS/Redis/Kafka integration tests
description:
# Message Queue E2E Test Suite

## Overview
Comprehensive end-to-end test suite for all message queue clients (NATS, Redis, Kafka)
with cancel-correctness verification and structured logging.

## Test Directory Structure
```
tests/e2e/mq/
├── mod.rs                       # Test module root
├── common/
│   ├── mod.rs                   # Shared utilities
│   ├── docker.rs                # Docker service management
│   └── assertions.rs            # Message queue assertions
├── nats/
│   ├── pubsub.rs                # Pub/sub tests
│   ├── request_reply.rs         # Request/reply pattern
│   ├── jetstream.rs             # JetStream durability
│   └── cancel.rs                # Cancellation tests
├── redis/
│   ├── commands.rs              # Basic command tests
│   ├── pubsub.rs                # Pub/sub tests
│   ├── streams.rs               # Streams consumer groups
│   └── cancel.rs                # Cancellation tests
├── kafka/
│   ├── producer.rs              # Producer tests
│   ├── consumer.rs              # Consumer group tests
│   ├── transactions.rs          # Transactional tests
│   └── cancel.rs                # Cancellation tests
└── lab/
    ├── deterministic.rs         # Lab runtime tests
    └── schedule_exploration.rs  # DPOR tests
```

## Docker Compose Setup
```yaml
version: '3.8'
services:
  nats:
    image: nats:latest
    ports:
      - "4222:4222"
    command: ["-js"]  # Enable JetStream
    
  redis:
    image: redis:7
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"
    
  kafka:
    image: confluentinc/cp-kafka:latest
    ports:
      - "9092:9092"
    environment:
      KAFKA_BROKER_ID: 1
      KAFKA_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://0.0.0.0:9092
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://localhost:9092
      KAFKA_OFFSETS_TOPIC_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      
  zookeeper:
    image: confluentinc/cp-zookeeper:latest
    environment:
      ZOOKEEPER_CLIENT_PORT: 2181
```

## Test Categories

### 1. Basic Functionality
- NATS: connect, publish, subscribe, wildcard
- Redis: GET/SET, HGET/HSET, EXPIRE
- Kafka: produce, consume, seek

### 2. Durability Tests
- NATS JetStream: persist, replay
- Redis Streams: consumer groups, ack
- Kafka: offset commit, rebalance

### 3. Cancel-Correctness Tests
- Subscription cancelled mid-receive
- Producer cancelled mid-send
- Consumer cancelled with uncommitted messages
- Region close with active connections

### 4. Backpressure Tests
- Slow consumer with fast producer
- Bounded queues fill up
- Credit window exhaustion

### 5. Lab Runtime Tests
- Deterministic message ordering
- Simulated network delays
- Partition simulation

## Logging Requirements

### Log Fields
```rust
tracing::info\!(
    test_name = %test_name,
    mq_type = %"nats",
    operation = %"publish",
    subject = %subject,
    message_count = count,
    latency_ms = latency.as_millis(),
    "Message queue operation"
);
```

### Metrics Collection
- Publish latency histogram
- Consume latency histogram
- Message throughput (msg/sec)
- Backpressure events
- Reconnection count

## Test Scripts

### Start Services
```bash
#\!/bin/bash
cd tests/e2e/mq
docker-compose up -d

# Wait for services
echo "Waiting for NATS..."
until nc -z localhost 4222; do sleep 1; done

echo "Waiting for Redis..."
until nc -z localhost 6379; do sleep 1; done

echo "Waiting for Kafka..."
until nc -z localhost 9092; do sleep 1; done

echo "All services ready"
```

### Run Tests
```bash
#\!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

export RUST_LOG="asupersync=debug,test=info"
export NATS_URL="nats://localhost:4222"
export REDIS_URL="redis://localhost:6379"
export KAFKA_BROKERS="localhost:9092"

echo "=== Message Queue E2E Tests ==="

# Run tests by MQ type
for mq in nats redis kafka; do
    echo "--- Testing $mq ---"
    cargo test -p asupersync --test e2e_mq $mq:: -- --test-threads=1 --nocapture 2>&1 | tee $mq_tests.log
done

echo "=== Summary ==="
grep -E '(PASS|FAIL|test result)' *_tests.log
```

title: Implement ObligationState and ObligationKind enums
description:
# ObligationState and ObligationKind Enums

## Purpose
These types define the two-phase effect system's tracking of linear resources. Obligations are tokens that MUST be resolved (committed or aborted) before their owning region closes.

## ObligationKind
```rust
enum ObligationKind {
    // Channel send permit (reserve capacity, then send)
    SendPermit,
    
    // Message acknowledgment (receive, process, then ack/nack)
    Ack,
    
    // Time-bounded resource lease (must renew or expire)
    Lease,
    
    // In-flight I/O operation (must complete or cancel)
    IoOp,
}
```

## ObligationState
```rust
enum ObligationState {
    // Obligation created, waiting for resolution
    Reserved,
    
    // Obligation fulfilled (effect took place)
    Committed,
    
    // Obligation cleanly cancelled (no effect)
    Aborted,
    
    // ERROR: Obligation lost (holder completed without resolving)
    Leaked,
}
```

## State Transitions

```
Reserved ──────► Committed
    │
    ├──────────► Aborted
    │
    └──────────► Leaked (error state, detected by runtime)
```

All three terminal states (Committed, Aborted, Leaked) are absorbing - once reached, no further transitions.

## Why These Obligation Kinds?

### SendPermit
Two-phase channel send prevents message loss under cancellation:
```rust
let permit = tx.reserve(cx).await?;  // Reserve capacity (cancel-safe)
permit.send(message);                 // Commit: actually send
// OR drop permit → Aborted (capacity released, no message lost)
```

### Ack
Two-phase receive with acknowledgment for reliable messaging:
```rust
let (item, ack) = rx.recv_with_ack(cx).await?;  // Receive but don't dequeue
process(item);
ack.commit();  // Dequeue permanently
// OR drop ack → Aborted (nack, message redelivered)
```

### Lease
Time-bounded resource ownership:
```rust
let lease = resource.lease(duration, cx).await?;
// Use resource...
lease.renew(duration);  // Extend lease
// OR lease expires → Aborted (resource released)
```

### IoOp
In-flight I/O operations bound to region:
```rust
let op = io.submit_read(buffer, cx).await?;  // Submit (region can't close yet)
let result = op.complete().await;             // Wait for completion
// OR op.cancel() → Aborted (I/O cancelled)
```

## ObligationState Semantics

### Reserved
- Obligation exists and must be resolved
- Blocks region close (quiescence requires zero reserved obligations)
- Shows up in obligation registry under holder's region

### Committed
- The effect took place successfully
- E.g., message was sent, ack was committed, I/O completed
- This is the "happy path" resolution

### Aborted
- The effect was cleanly cancelled
- No data loss, no side effects
- Capacity/resources released back
- This is the "safe cancellation" path

### Leaked
- ERROR STATE: Holder completed without resolving
- This indicates a bug in user code or library
- In lab mode: panic immediately
- In prod mode: log error, attempt recovery, continue
- Triggers futurelock detection

## Linear Resource Discipline

Obligations are LINEAR resources in the logic sense:
```
reserve : Cx → Obligation<K, 1>      // Introduce obligation
commit  : Obligation<K, 1> → Cx → () // Eliminate obligation
abort   : Obligation<K, 1> → Cx → () // Eliminate obligation
```

The `1` annotation means "exactly one use." Dropping without explicit resolution is detected and triggers Leaked.

## VASS/Petri Net View

For verification, obligations can be modeled as a vector addition system:
```
marking(r, k) = count of Reserved obligations of kind k in region r

reserve(k) → marking += 1
commit/abort(k) → marking -= 1
region_close requires marking = 0 for all kinds
```

## Implementation Requirements

1. **Both enums must be Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq**
2. **ObligationKind should have Display** for tracing
3. **ObligationState::is_terminal()**: Returns true for Committed/Aborted/Leaked
4. **ObligationState::is_resolved()**: Returns true for Committed/Aborted (not Leaked)
5. **ObligationState::is_error()**: Returns true only for Leaked

## Drop Semantics

When an obligation token is dropped:
- If Reserved → transition to Aborted AND emit trace event
- If already terminal → no-op

In lab mode, dropping a Reserved obligation can optionally panic (configurable).

## Testing Requirements

1. All terminal states are absorbing
2. Leaked is only reachable from Reserved
3. Committed/Aborted are mutually exclusive endpoints
4. Obligation tracking correctly counts per-region

## Invariant Support

### INV-OBLIGATION-BOUNDED
```rust
∀o: O[o].state = Reserved ⟹
    T[O[o].holder].state ∈ {Running, CancelRequested, Cancelling, Finalizing}
```

### INV-OBLIGATION-LINEAR
```rust
∀o: O[o].state ∈ {Committed, Aborted, Leaked} is absorbing
```

### I2: Region close = quiescence
```rust
R[r].state = Closed(_) requires
    ∀o where O[o].region = r: O[o].state ≠ Reserved
```

## Example Usage

```rust
// Two-phase send
let permit: SendPermit<T> = tx.reserve(cx).await?;
// permit.obligation_state() == Reserved

if should_send {
    permit.send(value);  // → Committed
} else {
    drop(permit);  // → Aborted
}

// If cx is cancelled and permit dropped without explicit resolution:
// → Aborted (safe default)
```

## References
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §1.7 (Obligation States)
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §3.4 (Obligations transitions)
- asupersync_plan_v4.md §8 (Two-phase effects + linear obligations)

## Acceptance Criteria
- Defines `ObligationKind` and `ObligationState` per the spec (Reserved/Committed/Aborted/Leaked).
- States are absorbing after resolution (Committed/Aborted/Leaked).
- Implements deterministic, trace-friendly formatting.
- Unit tests cover state ordering (if any), absorbing behavior, and conversions used by the registry.

title: Implement scheduler with cancel/timed/ready lanes
description:
# Scheduler with Cancel/Timed/Ready Lanes

## Purpose
The scheduler is the runtime’s execution engine. It decides which task to poll next under a lane priority system that is required for cancel-correctness and predictable shutdown.

## Lane Priority (Non-Negotiable)
1. **Cancel lane** (highest): tasks in cancel/drain/finalize protocol
2. **Timed lane** (middle): tasks with deadlines (EDF-ish)
3. **Ready lane** (lowest): normal runnable tasks

This ordering is essential for:
- bounded cancellation drain
- ensuring region close reaches quiescence

## Data Model (Sketch)

```rust
pub struct SchedulerState {
    cancel_queue: VecDeque<TaskId>,
    timed_queue: BinaryHeap<TimedEntry>,
    ready_queue: VecDeque<TaskId>,

    timers: TimerHeap,

    /// Membership set for dedup (order not relied on).
    queued: HashSet<TaskId>,
}

pub struct TimedEntry {
    task_id: TaskId,
    deadline: Time,
}
```

## Key Operations
### schedule(task_id)
- Dedup: if already queued, do nothing.
- Choose lane based on task state + budget deadline.

### pick_next(now)
- Prefer cancel lane.
- Otherwise consider timed lane vs ready lane (policy-driven fairness).
- Never starve cancel lane.

### wake(task_id)
- Only schedule if task is pollable.

## Wake Dedup
Wake dedup is required to avoid:
- queue blowup
- nondeterministic behavior from duplicate scheduling

Phase 0 can use a simple `woken` flag in `TaskRecord` plus scheduler membership set.

## Timers
Timer expiration produces wake events that feed back into scheduling.

## Deterministic Lab Tie-Breaking
When multiple tasks are equally eligible, the lab runtime must break ties deterministically.

Constraint: we must not introduce `rand` or OS entropy.

Plan-of-record:
- accept a `&mut DetRng` (internal PRNG) in lab-mode pick logic
- never rely on iteration order of hash structures for selection

## Budget Interaction
- Deadlines: timed lane ordering.
- Poll quotas/cost quotas: define enforcement semantics (may trigger cancellation or yielding). This must be consistent with the “budget exhaustion” decision bead.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Cancel lane always wins over timed/ready.
- Timer expiration wakes tasks deterministically.
- Lab runs are deterministic given the same seed/config.

## Testing
- Unit tests for lane priority and EDF ordering.
- E2E tests showing cancellation drains quickly and deterministically.

title: Phase 1+: Min-plus network calculus budgets (hard bounds)
description:
# Phase 1+: Min-Plus Network Calculus Budgets (Hard Bounds)

## Purpose
The design calls for upgrading scalar budgets (deadlines/quotas) into arrival/service curves in the min-plus semiring to provide provable backlog and latency bounds.

This is explicitly described as “required for hard bounds” and impacts:
- admission control
- backpressure
- buffer sizing

## Deliverables
- Curve representation types.
- min-plus convolution operations.
- integration points for scheduler/admission control.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Small demonstrator computing backlog/delay bounds for a simple pipeline.

title: [ALIEN][LAB][HOMO] Integrate scoring into exploration queue (priority scheduling)
description:
## Purpose

Replace or augment naive seed-sweep exploration with prioritized exploration.

## Integration approach

- Introduce an exploration frontier (priority queue) of nodes:
  - seeds
  - DPOR backtrack points (future)
  - targeted perturbations

- Pop next node by `(score, tie_break)`.

## Determinism constraints

- Priority queue ordering must be stable.
- Scoring must never consult wall-clock.

## Acceptance criteria

- Explorer can run in two modes:
  - baseline (seed sweep)
  - topology-prioritized
- Both modes remain deterministic.
close_reason: Explorer has both baseline (seed-sweep) and topology-prioritized modes. BinaryHeap frontier with TopologicalScore ordering. ExplorationMode enum, ExplorerConfig with mode flag. All exploration deterministic (no wall-clock). Tests verify both modes.

title: Setup project structure (Cargo.toml, modules, lib.rs)
description:
# Setup Project Structure (Cargo.toml, modules, lib.rs)

## Purpose
Create the initial Cargo crate and a *minimal, Phase-0-aligned* module layout that supports deterministic implementation and testing.

This task must respect the repo’s constraints:
- **No unsafe code** (`#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`)
- **Cargo only** (no other package managers)
- **Minimal dependencies** (avoid rand/tracing/etc. unless justified)
- **No file proliferation**: create files when they carry real functionality, not just placeholders

## Recommended Phase 0 Layout (minimal but extensible)

```
asupersync/
├── Cargo.toml
├── rust-toolchain.toml              # if we choose to pin toolchain
├── src/
│   ├── lib.rs
│   ├── error.rs
│   ├── util/
│   │   ├── mod.rs
│   │   ├── det_rng.rs               # deterministic PRNG (no rand)
│   │   └── arena.rs                 # internal Arena<T> for records
│   ├── types/
│   │   ├── mod.rs
│   │   ├── id.rs                    # RegionId, TaskId, ObligationId, Time
│   │   ├── outcome.rs               # Outcome severity lattice
│   │   ├── cancel.rs                # CancelReason/CancelKind (+ strengthen)
│   │   ├── budget.rs                # Budget product semantics
│   │   └── policy.rs                # Policy (aggregation/escalation)
│   ├── record/
│   │   ├── mod.rs
│   │   ├── task.rs                  # TaskRecord
│   │   ├── region.rs                # RegionRecord
│   │   └── obligation.rs            # ObligationRecord + registry
│   ├── trace/
│   │   ├── mod.rs
│   │   ├── event.rs                 # TraceEvent / TraceData
│   │   ├── buffer.rs                # TraceBuffer (ring)
│   │   └── format.rs                # formatting for tests/debug
│   ├── runtime/
│   │   ├── mod.rs
│   │   ├── state.rs                 # Σ = {regions,tasks,obligations,now}
│   │   ├── scheduler.rs             # 3-lane scheduler
│   │   ├── waker.rs                 # Waker (std::task::Wake) + wake dedup (no unsafe)
│   │   └── timer.rs                 # timer heap
│   ├── cx/
│   │   ├── mod.rs
│   │   ├── cx.rs                    # Cx trait + impls
│   │   └── scope.rs                 # Scope API
│   ├── combinator/
│   │   ├── mod.rs
│   │   ├── join.rs
│   │   ├── race.rs
│   │   └── timeout.rs
│   └── lab/
│       ├── mod.rs
│       ├── config.rs                # LabConfig
│       ├── runtime.rs               # LabRuntime loop
│       └── replay.rs                # replay/diff helpers
└── tests/
    ├── unit/                        # module-level unit tests
    └── e2e/                         # scenario tests (deterministic)
```

Notes:
- We **do not** pre-create Phase 2–5 modules here. Those should be added when their beads are started.
- The `util/` modules are intentionally explicit so we do not “accidentally” introduce heavy dependencies.

## Cargo.toml (Phase 0 defaults)

Goals:
- keep dependencies minimal
- keep determinism
- keep lints strict

Suggested starting point:

```toml
[package]
name = "asupersync"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"
license = "MIT"

[lib]
path = "src/lib.rs"

[dependencies]
# Phase 0: prefer std/core; avoid bringing in executors/runtimes.

[dev-dependencies]
proptest = "1.4"

[lints.rust]
unsafe_code = "forbid"
missing_docs = "warn"
unused = "warn"

[lints.clippy]
pedantic = "warn"
nursery = "warn"
module_name_repetitions = "allow"
must_use_candidate = "allow"
```

If we later want compile-fail tests (session types), add `trybuild` as a dev-dependency in the Phase 3 bead.

## lib.rs

```rust
#![forbid(unsafe_code)]
#![warn(missing_docs)]
#![warn(clippy::pedantic)]
#![warn(clippy::nursery)]

pub mod error;

pub mod util;
pub mod types;
pub mod record;
pub mod trace;
pub mod runtime;
pub mod cx;
pub mod combinator;
pub mod lab;

pub use types::{Budget, CancelKind, CancelReason, Outcome, Policy, RegionId, TaskId, ObligationId, Time};
pub use cx::{Cx, Scope};
pub use lab::{LabConfig, LabRuntime};
```

## Acceptance Criteria
1. `cargo check --all-targets` passes.
2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` passes.
3. `cargo fmt --check` passes.
4. `cargo test` runs (even if empty initially).

## Why This Is User-Friendly
- The module structure mirrors the runtime’s mental model (types → records → runtime → user API → lab).
- Determinism utilities are explicit and dependency-free.
- Tests have a clear home and are expected from day 1.
close_reason: Completed: Project structure set up with all modules, Cargo.toml configured, all quality gates pass (check, clippy, fmt, test)

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## Why

Without an explicit ordering contract, "works on my machine" interleavings will bleed into:
- trace fingerprints
- crashpack divergence
- DOWN/EXIT semantics
- supervisor restart decisions

This task makes ordering a *spec artifact* rather than incidental iteration order.

## Deliverable

A written contract (spec + tests) covering:

- App child start order: stable key derived from `ChildSpec` (name/id) + explicit tiebreaks.
- Stop/drain order: deterministic and explainable (reverse-topo or stable postorder).
- System message delivery order during shutdown:
  - DOWN delivery ordering
  - EXIT delivery ordering
  - timeout delivery ordering

## Dependencies

- Must align with `bd-12qan` deterministic ordering contracts.

## Acceptance

- Contract is referenced by:
  - supervisor conformance tests
  - monitor/link conformance tests
  - app harness trace canonicalization
- Unit tests lock the ordering (no accidental changes).

Goal: update scheduler and local queues to lock TaskTable instead of RuntimeState.

- Worker `execute` and LocalQueue `push/pop/steal` are hot; they only need task access.
- Narrowing lock scope is the main contention win.

- Update helper functions in `src/runtime/scheduler/three_lane.rs` that currently lock RuntimeState for task access.

Acceptance Criteria:
- No RuntimeState lock in worker execute path or LocalQueue hot path.
- Functionality preserved: task wake/dedup, local task invariants, cancellation promotion.
- Add targeted unit/regression tests + structured logs (seed, worker count, queue path) to prove TaskTable-only locking on hot paths.

title: Implement futurelock detector (lab/debug)
description:
# Futurelock Detector (lab/debug)

## Purpose
Detect and surface the design-rule violation:

> Never allow a primitive to stop being polled while holding an obligation without transferring it, aborting/nacking it, or escalating.

In practice this shows up as a *futurelock*: a task holds one or more unresolved obligations (permits/acks/leases/IoOps) but is no longer being polled (e.g. it awaited something that never wakes, or it was dropped/forgotten by a buggy primitive).

Phase 0 needs this in **lab/debug** mode so we can turn “subtle deadlocks/leaks” into deterministic test failures with actionable evidence.

## Spec Background
- Design Bible §8.6: “Futurelock detector”
- Operational Semantics §1.9 + §3.4: obligations are linear; leaks are semantic errors
- Key invariant: a region cannot close while obligations in the region remain `Reserved`

A futurelock is *strictly worse* than a normal leak:
- a leak is “task completed while holding obligation”
- a futurelock is “task *didn’t* complete, but is also no longer being polled, so it can’t resolve the obligation”

## Design (Plan-of-Record)
### Observable behavior
When enabled, the lab runtime MUST:
1. Detect tasks that hold ≥1 `Reserved` obligations and have not been polled for a bounded number of lab steps (configurable).
2. Emit a trace-visible event with enough context to debug.
3. Optionally fail-fast (panic) in lab mode when the threshold is exceeded.

### Data we need
- `last_polled_step: u64` per task (updated every time we poll the task).
- Ability to query “held obligations” per task (from the obligation registry).
- Global `step_counter: u64` in the lab runtime.

### Detection rule
On each lab step (or at least whenever the scheduler makes progress):
- For each task `t` that currently holds ≥1 `Reserved` obligation:
  - if `step_counter - last_polled_step(t) > futurelock_max_idle_steps` then `futurelock_detected(t, …)`.

We should explicitly ignore tasks that are already terminal.

### Trace model
Add a semantic trace event (names flexible):
- `TraceEvent::FuturelockDetected { task: TaskId, region: RegionId, idle_steps: u64, held: Vec<ObligationId>, kinds: Vec<ObligationKind> }`

Constraints:
- The trace event must be deterministic and stable.
- Do NOT allocate on the hot path in production; this is lab/debug functionality.

### Config knobs
Add lab config fields (names flexible):
- `futurelock_max_idle_steps: u64` (default: conservative but small, e.g. 10_000)
- `panic_on_futurelock: bool` (default: true in lab tests)

## Testing
### Unit tests
- Construct a tiny obligation registry state where a task holds a reserved obligation and has an old `last_polled_step`; assert detection triggers.

### E2E lab scenarios
- Scenario: task reserves a SendPermit and then awaits a future that never wakes; another task continues making progress so the lab runtime keeps stepping. Assert:
  - a FuturelockDetected trace event appears
  - (if enabled) the runtime panics with a message that includes task id + obligation ids

## Acceptance Criteria
- Deterministic detection in lab mode (same seed/config => same detection point and trace).
- Trace event contains enough context to debug (task, region, obligation ids/kinds, idle steps).
- Does not introduce stdout/stderr logging in core runtime (only trace + test harness output).
- Clear documentation in the issue text about what counts as a futurelock and what does not.
notes: Implemented futurelock detection in lab runtime (TraceEventKind::FuturelockDetected + TraceData::Futurelock) with config knobs + unit tests; still blocked in Beads by asupersync-1mm/asupersync-l6l/asupersync-jdg status.
close_reason: Implementation verified complete: FuturelockDetected trace event, TraceData::Futurelock, InvariantViolation::Futurelock, config knobs (futurelock_max_idle_steps, panic_on_futurelock), and detection logic all implemented in src/lab/runtime.rs. All dependencies satisfied.

description:
# Setup Project Structure (Cargo.toml, modules, lib.rs)

## Purpose
Create the initial Cargo crate and a *minimal, Phase-0-aligned* module layout that supports deterministic implementation and testing.

This task must respect the repo’s constraints:
- **No unsafe code** (`#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`)
- **Cargo only** (no other package managers)
- **Minimal dependencies** (avoid rand/tracing/etc. unless justified)
- **No file proliferation**: create files when they carry real functionality, not just placeholders

## Recommended Phase 0 Layout (minimal but extensible)

```
asupersync/
├── Cargo.toml
├── rust-toolchain.toml              # if we choose to pin toolchain
├── src/
│   ├── lib.rs
│   ├── error.rs
│   ├── util/
│   │   ├── mod.rs
│   │   ├── det_rng.rs               # deterministic PRNG (no rand)
```

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
SapphireHill: Pre-analysis of cross-table operations for refactoring.

## Lock Order Violations Mapped (state.rs)

Canonical order: B (Regions) → A (Tasks) → C (Obligations)

| Method | Line | Access Order | ShardGuard | Violation |
|--------|------|-------------|------------|-----------|
| create_obligation | 1162 | B→C | for_obligation (B→C) | NONE ✓ |
| commit_obligation | 1247 | C→B | for_obligation (B→C) | C→B ✗ CRITICAL |
| abort_obligation | 1310 | C→B | for_obligation (B→C) | C→B ✗ CRITICAL |
| task_completed | 1901 | A→C→B | for_task_completed (B→A→C) | A→C→B ✗ CRITICAL |
| cancel_request | 1626 | B→A→B | for_cancel (B→A) | B→A→B ✗ CRITICAL |
| cancel_sibling_tasks | 1561 | B→A | for_cancel (B→A) | B→A ✗ MEDIUM |
| advance_region_state | 2216 | B→A→C→B | for_task_completed (B→A→C) | RECURSIVE ✗ HIGH |
| can_region_complete_close | 2170 | B→A | for_cancel (B→A) | B→A ✗ MEDIUM |

## ShardGuard Already Handles Ordering

The guards acquire locks upfront in canonical order:
- for_obligation: B→C (fixes commit/abort_obligation)
- for_task_completed: B→A→C (fixes task_completed)
- for_cancel: B→A (fixes cancel_request/cancel_sibling_tasks)

## Refactoring Strategy Per Method

### 1. commit_obligation / abort_obligation (CRITICAL)
Current: accesses obligations first, then regions (C→B).
Fix: Under for_obligation guard (B→C), both tables are already locked. Rewrite to take &RegionTable and &ObligationTable as params instead of &mut self. Region access (resolve_obligation + advance_region_state) happens through the guard.

### 2. task_completed (CRITICAL)
Current: task removal → obligation scan → region update (A→C→B).
Fix: Under for_task_completed guard (B→A→C), all three locked. Restructure to:
  1. Read task record, extract owner/waiters (A)
  2. Remove task (A)
  3. Scan/abort orphaned obligations (C)
  4. Remove task from region, advance state (B)
No ordering issue since guard holds all three.

### 3. cancel_request / cancel_sibling_tasks (CRITICAL)
Current: collects regions, iterates tasks, re-accesses regions (B→A→B).
Fix: Under for_cancel guard (B→A), both locked. The re-access of regions is fine since it's the same guard. Just ensure methods take &RegionTable + &TaskTable.

### 4. advance_region_state (HARDEST - RECURSIVE)
Current: B→A→C→B with recursive self-calls.
Fix options:
  a) ITERATIVE LOOP: Replace recursion with a work queue of region IDs to advance. Single for_task_completed guard covers all three tables.
  b) TWO-PHASE: Phase 1 (under guard) gathers decisions. Phase 2 (new guard) executes.
  
RECOMMENDATION: Option (a) - iterative loop. The recursion only happens when:
  - Closing/Draining → Finalizing (line 2249)
  - Parent advance after child close (line 2299)
  
Convert to: let mut work = vec\![region_id]; while let Some(rid) = work.pop() { ... if transition { work.push(rid); } if closed { work.push(parent_id); } }

### 5. handle_obligation_leaks (MEDIUM-HIGH)
Current: calls abort_obligation (C→B) in Recover mode.
Fix: Under for_task_completed guard (B→A→C), all locked. No ordering issue.

## Key Principle
The ShardGuard design means methods no longer need to worry about acquisition order - the guard has already acquired everything needed. The refactoring is about changing method signatures from &mut self (single RuntimeState lock) to operating on guard fields (&RegionTable, &TaskTable, &ObligationTable).

## Deadlock Scenarios (Current Code, Single Lock = Safe)
These only become real when we switch from single Mutex<RuntimeState> to ShardedState:
1. Concurrent commit_obligation (C) + cancel_request (B→A) → 3-way if anything holds A→C
2. task_completed (A→C→B) + cancel_request (B→A) → circular wait
3. advance_region_state recursion → nested non-monotonic lock ordering

All resolved by guard-first approach.

## Implementation Order Recommendation
1. Flatten advance_region_state recursion → iterative loop (hardest, do first)
2. Refactor commit/abort_obligation to take table refs
3. Refactor task_completed to use guard pattern
4. Refactor cancel_request/cancel_sibling_tasks
5. Wire up to ShardGuard-based callers

SapphireHill: CRITICAL finding - ShardGuard::for_cancel (B→A) is insufficient.

cancel_request at state.rs:1836 calls advance_region_state, which in Finalizing state can call handle_obligation_leaks → abort_obligation → obligations table access. This means cancel_request needs obligation shard access too.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
SapphireHill: ARCHITECTURAL INSIGHT - advance_region_state table access analysis

advance_region_state accesses differ by state:

Closing/Draining branch (lines 2232-2257):
- Regions: YES (state check, begin_finalize/begin_drain)
- Tasks: NO (task_ids stored in region record itself)
- Obligations: NO
→ Guard needed: regions_only (B)

Finalizing branch (lines 2259-2311):
- Regions: YES (pending_obligations, task_ids, complete_close, remove_child)
- Tasks: YES (self.task(task_id) for terminal check at line 2273)
- Obligations: YES (collect_obligation_leaks at line 2276, handle_obligation_leaks at line 2279)
→ Guard needed: for_task_completed (B→A→C)

CONSEQUENCE: ANY caller of advance_region_state potentially needs all 3 locks. This means:
- for_obligation (B→C) is insufficient for commit/abort/mark_leaked (they also need A for task terminal checks)
- for_cancel (B→A) is insufficient (needs C for obligation leak handling)

RECOMMENDED APPROACH for bd-2utc3:
1. SHORT TERM: Use for_task_completed (B→A→C) for all callers of advance_region_state. This is correct but reduces concurrency gains.
2. MEDIUM TERM: Split advance_region_state into two phases:
   - Phase 1 (regions_only): Check Closing/Draining → Finalizing transition
   - Phase 2 (for_task_completed): Handle Finalizing state (needs all 3 tables)
   Callers do their primary work with narrow guard, then escalate only if Phase 2 needed.
3. LONG TERM: Deferred obligation leak handling - advance_region_state returns a 'deferred actions' list instead of executing them inline.

For initial sharding migration, recommend approach #1 (all callers use for_task_completed) to get correctness first, then optimize with #2/#3 as contention profiling reveals bottlenecks.

title: [EPIC-TOKIO] Service Layer (tower equivalent)
description:
# Service Abstraction Layer

## Overview
Composable service abstraction with middleware layers, equivalent to tower.

## Core Traits

### Service
```rust
pub trait Service<Request> {
    type Response;
    type Error;
    
    fn poll_ready(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<Result<(), Self::Error>>;
    fn call(&mut self, request: Request) -> Self::Future;
    
    type Future: Future<Output = Result<Self::Response, Self::Error>>;
}
```

### Layer
```rust
pub trait Layer<S> {
    type Service;
    fn layer(&self, inner: S) -> Self::Service;
}
```

## Standard Layers

### 1. TimeoutLayer
- Per-request timeout
- Integrates with budget deadlines

### 2. RetryLayer
- Configurable retry policy
- Backoff strategies
- Uses our retry combinator

### 3. RateLimitLayer
- Token bucket or leaky bucket
- Configurable rate
- Cancel-aware waiting

### 4. ConcurrencyLimitLayer
- Semaphore-based limiting
- Backpressure support

### 5. LoadShedLayer
- Reject when overloaded
- Configurable shed policy

### 6. BufferLayer
- Request buffering
- Bounded queue

### 7. FilterLayer
- Predicate-based filtering

### 8. MapRequestLayer / MapResponseLayer
- Request/response transformation

### 9. MapErrorLayer / MapResultLayer
- Error transformation

### 10. TraceLayer
- Observability integration
- Span per request

## ServiceBuilder
```rust
ServiceBuilder::new()
    .timeout(Duration::from_secs(10))
    .rate_limit(100, Duration::from_secs(1))
    .concurrency_limit(50)
    .layer(TracingLayer::new())
    .service(my_service)
```

## Cancel-Safety
- poll_ready: cancel-aware
- call: returns cancel-aware future
- Layers preserve cancel-safety

## Load Balancing
- p2c (power of two choices)
- round-robin
- least-loaded

title: [AUDIT] Deep correctness audit: cx/registry.rs
notes:
AUDIT COMPLETE: cx/registry.rs (3,414 lines) — SOUND, 0 bugs.

Zero concurrency primitives (pure &mut self). Name lease lifecycle with ObligationToken<LeaseKind> drop bomb: armed on creation, defused by release/abort. NamePermit::commit(mut self) transfers token by move — no duplication. commit_permit() aborts permit on error to defuse drop bomb.

Dual-map invariant (leases + pending): name in at most one map. All operations check both maps before insertion. Atomically moved by commit_permit.

Waiter FIFO: try_grant_to_first_waiter uses queue.remove(0). Cleanup operations abort granted leases to prevent drop-bomb panics.

Watcher tri-index (by_ref, by_name, by_region): each ref has one watcher_region. Notifications sorted by monotonic NameWatchRef u64 for determinism.

Cleanup ordering: watchers removed BEFORE release notifications emitted — prevents spurious notifications to closing region.

60+ tests cover lifecycle, conformance, collision policies, waiter FIFO, cross-region isolation, cleanup edge cases.

title: Implement TaskState enum and state machine
description:
# TaskState Enum and State Machine

## Purpose
TaskState represents the lifecycle of a task from creation to completion. The state machine is carefully designed to support the cancellation protocol with explicit drain and finalize phases.

## The Task States
```rust
enum TaskState {
    // Initial state after spawn
    Created,
    
    // Actively being polled
    Running,
    
    // Cancel requested but not yet acknowledged
    CancelRequested {
        reason: CancelReason,
        cleanup_budget: Budget,
    },
    
    // Task has acknowledged cancel, running cleanup code
    Cancelling {
        cleanup_budget: Budget,
    },
    
    // Cleanup done, running finalizers
    Finalizing {
        cleanup_budget: Budget,
    },
    
    // Terminal state
    Completed(Outcome),
}
```

## State Transitions

```
                    ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │                                      │
Created ──────────► Running ──────────────────────────────►│
    │                 │                                    │
    │                 │ cancel_request()                   │
    │                 ▼                                    │
    │           CancelRequested ─────────────────────────►│
    │                 │                                    │
    │                 │ checkpoint (mask=0)                │
    │                 ▼                                    │ Completed
    │              Cancelling ───────────────────────────►│
    │                 │                                    │
    │                 │ cleanup done                       │
    │                 ▼                                    │
    │              Finalizing ───────────────────────────►│
    │                 │                                    │
    │                 │ finalizers done                    │
    │                 ▼                                    │
    └────────────────►  Completed(Outcome)  ◄──────────────┘
```

## Valid Transitions

| From | To | Trigger | Label |
|------|-----|---------|-------|
| Created | Running | Scheduler selects | τ (silent) |
| Created | CancelRequested | Cancel before first poll | cancel(r,reason) |
| Running | Completed(Ok/Err) | Task body returns | complete(t,outcome) |
| Running | CancelRequested | Cancel request arrives | cancel(r,reason) |
| CancelRequested | Cancelling | Checkpoint with mask=0 | τ |
| CancelRequested | CancelRequested | Checkpoint with mask>0 (defer) | τ |
| Cancelling | Finalizing | Cleanup code completes | τ |
| Cancelling | Completed(Cancelled) | No cleanup needed | complete(t,Cancelled) |
| Finalizing | Completed(Cancelled) | All finalizers run | complete(t,Cancelled) |

## Why These States?

### Created vs Running
Separates "spawned but not yet scheduled" from "actively executing." This allows:
- Batch spawning before any execution
- Cancel before first poll (task never runs)
- Clear scheduling semantics

### CancelRequested
The task hasn't observed the cancel yet. This is important because:
- Task may be in the middle of a computation
- Task should reach a checkpoint to observe cancel
- Masking allows bounded deferral

### Cancelling
Task has acknowledged cancel and is running cleanup code. The cleanup_budget ensures bounded cleanup time.

### Finalizing
Cleanup code done, now running registered finalizers (defer_async, defer_sync). Finalizers run under cancel mask.

### Completed
Terminal and absorbing. Once Completed, the state never changes. This supports INV-OBLIGATION-LINEAR.

## Mask Budget

When in CancelRequested, the task has a `mask` count (in TaskRecord, not TaskState):
- Each checkpoint where mask>0 decrements mask and returns Ok
- When mask=0, checkpoint returns Cancelled
- This ensures bounded cancellation deferral (INV-MASK-BOUNDED)

## Implementation Requirements

1. **TaskState must be Clone, Debug**
2. **Completed(Outcome) stores the full outcome**
3. **is_terminal() method**: Returns true only for Completed
4. **is_cancelling() method**: Returns true for CancelRequested/Cancelling/Finalizing
5. **can_be_polled() method**: Returns true for Running/CancelRequested/Cancelling/Finalizing

## Invariant Support

### INV-TASK-OWNED
```rust
∀t: T[t].state ≠ Completed(_) ⟹ t ∈ R[T[t].region].children
```
Non-completed tasks are owned by their region.

### INV-MASK-BOUNDED  
```rust
∀t: T[t].mask ∈ ℕ and only decreases at CHECKPOINT-MASKED
```
Masking is finite.

### INV-OBLIGATION-BOUNDED
```rust
∀o: O[o].state = Reserved ⟹ T[O[o].holder].state ∈ {Running, CancelRequested, Cancelling, Finalizing}
```
Reserved obligations have live holders.

## Testing Requirements

1. Only valid transitions are possible
2. Completed is absorbing (can't transition out)
3. State machine handles all cancel timing scenarios
4. Mask budget decrements correctly

## Example Scenarios

### Normal Completion
```
Created → Running → Completed(Ok(value))
```

### Cancelled at Checkpoint
```
Created → Running → CancelRequested → Cancelling → Finalizing → Completed(Cancelled)
```

### Cancelled Before First Poll
```
Created → CancelRequested → Cancelling → Finalizing → Completed(Cancelled)
```

### Error During Cancellation
```
Created → Running → CancelRequested → Cancelling → Completed(Err(e))
// Error during cleanup is still an error, not Cancelled
```

## References
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §1.5 (Task States)
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §3.1-3.2 (Task lifecycle, Cancellation protocol)
- asupersync_plan_v4.md §7.1 (Task cancellation state machine)

## Acceptance Criteria
- Task lifecycle states match the spec: Created → Running → (CancelRequested → Cancelling → Finalizing) → Completed(outcome).
- Cancellation-related states carry the necessary metadata (reason, budgets/quotas) and strengthen idempotently.
- Completed is terminal/absorbing.
- Unit tests cover legal/illegal transitions and trace-level representation.
notes:
Implemented TaskState + core transitions aligned to formal semantics.

- `src/record/task.rs`: TaskState now `Created | Running | CancelRequested{reason, cleanup_budget} | Cancelling{cleanup_budget} | Finalizing{cleanup_budget} | Completed(TaskOutcome)` where `TaskOutcome = Outcome<(), crate::error::Error>` (Phase 0 concrete outcome storage). Added helpers `is_terminal`, `is_cancelling`, `can_be_polled`, plus TaskRecord transition helpers `start_running` + `complete`.
- Cancellation request handling is idempotent: repeated `request_cancel` strengthens `CancelReason` and tightens `cleanup_budget` via `Budget::combine`.
- Updated affected call sites/tests (notably `src/runtime/state.rs` live-task accounting + policy sibling-cancel tests).
- Added unit tests in `src/record/task.rs` covering cancel-before-first-poll, strengthening, Completed absorbing, and pollability predicate.

Gates: cargo fmt --check, cargo check --all-targets, cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings, cargo test all pass.

title: Implement Chase-Lev work-stealing deque (core primitive)
description:
# Chase–Lev Work-Stealing Deque

## Purpose
Implement the core work-stealing deque used by each worker:
- owner pushes/pops from the bottom (fast path)
- thieves steal from the top

This is the backbone of parallel scheduling.

## Constraints
- Must be correct under data-race-free Rust (use atomics).
- Must avoid `unsafe` in core if at all possible (unsafe is forbidden by project rules).
  - If a fully lock-free implementation requires unsafe, we must design an alternative:
    - use `Mutex`/`RwLock` in Phase 1 initially (correctness first), then optimize later
    - or encapsulate unsafe behind a separately-audited crate (only if allowed)

Given the project’s `unsafe` prohibition, the plan-of-record should start with a correct, deterministic, safe implementation even if it is not maximally performant.

## Plan-of-Record Options
### Option A: Safe deque with locks (Phase 1 baseline)
- Use `Mutex<VecDeque<TaskId>>` per worker.
- Steal = pop_front.
- Push/pop = push_back/pop_back.
- Determinism in lab is straightforward.

### Option B: Lock-free deque (requires careful review)
- Many lock-free implementations require unsafe and careful memory ordering.
- Likely incompatible with `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` in core.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Correctness properties:
  - no lost tasks
  - no duplicated tasks
  - owner pop and thief steal interleavings behave correctly
- Deterministic tests simulate concurrent accesses.

## Testing
- Model-based tests:
  - simulate multiple threads performing operations
  - verify resulting multiset of tasks matches expected
close_reason: LocalQueue implements safe lock-based work-stealing deque with tests

title: [Distributed] Integrate with Local Region Types
[EPIC-INFRA] First-Class Tracing Integration with Structured Causality
description:
# Overview

Integrate deeply with the `tracing` crate to automatically instrument task spawning, region 
entry/exit, cancellation events, obligation lifecycle, and budget consumption - with causality 
links between related spans.

## Why This Matters

Async debugging is notoriously difficult. Traditional tracing shows events but not causality.
Asupersync's structured concurrency model means causality IS explicit (parent regions, child 
tasks). Surfacing this through tracing is low-hanging fruit that transforms debugging.

This is foundational infrastructure that enables:
- Task Tree Visualization Dashboard (#4)
- Deterministic Replay Debugging (#6)
- OpenTelemetry Metrics Export (#15)
- Enhanced Cancel Reason Attribution (#10)

## Key Design Decisions

1. **Feature-gated**: `tracing` is an optional dependency behind a feature flag
2. **Zero-cost when disabled**: No overhead when tracing feature is off
3. **Causality links**: Use `tracing::Span::follows_from()` to link related operations
4. **Structured fields**: All spans include region_id, task_id, budget info
5. **Integration with DiagnosticContext**: Leverage existing observability infrastructure

## What Gets Instrumented

- Region lifecycle: enter, exit, state transitions (Open→Closing→Draining→Closed)
- Task lifecycle: spawn, poll, wake, complete, state transitions
- Cancellation flow: request, propagation path, drain, finalize
- Obligation lifecycle: reserve, commit, abort, leak detection
- Budget checkpoints: remaining quota, deadline proximity
- I/O operations: register, ready, complete

## Expected User Experience

```rust
// Users see spans like:
region[id=42, parent=1, state=Open] {
    task[id=100, region=42, state=Running] {
        checkpoint[remaining_polls=847, deadline_in=4.2s]
        cancel_requested[reason=Timeout, source=budget, propagated_from=region:1]
        obligation[kind=SendPermit, id=55, transition=Reserved→Aborted]
    } // task completed: Cancelled(Timeout)
} // region closed: quiescent
```

## Implementation Estimate

- ~300-400 lines of instrumentation code
- Touches: cx.rs, scope.rs, scheduler, obligation registry, reactor
- Dependencies: tracing crate (optional)

## Success Criteria

- [ ] All region state transitions emit spans
- [ ] All task state transitions emit spans  
- [ ] Cancellation propagation is fully traceable
- [ ] Obligation lifecycle is fully traceable
- [ ] Causality links connect parent/child relationships
- [ ] Zero overhead when feature disabled (verified by benchmark)
- [ ] Integration tests verify span structure

title: Watch channel blocks worker threads via Condvar::wait_timeout
description: watch::Receiver::changed() at src/channel/watch.rs:335-377 uses std::sync::Condvar::wait_timeout(10ms) which blocks the calling OS thread. If called from async tasks on scheduler worker threads, this can cause throughput collapse or deadlock with small worker pools. Same pattern in sync/rwlock.rs and sync/barrier.rs. Need async-aware waiting (waker-based notification) instead of blocking. Found during code audit.
notes: Fixed: replaced Condvar::wait_timeout(10ms) with async waker-based notification in watch channel. Receiver::changed() now returns a ChangedFuture that implements Future instead of blocking the OS thread. Sender::send/send_modify/drop wake all registered wakers. WatchStream properly delegates to the future. 24 tests pass including 2 new async-aware tests (Pending→Ready after send, sender drop wakes). Conformance test updated to .await the future.

title: [AUDIT] Deep correctness audit: fs/uring.rs
notes:
## Deep Correctness Audit: fs/uring.rs (975 lines)

### Concurrency Primitives Inventory
- 4 Mutex (parking_lot): ring, read_state, write_state, sync_state
- 1 AtomicU64: position (all Relaxed)
- 1 Arc<IoUringFileInner>

### Unsafe Blocks (9)
1. openat syscall (L189) — checked return
2. OwnedFd::from_raw_fd (L195, L218) — valid fd from prior syscall / caller responsibility
3. lseek syscall (L330) — checked return
4. ftruncate syscall (L349) — checked return
5. File::from_raw_fd+forget (L365-368, L375-378) — prevents double-close, panic-fragile but acceptable
6. ring.submission().push (L393-396, L692-695) — io_uring SQE push, valid entry

### Lock Analysis
- Single lock contention path: all I/O through submit_and_wait which holds ring Mutex
- OpState locks (read/write/sync_state) only touched in mark_op_complete (Drop path) and any_ops_pending
- No multi-lock ordering issues — each critical section touches at most one lock

### Key Patterns Verified
1. Drop drain correctness: strong_count==1 ensures no concurrent access during drain, submit_and_wait(1) blocks for CQEs
2. mark_op_complete wake-under-lock (L116): DEAD CODE — futures return Ready immediately, never set OpState::Pending with waker
3. Position TOCTOU in read()/write() (L238/L265): by design — _at variants (read_at/write_at) are the concurrent-safe API
4. set_len position clamp (L354-357): load-compare-store; could use fetch_min for hardening, but concurrent truncate+write is inherently undefined
5. File::from_raw_fd+forget in metadata/set_permissions: standard pattern, panic between from_raw_fd and forget would double-close but syscall wrappers are non-panicking
6. All futures block (return Poll::Ready), deferred true async noted at L486-487

### Latent Concerns (not bugs)
- mark_op_complete wake-under-lock will be a real hazard when futures become truly async
- Position tracking inherently racy for concurrent sequential access; intended usage is _at variants

### Verdict: SOUND — 0 bugs found

title: SEM-00 Semantic Harmonization Program: Canonical contract across runtime/docs/Lean/TLA
description: Program-level epic to eliminate semantic drift and make one canonical operational contract authoritative across implementation, documentation, theorem proving, and model checking.
design:
Background:
Asupersync currently has multiple semantic authorities (runtime behavior, formal semantics documentation, Lean model/proofs, and TLA model checks). This is powerful but high-risk when definitions or transition guards drift.

Intent:
Establish a single canonical semantic contract with stable rule IDs and explicit definitions for cancel, mask, region close, quiescence, obligation lifecycle, and severity ordering. All artifacts must project from or be validated against that contract.

Rationale:
1) Prevent contradictory assumptions across engineering and formal tracks.
2) Make regressions detectable in CI, not via late discovery.
3) Preserve deterministic/cancel-correct design goals while improving maintainability.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A canonical semantic contract artifact exists and is approved.
2. Runtime, docs, Lean, and TLA are all aligned to that contract with traceability links.
3. Conformance and anti-drift CI gates prevent untracked semantic divergence.
4. Harmonization report documents decisions, tradeoffs, and residual risks.
notes:
Program constraints:
- Keep determinism, structured concurrency, cancel-correctness, and no-leak invariants as non-negotiable.
- Prefer explicit semantics over implicit behavior.
- Use witness/counterexample style for ambiguity resolution.
- Ensure future contributors can understand intent without consulting external planning docs.
close_reason: All 12 SEM child epics are closed; canonical semantic contract artifacts and alignment surfaces are present across docs/runtime/Lean/TLA with anti-drift scripts and semantic verification harnesses in-repo.

1. Report groups outcomes by semantic domain and canonical rule ID.
2. First-failure and likely-root-cause sections are generated automatically.

notes: Direct user-value: reduces time-to-diagnosis after verification failures.

acceptance_criteria:
1. Smoke/full/forensics profiles are documented with explicit suite inclusion matrices.
2. Each profile has clear runtime budget and required artifact/log outputs.
3. Profile selection is consistent across local and CI runs.
4. Logs clearly declare selected profile and skipped components.
notes: User-value: faster feedback loops for day-to-day work, deep mode retained for incident forensics.

1. Repeated deterministic replay runs produce variance metrics and flake detection signals.
2. Dashboard/report identifies unstable suites, witness IDs, and likely variance sources.
3. Outputs include replay commands and logs for root-cause analysis.
4. Stability data feeds CI signal-quality tuning and recurring audit inputs.
notes: User benefit: fewer false alarms and faster triage when failures occur.

title: SEM-02 Semantic Inventory and Drift Matrix
description: Create complete cross-artifact inventory and classify alignment, divergence, ambiguity, and missing semantics.
design:
Purpose:
Produce a complete, evidence-backed inventory of semantic concepts and rules across runtime, docs, Lean, and TLA.

Method:
- Enumerate every core concept (state, transition, guard, invariant, definition).
- Build a row-wise drift matrix with artifact columns and explicit citations.
- Classify each row as Aligned, Divergent, Ambiguous, or Missing.

Why this matters:
This is the factual substrate for all later decisions; without it, ADR discussions become opinion-driven.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Drift matrix covers all core semantic areas (cancel, mask, region lifecycle, obligations, close/quiescence, severity ordering).
2. Every matrix row cites concrete source locations.
3. Divergences and ambiguities are explicitly tagged for ADR resolution.
4. Matrix is reviewed and accepted as complete input to SEM-03.
notes:
Quality bar:
- Prefer precise row granularity over broad summaries.
- Distinguish true contradiction from abstraction-level differences.
- Include known hotspots so future reviewers can retrace logic quickly.
close_reason: done

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
Inventory philosophy:
Treat disagreements as data, not arguments. Every row must be citation-backed and granular enough to support concrete decisions.

Future-self reminder:
If a row feels hard to classify, split it into narrower rows; ambiguity usually hides overloaded concepts.

title: SEM-03 Decision Framework and ADR Resolution
description: Resolve every divergence through explicit candidate evaluation, witness traces, and accepted ADR decisions.
design:
Purpose:
Resolve each divergence using a repeatable decision framework instead of ad hoc judgments.

Method:
- For each divergent/ambiguous row, define candidate semantic options.
- Evaluate with explicit rubric: safety, determinism, proof cost, model-check cost, runtime complexity, and operability.
- Attach witness traces/counterexamples where relevant.
- Record accepted outcome in ADR-style decision log with rationale and rejected alternatives.

Why this matters:
A transparent decision record is essential for future maintenance and prevents re-litigating settled semantics.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Every SEM-02 divergent or ambiguous row has a corresponding ADR decision.
2. Each decision includes alternatives, tradeoffs, and final rationale.
3. Unresolved items are escalated with explicit owner and deadline.
4. Approved decision set is ready to encode in canonical contract.
notes:
Decision discipline:
- Do not defer ambiguity into implementation.
- Prefer semantics that are explicit, deterministic, and testable.
- Mark any temporary compromises with sunset conditions.

title: Experiment: sheaf-theoretic consistency checks for distributed sagas
description:
# Experiment: Sheaf-Theoretic Consistency Checks

## Purpose
The design includes an advanced “global inconsistency detector” viewpoint:
- local states form a presheaf over network topology
- a globally consistent commit is a global section
- nontrivial cohomology (`H^1 != 0`) indicates an obstruction (split-brain-like inconsistency)

This task captures the experiment plan so it isn’t lost.

## Deliverables
- A simplified model for saga/lease state patches and overlaps.
- A diagnostic that reports “inconsistency” in a deterministic, debuggable way.

## Success Metrics
- Detects a constructed split-brain scenario that pairwise checks miss.

## Acceptance Criteria
- States a concrete distributed-saga consistency problem the sheaf lens is meant to detect (with a minimal example).
- Identifies the observable data to record (trace/overlap constraints) to support the check.
- Produces a minimal deterministic lab simulation test case (even if the check is stubbed initially).

title: Add environment variable and config file support to builder
description:
## Overview

Support 12-factor app configuration through environment variables and optional config file loading.

## Requirements

### Environment Variable Overrides
```rust
impl RuntimeBuilder {
    /// Load configuration from environment variables.
    /// Env vars override programmatic settings.
    pub fn with_env_overrides(mut self) -> Self;
}
```

Environment variable mapping:
- `ASUPERSYNC_WORKER_THREADS` -> scheduler.worker_threads
- `ASUPERSYNC_TASK_QUEUE_DEPTH` -> scheduler.task_queue_depth
- `ASUPERSYNC_TIMER_RESOLUTION_MS` -> timers.resolution
- `ASUPERSYNC_MAX_REGISTERED_IO` -> io.max_registered_sources
- `ASUPERSYNC_ENABLE_METRICS` -> metrics.enabled

### Config File Support
```rust
impl RuntimeBuilder {
    /// Load configuration from TOML file.
    pub fn from_toml(path: impl AsRef<Path>) -> Result<Self, ConfigError>;
    
    /// Load configuration from TOML string.
    pub fn from_toml_str(toml: &str) -> Result<Self, ConfigError>;
}
```

Config file format:
```toml
[scheduler]
worker_threads = 4
task_queue_depth = 1024

[timers]
resolution_ms = 1
max_duration_hours = 24

[io]
max_registered_sources = 10000
```

### Precedence Order
1. Programmatic settings (highest)
2. Environment variables
3. Config file
4. Defaults (lowest)

## Acceptance Criteria
1. `with_env_overrides()` method
2. `from_toml()` and `from_toml_str()` methods
3. Clear precedence documentation
4. Error messages for invalid env vars
5. Optional dependency on toml crate (feature-gated)

## Test Requirements
- Test env var parsing for all supported vars
- Test invalid env var values (should error)
- Test config file loading
- Test precedence: programmatic > env > file
- Test missing optional values use defaults
close_reason: done

title: Implement TraceReplayer for Lab runtime
description:
## Overview

Implement the TraceReplayer that feeds recorded decisions back into the Lab runtime to achieve exact execution replay.

## Background

This is the core replay mechanism. Instead of making scheduling decisions, the Lab runtime in replay mode reads the next decision from the trace and executes it.

## Design Requirements

### Exact Replay
- Every scheduling decision must match recorded
- Time advances must match exactly
- I/O results must be replayed, not simulated fresh

### Divergence Detection
- If execution diverges from trace, detect and report
- Divergence means bug or trace corruption
- Provide helpful error message with divergence point

### Stepping Support
- Support "step to next event" for debugging
- Support "continue to breakpoint" (e.g., specific tick or task)
- Support "run to completion"

## Implementation

```rust
pub struct TraceReplayer {
    reader: TraceReader,
    current_index: usize,
    mode: ReplayMode,
}

pub enum ReplayMode {
    Run,                    // Run to completion
    Step,                   // Stop after each event
    RunTo(Breakpoint),      // Run to specific point
}

pub enum Breakpoint {
    Tick(u64),
    Task(TaskId),
    Event(usize),           // Event index
}

impl TraceReplayer {
    pub fn new(reader: TraceReader) -> Self;
    pub fn next_event(&mut self) -> Option<&TraceEvent>;
    pub fn verify_matches(&self, actual: &TraceEvent) -> Result<(), DivergenceError>;
}

pub struct DivergenceError {
    pub index: usize,
    pub expected: TraceEvent,
    pub actual: TraceEvent,
    pub context: String,
}
```

## Lab Runtime Integration

```rust
impl LabRuntime {
    pub fn replay(trace: TraceReader) -> ReplayRuntime;
}

pub struct ReplayRuntime {
    lab: LabRuntime,
    replayer: TraceReplayer,
}
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Replayer correctly feeds decisions to Lab runtime
- [ ] Divergence is detected with helpful error
- [ ] Step mode allows event-by-event execution
- [ ] Complex scenario replays exactly
- [ ] Performance is similar to normal Lab execution

title: [AUDIT] Deep correctness audit: time/intrusive_wheel.rs
notes:
AUDIT VERDICT: SOUND — 0 bugs found

Module: src/time/intrusive_wheel.rs (1,212 lines)
Concurrency primitives: ZERO — entirely single-threaded (Cell-based, !Send, !Sync)

Unsafe analysis (~29 unsafe blocks, all pointer manipulation for intrusive linked lists):
1. TimerSlot push_back/remove/pop_front/drain/drain_nodes/collect_expired — standard doubly-linked list ops, all sound
2. TimerWheel insert/cancel — Pin get_unchecked_mut + NonNull creation, debug_assert on not-already-linked
3. TimerWheel tick/advance_to — collect_expired + cursor advance, advance_to handles >= SLOTS via full scan
4. HierarchicalTimerWheel cascade — drains higher-level slot, fires expired, re-inserts non-expired to correct lower level
5. TimerSlotIter::next — read-only traversal via NonNull
6. WheelLevel clear_slots/advance_and_drain — standard drain operations

Critical path analysis (cascade, L818-845):
- advance_and_drain pops nodes (linked=false), expired get waker taken + count--, non-expired re-inserted
- Wheel-level count preserved correctly: drain doesn't decrement wheel count, re-insert doesn't increment
- Recursion bounded: max depth 3 (levels 1→2→3, then _ => return)
- update_slot_level/push_node parameter ordering verified correct

Count tracking verified: insert(+1), cancel(-1), tick/advance_to(-expired), cascade(-expired, re-insert=neutral), clear(=0)

Design notes (not bugs):
- HierarchicalTimerWheel::advance_to loops tick() which uses Instant::now() internally — may fire slightly beyond requested time (real-time behavior, deterministic time handled by lab runtime)
- advance_to could be slow for large time jumps (tick-by-tick loop)
- next_expiration scans ALL nodes — O(n)
- Double-insert only guarded by debug_assert (acceptable: unsafe API with documented preconditions)

title: Phase 1: Region Heap + Send Task Model
description:
# Phase 1: Region Heap + Send Task Model

## Purpose
Make the “task tier” sound:
- allow `Send` tasks to migrate across workers
- preserve region ownership and lifetimes via region-owned allocation

This is the “soundness frontier” encoded into the runtime:
- fibers (Phase 0): borrow-friendly, same-thread
- tasks (Phase 1): `Send`, parallel, region-heap-backed

## Requirements
- Region-owned allocation arena that is reclaimed only after region close/quiescence.
- A `RRef<'r, T>`-style handle (or equivalent) to store data with region lifetime.

title: Phase 0: Scheduler, Waker, and Timers
description:
# Phase 0: Scheduler, Waker, and Timers

## Purpose
This feature implements the Phase 0 execution engine that turns the operational semantics into a running system:
- a deterministic, single-thread scheduler with **3 priority lanes**
- a safe waker bridge from Rust `Future` polling → scheduler enqueueing
- a timer heap for `sleep_until` and virtual-time advancement in the lab runtime

This is where several non-negotiable invariants become *mechanically enforceable*:
- cancellation progress (cancel lane priority)
- bounded, deterministic drain paths
- deterministic scheduling for lab tests and replay

## What This Feature Covers

### 1) 3-lane scheduler (Cancel > Timed > Ready)
Normative lane priority (spec):
1. **Cancel lane** (highest) — tasks in cancel/drain/finalize protocol
2. **Timed lane** — deadline-driven readiness (EDF-ish ordering)
3. **Ready lane** — ordinary runnable tasks

Key constraints:
- cancel lane must never be starved
- timed lane must not violate deadline ordering assumptions
- all tie-breaking that can influence behavior in lab must be deterministic

### 2) Waker (`std::task::Wake`) + wake dedup
We must provide a `Waker` for polling tasks, but repo policy forbids `unsafe`.

Plan-of-record:
- implement wakers via `std::task::Wake` (safe)
- waker carries `TaskId` + an explicit runtime handle (no TLS / no ambient globals)
- wake dedup is mandatory to prevent queue blowup and nondeterministic behavior

Wake dedup strategy (Phase 0):
- a per-task `woken` bit (or equivalent) in `TaskRecord`
- scheduler membership tracking to avoid duplicate enqueues

### 3) Timer heap + virtual time integration
Timers are a core kernel primitive:
- `sleep_until(t)` parks the current task until virtual time reaches `t`
- `tick` advances time when no immediate progress is possible (lab runtime)

Implementation expectations:
- timer heap is deterministic (stable ordering for same deadlines)
- timer expiry produces wake events that feed back into scheduler lanes

## Determinism Contract (Lab)
The lab runtime must produce identical traces given identical configuration/seed:
- no ambient randomness
- do not rely on hash-map iteration order
- explicit tie-breaking (ordered structures or deterministic PRNG)

## Testing Strategy
- unit tests for lane priority and timer ordering
- E2E tests that demonstrate:
  - cancellation drains quickly and deterministically
  - timer wakeups are reproducible
  - wake dedup prevents duplicate queue entries

## Acceptance Criteria
- Scheduler implements lane priority: cancel > timed > ready.
- Wakers are implemented with `std::task::Wake` (no unsafe, no TLS).
- Wake dedup prevents duplicate queue entries for the same `TaskId`.
- Timer expiry deterministically wakes the correct tasks.
- Lab runs are deterministic given the same seed/config.
close_reason: All implementations complete: scheduler (845), waker (fzl), timer heap (tgl). 163 tests passing including scheduler and timer tests.

title: Budget monitor: real-time budget consumption across regions
description:
# Budget Monitor

## Overview
Real-time dashboard for monitoring budget consumption across all regions,
with alerts, trends, and exhaustion prediction.

## Design

### Budget Monitor
```rust
pub struct BudgetMonitor {
    state: Arc<RuntimeState>,
    console: Console,
    history: BudgetHistory,
}

impl BudgetMonitor {
    /// Get current budget status for all regions.
    pub fn status(&self) -> Vec<RegionBudgetStatus> {
        self.state.all_regions()
            .map(|r| RegionBudgetStatus {
                region_id: r.id(),
                region_name: r.name(),
                total: r.budget().total(),
                remaining: r.budget().remaining(),
                consumed: r.budget().consumed(),
                percent_used: r.budget().percent_used(),
                exhaustion_eta: self.predict_exhaustion(&r),
            })
            .collect()
    }
    
    /// Predict when a region will exhaust its budget.
    fn predict_exhaustion(&self, region: &Region) -> Option<Duration> {
        let history = self.history.get(region.id());
        let rate = history.consumption_rate()?;
        let remaining = region.budget().remaining();
        
        if rate > 0.0 {
            Some(Duration::from_secs_f64(remaining as f64 / rate))
        } else {
            None
        }
    }
    
    /// Get budget breakdown by resource type.
    pub fn breakdown(&self, region_id: RegionId) -> BudgetBreakdown {
        let region = self.state.get_region(region_id);
        BudgetBreakdown {
            ops: region.budget().ops_consumed(),
            bytes: region.budget().bytes_consumed(),
            time: region.budget().time_consumed(),
            connections: region.budget().connections_consumed(),
        }
    }
}
```

### Output Format
```

│ Region                     Budget          ETA     Rate        │

│   Request-1 consumption rate increasing (+15% last 30s)        │
╰─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

title: Implement Budget type with product semiring semantics
description:
# Budget Type with Product Semiring Semantics

## Purpose
Budget encapsulates resource limits that propagate through the region tree. It uses product semiring semantics where components combine by "stricter wins" (min), ensuring children can never exceed parent budgets.

## Budget Structure
```rust
struct Budget {
    deadline: Option<Time>,      // Absolute deadline (None = no deadline)
    poll_quota: u64,             // Max polls before forced yield (u64::MAX = unlimited)
    cost_quota: Option<u64>,     // Abstract cost units (None = unlimited)
    priority: u8,                // 0-255, higher = more important
}
```

## Why Product Semiring?
A product semiring allows independent composition of each component:
- Each component has its own combination rule
- Combined budget = componentwise combination
- This gives automatic propagation without manual threading

The combination rules:
- **deadline**: min (earlier deadline wins)
- **poll_quota**: min (stricter quota wins)
- **cost_quota**: min (stricter cost wins)
- **priority**: max (higher priority wins - inverse for scheduling)

## Mathematical Structure

### The Semiring Laws
For each component (except priority):
```
combine(a, combine(b, c)) = combine(combine(a, b), c)  // Associativity
combine(a, identity) = a                                // Identity
combine(a, b) = combine(b, a)                           // Commutativity
combine(a, a) = a                                       // Idempotence (min is idempotent)
```

This is actually an **idempotent semiring** (also called a tropical semiring for min/max operations).

### Tropical Interpretation
The budget algebra connects to tropical geometry:
- Sequential composition: budgets ADD (time/cost accumulates)
- Constraint propagation: budgets MIN (stricter wins)

This enables:
- Critical path computation in task DAGs
- "Where did my budget go?" explanations
- Automatic deadline propagation

## Key Operations

### combine(parent: &Budget, child: &Budget) -> Budget
```rust
fn combine(parent: &Budget, child: &Budget) -> Budget {
    Budget {
        deadline: min_option(parent.deadline, child.deadline),
        poll_quota: min(parent.poll_quota, child.poll_quota),
        cost_quota: min_option(parent.cost_quota, child.cost_quota),
        priority: max(parent.priority, child.priority),
    }
}
```

### remaining(&self, now: Time) -> Option<Duration>
Calculates time remaining until deadline.

### has_poll_quota(&self) -> bool
Returns true if poll_quota > 0.

### consume_poll(&mut self) -> bool
Decrements poll_quota, returns false if exhausted.

### consume_cost(&mut self, cost: u64) -> bool
Decrements cost_quota, returns false if insufficient.

### is_expired(&self, now: Time) -> bool
Returns true if deadline has passed.

## Budget Propagation

When a child region/task is created:
1. Parent's effective budget is computed
2. Child specifies its own budget (or None for defaults)
3. Effective child budget = combine(parent_effective, child_requested)

This ensures INV-DEADLINE-MONOTONE: children can never outlive parents.

## Cleanup Budgets

Cancellation provides a cleanup_budget for the drain phase:
```rust
fn cleanup_budget_for(reason: CancelKind) -> Budget {
    match reason {
        User | Timeout => Budget::generous(),   // Normal cleanup time
        FailFast => Budget::moderate(),         // Faster cleanup
        ParentCancelled => Budget::moderate(),
        Shutdown => Budget::minimal(),          // Emergency cleanup
    }
}
```

## Implementation Requirements

1. **Budget must be Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq**
2. **Default budget**: generous (no deadline, high poll quota)
3. **Infinite budget**: truly unlimited (for root region)
4. **Zero budget**: immediate expiry (for testing)

## Testing Requirements

1. combine() is associative
2. combine() is commutative (except priority direction)
3. combine() is idempotent
4. combine(x, infinite) = x
5. combine(x, zero) = zero (for deadline at least)
6. Children never get looser budgets than parents

## Performance Considerations

- Budget should be 32 bytes or less (fits in 2 cache lines with padding)
- All operations should be branchless where possible
- Copy is trivial (no heap allocation)

## Example Usage
```rust
let parent_budget = Budget {
    deadline: Some(Time::from_secs(10)),
    poll_quota: 1000,
    cost_quota: Some(100),
    priority: 5,
};

let child_request = Budget {
    deadline: Some(Time::from_secs(5)),  // Tighter
    poll_quota: 2000,                     // Looser (will be ignored)
    cost_quota: None,                     // Use parent's
    priority: 7,                          // Higher
};

let effective = Budget::combine(&parent_budget, &child_request);
// effective.deadline = Some(5)    -- tighter wins
// effective.poll_quota = 1000     -- stricter wins
// effective.cost_quota = Some(100) -- parent's wins
// effective.priority = 7          -- higher wins
```

## References
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §1.4 (Budgets)
- asupersync_plan_v4.md §3.3 (Budget algebra as tropical structure)
- asupersync_plan_v4.md §11.7 (Network calculus view for Phase 1+)

## Acceptance Criteria
- Budget combines via componentwise meet (deadline/poll/cost: min; priority: max) and is monotone.
- Child budgets can never be looser than parent budgets (deadline monotonicity invariant).
- Budget consumption/exhaustion behavior is defined and consistent with the budget-exhaustion decision bead.
- Unit tests cover algebraic laws (assoc/comm/idempotent where applicable) and key edge cases.

title: Implement test oracle: no_obligation_leaks invariant checker
description:
## Purpose
Implement a test oracle that verifies the "no obligation leaks" invariant: all obligations (SendPermit, Ack, Lease, IoOp) are either committed or aborted before their owning region closes.

## The Invariant
From asupersync_plan_v4.md:
> Permits/acks/leases must be committed or aborted; no silent drops

Formally: `∀o ∈ obligations: state(o) ∈ {Committed, Aborted}` at region close

## Obligation Lifecycle
```
Created → [Committed | Aborted]
```

An obligation leak occurs when an obligation exists in Created state when its region closes.

## Oracle Design

```rust
pub struct ObligationLeakOracle {
    // Tracks all obligation lifecycle events
    creates: Vec<(ObligationId, ObligationKind, RegionId, Time)>,
    resolutions: Vec<(ObligationId, ObligationState, Time)>,  // Committed or Aborted
    region_closes: Vec<(RegionId, Time)>,
}

impl ObligationLeakOracle {
    /// Called when reserve() creates obligation
    pub fn on_create(&mut self, id: ObligationId, kind: ObligationKind, region: RegionId, time: Time);
    
    /// Called when commit() or abort() resolves obligation
    pub fn on_resolve(&mut self, id: ObligationId, state: ObligationState, time: Time);
    
    /// Called when region closes
    pub fn on_region_close(&mut self, region: RegionId, time: Time);
    
    /// Verify invariant holds
    pub fn check(&self) -> Result<(), ObligationLeakViolation>;
}
```

## Violation Detection
```rust
pub struct ObligationLeakViolation {
    pub region: RegionId,
    pub leaked_obligations: Vec<ObligationId>,
    pub kinds: Vec<ObligationKind>,  // SendPermit, Ack, Lease, IoOp
    pub region_close_time: Time,
}
```

A violation occurs when:
1. Region R closes at time T
2. ∃ obligation O in R with state ∉ {Committed, Aborted} at time T

## Obligation Kinds and Their Semantics
| Kind | Created By | Committed By | Aborted By |
|------|-----------|--------------|------------|
| SendPermit | tx.reserve() | permit.send() | permit.abort() or Drop |
| Ack | receive message | ack.commit() | ack.nack() |
| Lease | acquire_lease() | lease.release() | lease.expire() |
| IoOp | io.start() | io.complete() | io.cancel() |

## Linear Type Enforcement
The oracle complements Rust's ownership model:
- In ideal code, obligations are `#[must_use]` and consumed exactly once
- Oracle catches runtime violations that slip through static checks
- Particularly important for dynamic scenarios (vec of obligations, etc.)

## Testing the Oracle
1. **Correct case**: All obligations resolved → check passes
2. **Leak cases by kind**: Each obligation type can leak → check catches
3. **Nested regions**: Inner region obligations must resolve before inner closes
4. **Cancellation**: Cancelled tasks must still resolve their obligations (via abort)

## References
- asupersync_plan_v4.md: §4.4 Obligation Registry, §6.5 Two-Phase Operations
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md: Invariant I2 (obligation_resolved)

## Acceptance Criteria
- Oracle flags any leaked obligation (task completes with unresolved reserved obligations).
- Supports per-kind accounting (permits/acks/leases/ioops) and region-scoped checks.
- Diagnostics include obligation id, kind, holder task, and owning region.
- Deterministic; usable on both trace events and direct registry snapshots.

title: Design TraceEvent schema for recording
description:
## Overview

Design the TraceEvent enum that captures all sources of non-determinism in the Lab runtime.

## Background

For deterministic replay, we need to capture every decision point that could vary between runs. The existing trace module provides some infrastructure, but we need a comprehensive schema that covers all non-determinism.

## Sources of Non-Determinism to Capture

### Scheduling Decisions
- Which task was chosen when multiple are ready
- Task spawn ordering
- Task completion notification ordering

### Time Events
- Virtual time advances
- Timer creation and expiration
- Deadline checks

### I/O Simulation
- Simulated I/O results (success, error, bytes)
- I/O ordering when multiple pending

### RNG
- Deterministic RNG seed
- Each RNG call result (for verification)

### External Inputs
- Any future injection points
- Test oracle responses

## Deliverables

1. `TraceEvent` enum with variants for each category
2. `TraceMetadata` struct with version, timestamp, runtime config
3. Serialization derive macros (serde)
4. Size estimation (traces should be compact)

## Implementation Notes

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub enum TraceEvent {
    // Scheduling
    TaskScheduled { task_id: TaskId, at_tick: u64 },
    TaskYielded { task_id: TaskId },
    TaskCompleted { task_id: TaskId, outcome: Outcome<()> },
    
    // Time
    TimeAdvanced { from: u64, to: u64 },
    TimerCreated { id: u64, deadline: u64 },
    TimerFired { id: u64 },
    
    // I/O (simulated)
    IoResult { token: u64, result: SimulatedIoResult },
    
    // RNG
    RngSeed { seed: u64 },
    RngValue { value: u64 },
}
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] All non-determinism sources identified and covered
- [ ] Events are compact (estimate < 64 bytes typical)
- [ ] Format is versioned for forward compatibility
- [ ] Unit tests for serialization round-trip
