title: [EPIC] Cancellation Injection Testing Framework
description:
# Overview

A testing framework that systematically injects CancelRequested at every await point
in async code, then verifies that all invariants hold: obligations committed or aborted,
no leaked tasks, finalizers run, resources released.

## Why This Is The #1 Priority

This directly validates asupersync's core promise of "cancel-correctness." Without 
systematic testing, that's just marketing. This framework makes it PROVABLE.

The project's formal semantics (asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md) defines exactly what
invariants must hold. This framework tests those invariants exhaustively.

## How It Works

1. **First run**: Execute the test, recording all await points reached
2. **Subsequent runs**: For each await point N, inject cancellation at that point
3. **Verification**: After each injection, run all oracles to verify invariants

```rust
#[test]
fn test_http_request_cancel_correct() {
    Lab::new()
        .with_oracle(CancellationProtocolOracle)
        .with_oracle(ObligationLeakOracle)
        .with_oracle(TaskLeakOracle)
        .with_cancellation_injection(InjectionStrategy::AllPoints)
        .run(|cx| async {
            let client = HttpClient::new(cx);
            client.get("https://example.com").await
        });
    // Automatically runs N times, injecting at each await point
}
```

## Invariants Verified (from formal semantics)

1. **Task Leak**: All spawned tasks must complete before parent region closes
2. **Obligation Linearity**: All obligations must be Committed or Aborted, never Leaked
3. **Quiescence**: Region close implies no live children
4. **Loser Drain**: Race losers are fully drained before winner returns
5. **Cancellation Protocol**: State machine transitions are valid
6. **Finalizer Guarantee**: Finalizers run exactly once

## Implementation Approach

1. Create `InstrumentedFuture<F>` wrapper that tracks await points
2. On first poll, record await point ID (file:line or unique counter)
3. `InjectionStrategy` determines which points to test
4. For each point, re-run test with cancellation injected at that point
5. Run oracles after each injected run
6. Report: which points were tested, which failed, why

## User Value

- **Library authors**: "I can prove my async code is cancel-safe"
- **Application developers**: "My critical paths are verified"
- **Adopters**: "This runtime has rigor I can't get elsewhere"

## Implementation Estimate

- ~500-800 lines of new code
- Builds on existing LabReactor and Oracle infrastructure
- Touches: lab/, new test utilities

## Success Criteria

- [ ] Can specify injection strategy (all points, random sample, specific points)
- [ ] Captures all await points in a test
- [ ] Injects cancellation at each point reliably
- [ ] Runs all configured oracles after each injection
- [ ] Reports clear failure information
- [ ] Works with existing Lab infrastructure
- [ ] Documentation with examples

title: Actor mailbox: bounded channel with backpressure
description:
# Actor Mailbox Implementation

## Goal

Implement bounded mailboxes for actors that provide backpressure and integrate with the cancellation protocol.

## Background

Actors receive messages through mailboxes. Unlike unbounded queues (which can cause OOM), bounded mailboxes provide backpressure: when full, senders must wait or get backpressure signals.

## Design

### Mailbox<M>
- Wrapper around bounded mpsc channel
- Capacity specified at actor spawn time
- Integrates with two-phase send (reserve→commit)

### MailboxConfig
- capacity: usize (default: 64)
- overflow_policy: OverflowPolicy (Block, DropOldest, DropNewest, Error)
- priority_levels: Option<u8> (for priority mailboxes)

### MailboxHandle<M>
- Sender half given to ActorRef
- Methods: send(msg), try_send(msg), reserve() -> SendPermit

### MailboxReceiver<M>
- Receiver half held by ActorCell
- Methods: recv() -> Option<M>, try_recv(), is_empty(), len()

## Backpressure Semantics

When mailbox is full:
1. Block (default): Sender awaits until space available
2. DropOldest: Remove oldest message, insert new one
3. DropNewest: Reject new message immediately
4. Error: Return MailboxFull error

## Cancellation Integration

- recv() respects cancellation checkpoints
- Pending sends are aborted cleanly on actor cancellation
- SendPermit is an obligation (must commit or abort)

## Priority Mailbox (Optional)

For actors that need priority message handling:
- Multiple internal queues by priority level
- High-priority messages processed first
- Prevents priority inversion

## Implementation Notes

- Build on existing channel primitives in src/channel/
- MailboxConfig stored in ActorCell
- Metrics: messages_received, messages_dropped, current_depth

## Testing

- Backpressure: verify senders block when full
- Cancellation: verify clean abort of pending sends
- Priority: verify high-priority messages processed first
- Lab runtime: deterministic message ordering

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Mailbox<M> with configurable capacity
- [ ] OverflowPolicy enum with 4 strategies
- [ ] Two-phase send integration (SendPermit)
- [ ] Cancellation-safe recv()
- [ ] Optional priority levels
- [ ] Metrics for observability

title: [EPIC] Phase 2: Real Async I/O Reactor Implementation
description:
# Epic: Real Async I/O Reactor Implementation

## Background & Context

asupersync is a spec-first, cancel-correct, capability-secure async runtime for Rust. It is currently in **Phase 0**: a single-threaded deterministic kernel with no real I/O reactor. Instead, networking primitives use a "busy-loop on WouldBlock" pattern via `yield_now()`.

### Current Phase 0 Behavior (src/net/tcp/stream.rs)
```rust
// Phase 0: Busy-loop on WouldBlock
Err(ref e) if e.kind() == io::ErrorKind::WouldBlock => {
    cx.waker().wake_by_ref();  // Re-poll immediately
    Poll::Pending
}
```

This works for deterministic testing but is unsuitable for production:
- No efficient I/O multiplexing (epoll/kqueue/IOCP)
- Wastes CPU cycles spinning
- Cannot scale to many concurrent connections

## Why This Epic Matters

For rchd (remote compilation helper daemon) and similar production uses, we need:
1. **Unix socket server** - Real async accept/read/write for local IPC
2. **HTTP server capability** - Foundation for axum/hyper integration
3. **SSH connections** - Foundation for openssh-rs integration
4. **Event streaming** - Concurrent broadcast to multiple clients

## Design Philosophy (CRITICAL - Must Be Preserved)

This implementation MUST respect asupersync's core design principles:

1. **Structured Concurrency by Construction**
   - Tasks owned by regions forming a tree
   - Region close guarantees quiescence
   - No orphaned work possible

2. **Cancellation as a Protocol**
   - Not silent drops but explicit request → drain → finalize
   - Bounded cancellation budgets
   - Cancel-correct I/O operations

3. **Capability Security**
   - All effects flow through explicit `Cx` tokens
   - No ambient authority
   - IoCap<'r> capability tier for I/O operations

4. **Deterministic Testing**
   - Lab runtime with virtual time
   - Deterministic scheduling
   - Trace replay capability
   - LabReactor for simulated I/O

5. **Two-Phase Effects (Reserve/Commit)**
   - I/O operations should follow the reserve/commit pattern where applicable
   - ObligationRecord tracking for in-flight I/O

## Phase Roadmap Context
```
Phase 0: Single-thread deterministic kernel    ✅ COMPLETE
Phase 1: Parallel scheduler + region heap      🔜 In Progress
Phase 2: I/O integration                       📍 THIS EPIC
Phase 3: Actors + session types                Planned
Phase 4: Distributed structured concurrency    Planned
Phase 5: DPOR + TLA+ tooling                   Planned
```

## Implementation Strategy

We will build:
1. **Core Reactor Abstraction** - Platform-agnostic trait + IoDriver integration
2. **Linux Reactor (epoll)** - Primary target, most common production env
3. **macOS Reactor (kqueue)** - Developer machines
4. **Lab Reactor** - Deterministic testing with simulated I/O
5. **TCP/UDP Primitives Rewrite** - True async with reactor registration
6. **Unix Domain Sockets** - UdsListener/UdsStream for local IPC
7. **Integration Tests** - Prove correctness across platforms

## Success Criteria

- [ ] TCP server can accept thousands of connections efficiently
- [ ] Unix socket server works with real async I/O
- [ ] Lab runtime still provides deterministic testing
- [ ] Cancellation works correctly (tasks can be cancelled mid-I/O)
- [ ] Obligations are tracked for all in-flight I/O operations
- [ ] No CPU spinning on idle connections
- [ ] All existing tests still pass

title: [ALIEN][SCHED][LYAP] Spec: scheduler policy seam + determinism rules
description:
## Purpose

Define exactly how the Lyapunov governor is allowed to influence scheduling without breaking correctness or determinism.

This is the "policy object" seam: the scheduler remains correct by construction; the governor only affects deterministic tie-breaking and queue selection within allowed constraints.

## Conceptual model

We maintain a potential function over the runtime state Sigma:

V(Sigma) = w1 * obligations_unresolved
         + w2 * cancel_debt
         + w3 * deadline_slack_penalty
         + w4 * region_close_pressure
         + ...

The governor proposes actions that maximize drift reduction (-Delta V), subject to hard invariants.

In the deterministic lab runtime, "expected" is implemented as deterministic evaluation of candidate actions using the same snapshot function; no sampling.

## Allowed influence surface (must be explicit)

- tie-breaking among runnable tasks within the same lane
- selection among multiple ready queues when semantics permits
- optional: promotion within bounds (e.g., run cancel-debt tasks earlier)

## Hard invariants (non-negotiable)

- cancel lane strictness unless formally justified (cancel protocol must not be delayed)
- determinism: no wall-clock, no ambient RNG
- bounded fairness: governor cannot starve a runnable task indefinitely
- no semantic changes: only reordering of runnable work, not skipping required protocol steps

## Evidence ledger (galaxy-brain mode)

When enabled for debugging (trace-backed, bounded):
- record V decomposition for each decision
- record candidate comparisons: why task X beat task Y (Delta V components)
- record any policy constraints that forced a suboptimal choice

This must be emitted via tracing/trace events, not stdout.

## Acceptance criteria

- A clear policy interface exists (trait or config) specifying inputs/outputs and allowed hooks.
- Explicit deterministic ordering/tie-break rules are specified (including stable iteration order for candidate sets).
- A fairness story exists (e.g., governor score + age-based tiebreak, or bounded round-robin within score bands).

title: Unit and integration tests for Separation Logic specifications and proofs
description:
Comprehensive test suite for the Separation Logic proof infrastructure (specifications in bd-1xwvk.1, no-aliasing proof in bd-1xwvk.2, no-leak proof in bd-1xwvk.3).

BACKGROUND: While the formal proofs are verified by the proof tool (Creusot/Verus), we need a complementary runtime test suite that: (1) validates the proof assumptions hold in practice, (2) provides defense-in-depth with dynamic checking, (3) catches regressions when the implementation changes, and (4) verifies the proof tool integration with CI.

UNIT TESTS:
(1) Proof tool integration: verify cargo creusot (or verus) runs successfully on all annotated files and produces a verified result. This is a CI gate -- any proof regression fails the build.
(2) Ghost state consistency: add debug-mode runtime checks that mirror the ghost state in proofs. For each obligation lifecycle (create, transfer, release), verify the runtime ghost counter matches expected values.
(3) Specification coverage: for each formal specification in bd-1xwvk.1, write a runtime test that exercises the specified behavior and verifies the pre/post conditions hold dynamically.
(4) No-aliasing dynamic check: use a global debug-mode registry of outstanding permits. On create, insert. On transfer, move entry. On release, remove. At any point, assert each permit has exactly one owner. Test with 100 concurrent permit lifecycles.
(5) No-leak dynamic check: at region quiescence, assert the obligation counter for that region is zero. Test with 50 regions, each spawning 10 tasks with random obligations.
(6) Cancellation path coverage: verify Drop runs on all cancellation severities (Ok, Err, Cancelled, Panicked) and releases obligations correctly.
(7) Mutation testing: introduce known-bad mutations (clone a permit, skip release on one path) and verify either the proof tool rejects or the runtime check catches the violation.

INTEGRATION TESTS:
(8) Full obligation lifecycle under FrankenLab: run all obligation types through complete lifecycles with deterministic scheduling. Verify ghost counters are zero at completion.
(9) Cross-obligation interaction: test scenarios where multiple obligation types interact (SendPermit held while Lease is active), verify no cross-contamination.

PROPERTY-BASED TESTS (proptest):
(10) Random obligation lifecycle sequences: generate random create/transfer/release sequences, verify invariants (no aliasing, no leak) hold for all valid sequences.
(11) Random cancellation injection: generate random task trees with random cancel points, verify all obligations released after quiescence.

LOGGING REQUIREMENTS: Each test logs: test_name, proof_tool_used, verification_time_ms, ghost_counter_final, obligations_created, obligations_released, obligations_leaked (must be 0). On ghost counter mismatch: log full obligation lifecycle trace with create/transfer/release events. CI summary: proofs_verified, runtime_checks_passed, mutations_caught.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: (1) All formal proofs verify successfully in CI. (2) Runtime ghost counter checks pass for 10000 random obligation lifecycles. (3) All mutation tests detect the injected bug (either proof tool or runtime check). (4) Zero obligation leaks across all cancellation scenarios. (5) Tests complete in under 5 minutes on CI.

title: Implement futurelock detector (lab/debug)
description:
# Futurelock Detector (lab/debug)

## Purpose
Detect and surface the design-rule violation:

> Never allow a primitive to stop being polled while holding an obligation without transferring it, aborting/nacking it, or escalating.

In practice this shows up as a *futurelock*: a task holds one or more unresolved obligations (permits/acks/leases/IoOps) but is no longer being polled (e.g. it awaited something that never wakes, or it was dropped/forgotten by a buggy primitive).

Phase 0 needs this in **lab/debug** mode so we can turn “subtle deadlocks/leaks” into deterministic test failures with actionable evidence.

## Spec Background
- Design Bible §8.6: “Futurelock detector”
- Operational Semantics §1.9 + §3.4: obligations are linear; leaks are semantic errors
- Key invariant: a region cannot close while obligations in the region remain `Reserved`

A futurelock is *strictly worse* than a normal leak:
- a leak is “task completed while holding obligation”
- a futurelock is “task *didn’t* complete, but is also no longer being polled, so it can’t resolve the obligation”

## Design (Plan-of-Record)
### Observable behavior
When enabled, the lab runtime MUST:
1. Detect tasks that hold ≥1 `Reserved` obligations and have not been polled for a bounded number of lab steps (configurable).
2. Emit a trace-visible event with enough context to debug.
3. Optionally fail-fast (panic) in lab mode when the threshold is exceeded.

### Data we need
- `last_polled_step: u64` per task (updated every time we poll the task).
- Ability to query “held obligations” per task (from the obligation registry).
- Global `step_counter: u64` in the lab runtime.

### Detection rule
On each lab step (or at least whenever the scheduler makes progress):
- For each task `t` that currently holds ≥1 `Reserved` obligation:
  - if `step_counter - last_polled_step(t) > futurelock_max_idle_steps` then `futurelock_detected(t, …)`.

We should explicitly ignore tasks that are already terminal.

### Trace model
Add a semantic trace event (names flexible):
- `TraceEvent::FuturelockDetected { task: TaskId, region: RegionId, idle_steps: u64, held: Vec<ObligationId>, kinds: Vec<ObligationKind> }`

Constraints:
- The trace event must be deterministic and stable.
- Do NOT allocate on the hot path in production; this is lab/debug functionality.

### Config knobs
Add lab config fields (names flexible):
- `futurelock_max_idle_steps: u64` (default: conservative but small, e.g. 10_000)
- `panic_on_futurelock: bool` (default: true in lab tests)

## Testing
### Unit tests
- Construct a tiny obligation registry state where a task holds a reserved obligation and has an old `last_polled_step`; assert detection triggers.

### E2E lab scenarios
- Scenario: task reserves a SendPermit and then awaits a future that never wakes; another task continues making progress so the lab runtime keeps stepping. Assert:
  - a FuturelockDetected trace event appears
  - (if enabled) the runtime panics with a message that includes task id + obligation ids

## Acceptance Criteria
- Deterministic detection in lab mode (same seed/config => same detection point and trace).
- Trace event contains enough context to debug (task, region, obligation ids/kinds, idle steps).
- Does not introduce stdout/stderr logging in core runtime (only trace + test harness output).
- Clear documentation in the issue text about what counts as a futurelock and what does not.
notes: Implemented futurelock detection in lab runtime (TraceEventKind::FuturelockDetected + TraceData::Futurelock) with config knobs + unit tests; still blocked in Beads by asupersync-1mm/asupersync-l6l/asupersync-jdg status.
close_reason: Implementation verified complete: FuturelockDetected trace event, TraceData::Futurelock, InvariantViolation::Futurelock, config knobs (futurelock_max_idle_steps, panic_on_futurelock), and detection logic all implemented in src/lab/runtime.rs. All dependencies satisfied.

title: [SUB-EPIC] Core Reactor Abstraction & IoDriver
description:
# Sub-Epic: Core Reactor Abstraction & IoDriver

## Purpose

Define the platform-agnostic reactor interface and integrate it with the runtime's IoDriver. This is the foundation upon which all platform-specific reactors (epoll, kqueue, IOCP) are built.

## Background

The reactor abstraction already exists in stub form at `src/runtime/reactor/mod.rs`:

```rust
pub trait Reactor {
    fn register(&self, source: &dyn Source, interest: Interest) -> io::Result<Registration>;
    fn deregister(&self, registration: Registration) -> io::Result<()>;
    fn poll(&self, events: &mut Events, timeout: Option<Duration>) -> io::Result<usize>;
    fn wake(&self) -> io::Result<()>;
}
```

We need to:
1. Finalize this trait design
2. Implement proper Registration/Token management
3. Integrate with IoDriver for waker coordination
4. Design the Source trait for I/O sources (sockets, pipes, etc.)

## Design Considerations

### Waker Efficiency
Phase 0 uses `wake_by_ref()` which causes immediate re-poll. Real reactor needs:
- Slab-based waker storage (like mio/tokio)
- Token → TaskId mapping for targeted wakeups
- Batch processing of ready events

### Cancel-Correctness for I/O
When a task is cancelled mid-I/O:
- Deregister interest immediately
- Any in-flight data may be lost (documented behavior)
- Registration cleanup must be atomic

### Two-Phase I/O Operations
For cancel-safety, consider:
```rust
// Reserve phase: register interest, get permit
let permit = stream.reserve_read(cx).await?;
// Commit phase: perform actual read
let bytes = permit.read(buf)?;  // Linear, must happen
```

This is optional for basic I/O but important for advanced patterns.

## Key Types to Define/Refine

1. **Registration** - Handle to registered I/O source
2. **Token** - Compact ID for mapping events to wakers
3. **Interest** - Bitflags for READABLE/WRITABLE/ERROR
4. **Source** - Trait for things that can be registered (sockets, pipes)
5. **Events** - Container for ready events from poll()

## Integration Points

- `RuntimeState`: Hold reactor instance
- `IoDriver`: Bridge between reactor events and task wakers
- `Cx`: Provide IoCap capability tier for I/O registration
- `Scheduler`: Wake tasks when their I/O is ready

## Deliverables

1. Finalized `Reactor` trait with complete documentation
2. `Source` trait for registerable I/O sources
3. `Registration`, `Token`, `Interest`, `Events` types
4. `IoDriver` implementation with slab-based waker storage
5. Runtime integration (reactor in RuntimeState)
6. Unit tests for token allocation/deallocation

title: Epic: Distributed Structured Concurrency (Phase 4)
description:
# Epic: Distributed Structured Concurrency (Phase 4)

## Overview

This epic extends Asupersync's structured concurrency guarantees to distributed systems. Tasks can span multiple machines while preserving the region ownership model, cancel-correctness, and quiescence guarantees.

## Background & Context

The Asupersync roadmap defines Phase 4 as distributed structured concurrency. This is the most ambitious phase, applying the runtime's formal semantics across network boundaries.

Key insight: **The same invariants that make local concurrency safe also make distributed systems reliable.**

- Region close = quiescence → Graceful distributed shutdown
- Cancellation protocol → Network-aware cancellation propagation
- Obligation tracking → Distributed transaction guarantees
- Two-phase effects → Saga/compensating transactions

## Challenges

Distributed systems introduce:
1. **Partial failure**: Some nodes fail while others continue
2. **Network partitions**: Nodes can't communicate temporarily
3. **Clock skew**: No global time, only happens-before
4. **At-most-once vs at-least-once**: Message delivery semantics

## Design Principles

1. **Remote regions are regions**: Same ownership model, same close semantics
2. **Leases for remote resources**: Time-bounded claims, renewable
3. **Idempotency tokens**: Safe retries for at-least-once delivery
4. **Saga pattern**: Compensating transactions for multi-step operations
5. **Logical clocks**: Lamport/vector clocks, not wall time

## Architecture

```
LocalRuntime ←→ RemoteProxy ←→ Network ←→ RemoteRuntime

RemoteSpawn:
  - Create task/actor on remote node
  - Returns RemoteHandle with lease
  
RemoteRegion:
  - Distributed region spanning multiple nodes
  - Close requires quiescence across all nodes
  
Lease:
  - Time-bounded claim on remote resource
  - Must renew before expiry or resource released
  
IdempotencyToken:
  - Unique ID for deduplication
  - Enables safe retry on failure
```

## Components

1. **RemoteSpawn**: Spawn tasks on remote nodes
2. **Lease Manager**: Track and renew resource leases
3. **Idempotency Registry**: Deduplicate retried operations
4. **Saga Executor**: Multi-step transactions with compensation
5. **Distributed Cancel**: Propagate cancellation across nodes
6. **Logical Clocks**: Happens-before ordering

## Success Criteria

- Tasks can spawn on remote nodes
- Remote regions close to quiescence
- Cancellation propagates across network
- Leases prevent orphaned resources
- Sagas provide transaction guarantees
- Lab runtime can simulate network conditions

## Dependencies

This epic BLOCKS on:
- bd-3t9g: Actor System (remote actors build on local actors)
- bd-1j64: Runtime Core Maturity (stable local runtime first)

## References

- asupersync_plan_v4.md Section 4.3: Execution Tiers (Remote)
- asupersync_plan_v4.md Section 6: Distributed Extensions
- Pat Helland: 'Life Beyond Distributed Transactions'

## Non-Goals (for Phase 4)

- Full consensus protocol implementation (use external like Raft)
- Persistent storage layer (integrate with existing DBs)
- Service mesh / network infrastructure

# Async Networking Layer

## Overview
Full async networking with TCP, UDP, and Unix sockets, all with cancel-correct I/O obligations.

## Components

### 1. TCP
- TcpListener: bind, accept with obligations
- TcpStream: connect, read, write with obligations
- TcpSocket: advanced socket options before bind/connect

### 2. UDP
- UdpSocket: bind, send_to, recv_from
- Connected UDP: connect, send, recv

### 3. Unix Sockets (cfg(unix))
- UnixListener, UnixStream
- UnixDatagram
- Ancillary data (file descriptors)

### 4. I/O Obligations
Every I/O operation returns an IoObligation that must be:
- Completed (operation finished)
- Cancelled (cleanup performed)
- Never leaked

### 5. Cancel-Correct Patterns
- Read operations: cancel = discard partial data (acceptable)
- Write operations: two-phase (reserve buffer, commit)
- Accept: cancel = reject pending connection

### 6. Socket Options
- SO_REUSEADDR, SO_REUSEPORT
- TCP_NODELAY, SO_KEEPALIVE
- Timeouts (integrate with budgets)

## Platform Abstraction
- Linux: io_uring or epoll
- macOS: kqueue  
- Windows: IOCP

## Lab Runtime
- Virtual sockets for deterministic testing
- Fault injection (connection refused, reset, timeout)
- Latency simulation

## Success Criteria
- All socket types working
- Cancel-safety verified
- No obligation leaks in any scenario
- Deterministic tests for all network operations

title: Instrument obligation lifecycle with tracing
description:
# Task

Add tracing instrumentation for the obligation (two-phase commit) system.

## Background

Obligations are the mechanism for cancel-safe resource management:
- SendPermit: Channel send slots
- Ack: Message processing confirmation  
- Lease: Borrowed resources (RPC slots, etc.)
- IoOp: In-flight I/O operations

The lifecycle is: Reserved → (Committed | Aborted | Leaked)

Leaked obligations indicate bugs - a task completed while holding an uncommitted obligation.

## What to Instrument

1. **Reserve**: Obligation created
   - Fields: obligation_id, kind, holder_task, owning_region
   
2. **Commit**: Obligation fulfilled
   - Fields: obligation_id, duration_held
   
3. **Abort**: Obligation explicitly cancelled
   - Fields: obligation_id, abort_reason (cancel, error, explicit)
   
4. **Leak detection**: Obligation not resolved when task completes
   - Level: ERROR
   - Fields: obligation_id, kind, holder_task, held_duration
   - This is a BUG indicator

## Integration with Cancellation

When a task is cancelled:
1. Cancel requested → obligations should start aborting
2. If task completes with Reserved obligations → LEAK ERROR

Tracing should make this flow visible:

```
obligation[id=55, kind=SendPermit, state=Reserved]
  task_cancel_requested[task=100]
    obligation[id=55, transition=Reserved→Aborted, reason=task_cancelled]
```

vs the bug case:

```
obligation[id=55, kind=SendPermit, state=Reserved]
  task_completed[task=100, outcome=Ok]
    obligation_leaked[id=55, kind=SendPermit] // ERROR!
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Reserve emits span with full context
- [ ] Commit/Abort emit events with duration
- [ ] Leak detection emits ERROR level event
- [ ] Cancellation→abort flow is traceable
- [ ] Integration tests verify obligation tracing

```rust
    "region",
    id = %region_id,
    parent = %parent_id,
    state = %"Open",
);

#[cfg(feature = "tracing")]

```

- [ ] Region entry creates span with correct fields
- [ ] State transitions update span or emit events
- [ ] Region exit closes span with final state
- [ ] Parent/child causality linked via follows_from
- [ ] No compilation when tracing feature disabled

title: Implement test oracle: losers_always_drained invariant checker
description:
## Purpose
Implement a test oracle that verifies the "losers always drained" invariant: in any race/select operation, losing tasks are cancelled AND fully drained before the operation returns.

## The Invariant
From asupersync_plan_v4.md:
> Races must cancel and fully drain losers

This prevents resource leaks, ensures cleanup runs, and maintains predictable behavior.

## What "Drained" Means
A task is drained when it has:
1. Received cancel request (`CancelRequested` state)
2. Run to next checkpoint (`Cancelling` state)
3. Executed finalizers (`Finalizing` state)
4. Reached `Completed(Cancelled)` state

Simply requesting cancellation is NOT sufficient. The task must actually complete.

## Oracle Design

```rust
pub struct LoserDrainOracle {
    // Tracks race/select operations
    race_starts: Vec<RaceEvent>,
    race_completes: Vec<RaceCompletion>,
    task_drains: HashMap<TaskId, DrainRecord>,
}

pub struct RaceEvent {
    pub race_id: RaceId,
    pub participants: Vec<TaskId>,
    pub start_time: Time,
}

pub struct RaceCompletion {
    pub race_id: RaceId,
    pub winner: TaskId,
    pub losers: Vec<TaskId>,
    pub complete_time: Time,
}

pub struct DrainRecord {
    pub cancel_requested: Option<Time>,
    pub drain_started: Option<Time>,
    pub finalizers_complete: Option<Time>,
    pub fully_drained: Option<Time>,
}

impl LoserDrainOracle {
    /// Called when race/select starts
    pub fn on_race_start(&mut self, race_id: RaceId, participants: Vec<TaskId>, time: Time);
    
    /// Called when race determines winner
    pub fn on_race_complete(&mut self, race_id: RaceId, winner: TaskId, time: Time);
    
    /// Called when task fully drains
    pub fn on_task_drained(&mut self, task: TaskId, time: Time);
    
    /// Verify all losers are drained before race returns
    pub fn check(&self) -> Result<(), LoserDrainViolation>;
}
```

## Violation Detection
```rust
pub struct LoserDrainViolation {
    pub race_id: RaceId,
    pub winner: TaskId,
    pub undrained_losers: Vec<(TaskId, DrainRecord)>,
    pub race_return_time: Time,
}
```

A violation occurs when:
1. Race R completes at time T
2. ∃ loser L where `fully_drained` time > T or is None

## Operations That Must Drain Losers
| Operation | Winner | Losers |
|-----------|--------|--------|
| `race(a, b)` | First to complete | Other participants |
| `select\!{...}` | Selected branch | Unselected branches |
| `quorum(M, N)` | First M successes | Remaining N-M |
| `first_ok(...)` | First success | Operations after success |
| `timeout(op, d)` | Whichever wins | Timeout or op |

## Testing the Oracle
1. **Two-way race**: Winner and loser properly handled
2. **N-way race**: Multiple losers all drained
3. **Nested races**: Inner race losers drained before outer race proceeds
4. **Loser with finalizers**: Finalizers run during drain
5. **Loser with obligations**: Obligations resolved during drain
6. **Slow drain**: Loser takes time to reach checkpoint

## Drain Timing Verification
The oracle tracks timing to ensure:
- `race_return_time > max(loser_drain_times)`
- Race does NOT return until all losers fully drained

## References
- asupersync_plan_v4.md: §5.5 Race with Loser Draining, §1.1 Non-negotiable invariants
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md: RACE-LOSER-DRAIN rule

## Acceptance Criteria
- Oracle identifies each race and validates that all losers reach terminal completion before the race returns.
- Also validates losers are cancelled (or otherwise transitioned out of running) promptly.
- Produces actionable diagnostics (winner/loser ids, missing completion event).
- Deterministic and runs on every E2E scenario trace.
close_reason: Implemented oracle module with TaskLeakOracle, ObligationLeakOracle, QuiescenceOracle, LoserDrainOracle, FinalizerOracle. All tests passing, clippy clean.

title: Implement TraceRecorder for Lab runtime
description:
## Overview

Implement the TraceRecorder that instruments the Lab runtime to emit trace events during execution.

## Background

Once we have the TraceEvent schema, we need to hook into Lab runtime's decision points to capture events without adding significant overhead.

## Design Requirements

### Low Overhead
- Recording should not significantly slow down test execution
- Use buffered writes
- Consider memory-mapped file for large traces

### Non-Invasive
- Lab runtime code changes should be minimal
- Use callback/observer pattern
- Recording should be opt-in (disabled by default)

### Thread-Safe
- Handle recording from multiple Lab runtime threads
- Use lock-free structures where possible

## Implementation Approach

```rust
pub struct TraceRecorder {
    events: Vec<TraceEvent>,
    metadata: TraceMetadata,
    enabled: bool,
}

impl TraceRecorder {
    pub fn new(config: RecorderConfig) -> Self;
    pub fn record(&mut self, event: TraceEvent);
    pub fn finish(self) -> RecordedTrace;
}

// In Lab runtime, add hooks:
impl LabRuntime {
    pub fn with_recorder(config, recorder: TraceRecorder) -> Self;
}
```

## Integration Points

1. `Scheduler::pick_next_task()` - record choice
2. `VirtualClock::advance()` - record time changes
3. `SimulatedIo::complete()` - record I/O results
4. `DeterministicRng::next()` - record RNG values

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] TraceRecorder captures all TraceEvent variants
- [ ] Recording adds < 5% overhead to test execution
- [ ] Events are captured in correct causal order
- [ ] Integration with Lab runtime is clean and minimal
- [ ] Unit tests verify recording correctness

title: [EPIC-PHASE] Phase 1 - Parallel Scheduler and Region Heap
description:
## Overview
Phase 1 extends the single-threaded deterministic kernel (Phase 0) to support parallel execution with work-stealing, region-isolated heaps, and multi-threaded scheduling while preserving all invariants.

## Goals
1. Enable true parallelism for throughput
2. Maintain determinism in lab runtime (parallel simulation)
3. Implement region heap for memory isolation
4. Work-stealing scheduler for load balancing
5. All Phase 0 invariants MUST be preserved

## Key Components

### 1. Work-Stealing Scheduler
- Per-worker local queues
- Global steal queue for overflow
- Lock-free deque implementation
- Maintain scheduling determinism via virtual schedule in lab mode

### 2. Region Heap
- Each region owns its allocations
- Mass deallocation on region close
- Thread-safe allocation within region
- Region-local bump allocator (fast path)
- Fallback to global allocator

### 3. Parallel Task Model
- `Task<T>` is `Send` - can migrate between workers
- Wake deduplication across threads
- Atomic task state transitions
- Thread-safe RegionRecord access

### 4. Synchronization Primitives (Parallel Versions)
- Lock-free MPSC queue
- Sharded counters for obligations
- Atomic region state machine

## Dependencies
- Requires complete Phase 0 kernel
- Requires all Phase 0 invariants proven/tested
- Requires two-phase primitives from Phase 0

## Constraints
- No additional invariants beyond Phase 0
- Must support lab runtime schedule replay
- Must support deterministic parallel simulation
- Cannot break cancel-correctness

## Non-Goals for Phase 1
- I/O integration (Phase 2)
- Actor model (Phase 3)
- Distributed execution (Phase 4)
- DPOR/TLA+ tooling (Phase 5)

## Mathematical Foundation
From the spec:
- Work-stealing preserves eventual quiescence
- Region heap uses arena allocation semantics
- Parallel near-semiring: join/race laws still hold under parallelism

## Testing Strategy
- All Phase 0 tests must pass
- Add parallel stress tests
- Add work-stealing correctness tests
- Verify determinism under parallel lab runtime

## References
- asupersync_plan_v4.md: §7 Phase 1 (Parallel)
- Chase-Lev work-stealing deque
- Region-based memory management (Tofte-Talpin)

## Success Criteria
- Parallel scheduler executes `Send` tasks across multiple workers while preserving Phase 0 invariants.
- Region heap enables safe region-owned allocation and quiescent reclamation on close.
- Lab runtime can deterministically *simulate* multi-worker schedules (repeatable traces).
- Stress/E2E tests cover work stealing, cancellation drain, and quiescence under contention.

title: Implement Chase-Lev work-stealing deque (core primitive)
description:
# Chase–Lev Work-Stealing Deque

## Purpose
Implement the core work-stealing deque used by each worker:
- owner pushes/pops from the bottom (fast path)
- thieves steal from the top

This is the backbone of parallel scheduling.

## Constraints
- Must be correct under data-race-free Rust (use atomics).
- Must avoid `unsafe` in core if at all possible (unsafe is forbidden by project rules).
  - If a fully lock-free implementation requires unsafe, we must design an alternative:
    - use `Mutex`/`RwLock` in Phase 1 initially (correctness first), then optimize later
    - or encapsulate unsafe behind a separately-audited crate (only if allowed)

Given the project’s `unsafe` prohibition, the plan-of-record should start with a correct, deterministic, safe implementation even if it is not maximally performant.

## Plan-of-Record Options
### Option A: Safe deque with locks (Phase 1 baseline)
- Use `Mutex<VecDeque<TaskId>>` per worker.
- Steal = pop_front.
- Push/pop = push_back/pop_back.
- Determinism in lab is straightforward.

### Option B: Lock-free deque (requires careful review)
- Many lock-free implementations require unsafe and careful memory ordering.
- Likely incompatible with `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` in core.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Correctness properties:
  - no lost tasks
  - no duplicated tasks
  - owner pop and thief steal interleavings behave correctly
- Deterministic tests simulate concurrent accesses.

## Testing
- Model-based tests:
  - simulate multiple threads performing operations
  - verify resulting multiset of tasks matches expected
close_reason: LocalQueue implements safe lock-based work-stealing deque with tests

Each worker maintains (at minimum):

- cancel work is not starved by ready work

description:
# Phase 1: Region Heap + Send Task Model

## Purpose
Make the “task tier” sound:
- allow `Send` tasks to migrate across workers
- preserve region ownership and lifetimes via region-owned allocation

This is the “soundness frontier” encoded into the runtime:
- fibers (Phase 0): borrow-friendly, same-thread
- tasks (Phase 1): `Send`, parallel, region-heap-backed

## Requirements
- Region-owned allocation arena that is reclaimed only after region close/quiescence.
- A `RRef<'r, T>`-style handle (or equivalent) to store data with region lifetime.
- Clear rules for what can be captured in a migrating task.

## Acceptance Criteria
- It is impossible (by construction or by runtime checks) for a migrating task to hold references that outlive the region heap.
- Region close safely reclaims region heap after quiescence.

## Testing
- Parallel tests that allocate in region heap, migrate tasks, and verify data remains valid.
- Leak tests: ensure region heap reclaimed only after close.

title: Implement region heap allocator + quiescent reclamation
description:
# Region Heap Allocator + Quiescent Reclamation

## Purpose
Enable safe parallel tasks by allocating captured data in a region-owned heap that is reclaimed only when the region closes to quiescence.

This is the memory backbone for the “task tier.”

## Requirements
- Region heap lifetime = region lifetime.
- Reclamation only after:
  - all child tasks terminal
  - all finalizers complete
  - all obligations resolved

## Design Notes
- Start with a simple allocator design:
  - bump allocator per region for fast-path
  - fallback to global allocator when necessary
- Determinism: allocation addresses must not be used as observable identifiers.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Region heap allocations remain valid for all tasks owned by the region.
- Region heap is reclaimed on region close without leaks.

## Testing
- Allocate values in region heap, spawn tasks that read them, close region, ensure memory is reclaimed (via debug counters, not UB).

title: Implement RRef<'r, T> (region-owned Send reference)
description:
# RRef<'r, T> (Region-Owned Reference)

## Purpose
Provide a way for migrating (`Send`) tasks to reference data allocated in the region heap safely.

## Requirements
- `RRef<'r, T>` ties to region lifetime `'r`.
- `RRef<'r, T>` can be `Send`/`Sync` when `T` is.
- No unsafe code in core (if possible). If unavoidable, redesign.

## Design Sketch
- Internally represent as:
  - `Arc<RegionHeap>` + offset/index into heap
  - OR `Arc<T>` allocated via region heap wrapper (but `Arc` implies refcount overhead)

Given performance goals, prefer region heap + offset, but we must reconcile with `unsafe` prohibition.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Users can spawn Send tasks that capture `RRef`s without lifetime violations.
- Region close guarantees memory validity until tasks are done.

## Testing
- Compile-time tests for trait bounds (`Send`/`Sync` conditions).
- Runtime tests: create `RRef`, spawn tasks across workers, validate reads.
close_reason: RRef implemented in src/types/rref.rs with Send/Sync bounds + tests

title: Define Send task tier API and soundness rules
description:
# Send Task Tier API + Soundness Rules

## Purpose
Make the “soundness frontier” explicit:
- Phase 0 supports single-thread fibers that can borrow.
- Phase 1 adds Send tasks that may migrate across workers.

This task defines the API and rules for spawning Send tasks.

## Rules to Encode
- A migrating task must be `Send`.
- Captured data must be safe across threads:
  - either `'static`
  - or allocated in region heap and referenced via `RRef<'r, T>`.
- Cancellation and obligations semantics are identical to fibers.

## API Sketch
```rust
impl<'r> Scope<'r> {
    pub fn spawn_task<T: Send + 'r>(...) -> JoinHandle<'r, T>;
}
```

We may also model capabilities:
- `FiberCap` vs `TaskCap`

## Acceptance Criteria
- API prevents accidental unsound captures.
- Lab runtime can simulate this tier deterministically.

## Testing
- Compile-fail tests for borrowing captures in Send tasks.
- Runtime tests for cross-thread execution.

title: [fastapi-integration] Cross-Project Coordination Protocol
description:
# Cross-Project Coordination Protocol

## Objective
Establish communication and dependency management protocols between the Asupersync and fastapi_rust projects.

## Background

### Why Cross-Project Coordination?
- fastapi_rust depends on Asupersync APIs
- API changes in Asupersync can break fastapi_rust
- Shared development benefits from synchronized planning
- Bug reports may span both projects

## Requirements

### 1. Communication Channels

#### Beads Thread Prefix
All integration-related beads use thread_id prefix:
- `fastapi-asupersync-integration`

Example:
```
bd create --title="[fastapi-integration] ..." --thread=fastapi-asupersync-integration
```

#### Agent Mail Threads
For async agent coordination:
- Thread: `fastapi-asupersync-sync`
- Subject format: `[fastapi-asupersync] <topic>`

### 2. Dependency Management

#### Cargo.toml Pattern
```toml
# In fastapi_rust/Cargo.toml

[dependencies]
# During development: path dependency
asupersync = { path = "../asupersync" }

# For release: crates.io with version
# asupersync = "0.1"
```

#### Version Pinning Strategy
- fastapi_rust pins Asupersync to minor version: `"0.1"`
- Breaking changes require coordination before release
- Pre-release testing with git dependency

### 3. API Stability Contract

#### Stable APIs (semver guaranteed)
- `Cx` capability token
- `Outcome` type and variants
- `Budget` type and methods
- Core combinators (join, race, timeout)

#### Unstable APIs (may change)
- Internal scheduler details
- Lab runtime internals
- Platform-specific I/O backends

### 4. Shared Type Considerations

#### Option A: Re-export
fastapi_rust re-exports Asupersync types:
```rust
// In fastapi_rust
pub use asupersync::{Outcome, Budget, Cx};
```

#### Option B: Thin API Crate
Create `asupersync-api` crate with just types:
```
asupersync-api/
├── Outcome
├── Budget
├── CancelReason
└── Error types
```

Both asupersync and fastapi_rust depend on asupersync-api.

#### Recommendation
Start with Option A (re-export), consider Option B if:
- Multiple downstream projects need shared types
- Compile times become an issue
- Need to decouple version cycles

### 5. Breaking Change Protocol

When Asupersync makes a breaking change:
1. Open bead in both projects
2. Document migration path
3. fastapi_rust tests against branch BEFORE merge
4. Coordinate release timing

### 6. Bug Report Protocol

Cross-project bugs:
1. Determine root cause location
2. File bead in appropriate project
3. Link beads if fix spans both projects
4. Coordinate testing

### 7. Sync Meetings (if needed)

For complex coordination:
- Ad-hoc via Agent Mail thread
- Decision log in bead comments

## Deliverables
1. [ ] Thread naming convention documented
2. [ ] Cargo.toml pattern documented
3. [ ] API stability classification documented
4. [ ] Breaking change protocol documented
5. [ ] Bug report protocol documented

## References
- AGENTS.md: Agent coordination via beads and Agent Mail
- Cargo documentation: dependency specifications

title: EPIC: Asupersync ↔ fastapi_rust Integration
description:
# EPIC: Asupersync ↔ fastapi_rust Integration

## Executive Summary

This epic tracks the co-development coordination between Asupersync (spec-first async runtime) and fastapi_rust (Rust web framework). fastapi_rust will use Asupersync as its async runtime foundation, requiring close API alignment and coordinated development.

## Background

**Asupersync** provides:
- Structured concurrency with region-based task ownership
- Cancel-correct operations with bounded cleanup
- Two-phase effects (reserve/commit) preventing data loss
- Capability-secured effects through explicit `Cx` tokens
- Deterministic lab runtime for testing

**fastapi_rust** needs:
- Async runtime for HTTP request handling
- Request context (similar to Cx) for per-request state
- Error handling compatible with HTTP semantics
- TCP I/O for network operations
- Graceful shutdown for zero-downtime deployments
- Deterministic testing for request handlers

## Integration Architecture

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      fastapi_rust Application                     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                   │
│  ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐          │
│  │   Router    │ →  │  Middleware │ →  │   Handler   │          │
│  └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └──────┬──────┘          │
│                                               │                   │
│                                               ▼                   │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │                    RequestContext (Cx)                     │  │
│  │  • Request metadata    • Response builder                  │  │
│  │  • Budget (timeout)    • Cancellation token                │  │
│  │  • Trace/span context  • Capability tokens                 │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                              │                                    │
└──────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┘
                               │
                               ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      Asupersync Runtime                           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                   │
│  ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐          │
│  │   Regions   │    │    Tasks    │    │ Obligations │          │
│  │  (per-req)  │    │  (handlers) │    │  (2-phase)  │          │
│  └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘          │
│                                                                   │
│  ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐          │
│  │  Scheduler  │    │   TCP I/O   │    │ Lab Runtime │          │
│  └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘          │
│                                                                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Development Phases

### Phase 0 (Immediate) - Foundation
- Cx capability token integration for RequestContext
- Outcome type exposure for HTTP error handling  
- Public API surface documentation
- Cross-crate compilation verification

### Phase 1 (Core HTTP) - Networking
- TCP I/O traits (TcpListener, TcpStream)
- Budget integration for request timeouts
- Connection lifecycle management
- Accept loop with backpressure

### Phase 2+ (Advanced) - Full Integration
- Request handlers as regions (structured concurrency)
- Lab runtime for deterministic HTTP testing
- Graceful shutdown coordination
- Distributed tracing integration

## Key Design Decisions

### 1. RequestContext as Cx Extension
fastapi_rust's RequestContext will WRAP Asupersync's Cx, not replace it:
```rust
pub struct RequestContext<'a> {
    cx: Cx<'a>,              // Asupersync capability
    request: &'a Request,     // HTTP request
    response: ResponseBuilder, // HTTP response
    // ... fastapi-specific fields
}
```

### 2. Outcome ↔ HTTP Status Mapping
```
Outcome::Ok(T)        → 200 OK / custom success status
Outcome::Err(E)       → 4xx/5xx based on error kind
Outcome::Cancelled    → 499 Client Closed Request
Outcome::Panicked     → 500 Internal Server Error
```

### 3. Request Budget = Request Timeout
HTTP request timeouts map directly to Asupersync Budget:
- deadline_ns: request timeout
- poll_quota: optional compute limit
- cost_quota: optional memory limit

### 4. Connection as Region
Each HTTP connection spawns a region; each request spawns a sub-region:
```
Server Region
├── Connection Region (long-lived)
│   ├── Request Region (short-lived)
│   ├── Request Region
│   └── ...
└── Connection Region
    └── ...
```

## Success Criteria

1. fastapi_rust can depend on asupersync as sole async runtime
2. RequestContext provides full Cx capability access
3. HTTP errors map cleanly to Outcome semantics
4. Request timeouts use Budget system
5. Graceful shutdown cancels all in-flight requests correctly
6. Lab runtime can test HTTP handlers deterministically
7. No orphaned connections or leaked resources

## Cross-Project Coordination

### Communication
- Use thread_id prefix: `fastapi-asupersync-integration`
- Beads reference each other via ID
- Agent Mail for async coordination

### Dependency Management
- fastapi_rust depends on asupersync (Cargo.toml)
- API breaking changes require coordination
- Shared types may need `asupersync-api` crate

## References
- Asupersync README.md: Architecture and design philosophy
- asupersync_plan_v4.md: Detailed specification
- AGENTS.md: Non-negotiable invariants (fastapi must not violate)

## Owner
Joint: Asupersync team + IvoryWolf (fastapi_rust)

title: [EPIC-INFRA] Symbol-Native Distributed Regions
description:
# EPIC: Symbol-Native Distributed Regions

**Bead ID:** asupersync-y1p
**Type:** EPIC
**Priority:** P1
**Status:** OPEN
**Owner:** Dicklesworthstone

---

## Vision

Symbol-Native Distributed Regions extend asupersync's structured concurrency model across machine boundaries using RaptorQ erasure coding for fault-tolerant state replication. This EPIC transforms local regions - with their guarantees of task containment, cancellation propagation, and orderly shutdown - into distributed regions that maintain these same guarantees despite network partitions, node failures, and Byzantine conditions.

The core insight is that region state (task trees, pending obligations, finalizers) can be serialized into RaptorQ symbols and distributed to replica nodes. When quorum is maintained, the distributed region operates normally. When failures occur, the region can recover from any subset of replicas that collectively hold enough symbols to reconstruct the state. This is erasure coding applied to structured concurrency itself.

The distributed region model preserves the local programming model: developers spawn tasks into regions, regions nest hierarchically, cancellation flows from parent to child. The difference is that the region's state is durably replicated, making the structured concurrency tree resilient to infrastructure failures without requiring developers to think about replication.

---

## Goals

- **Define distributed region state model** with clear state machine for initialization, active operation, degradation, and recovery
- **Implement state encoding** that serializes region snapshots into RaptorQ symbols with configurable redundancy
- **Implement symbol distribution** that replicates encoded state to replicas using quorum-based writes
- **Implement recovery protocol** that reconstructs region state from surviving replicas when quorum is lost
- **Integrate with local regions** providing transparent upgrade path from local to distributed operation
- **Preserve structured concurrency guarantees** across the distributed boundary

---

## Non-Goals

- **Distributed consensus**: This layer uses RaptorQ for data redundancy, not Raft/Paxos for agreement
- **Distributed transactions**: ACID transactions across regions are a higher-level concern
- **Automatic sharding**: Horizontal partitioning of regions is not addressed
- **Cross-datacenter replication**: WAN-optimized replication strategies are future work
- **Persistent storage**: Durable storage backends (disk, S3) are external to this layer

---

## Child Beads

| ID | Title | Status | Priority | Description |
|----|-------|--------|----------|-------------|
| asupersync-qqw | Define DistributedRegion State Model | OPEN | P1 | State machine for distributed region lifecycle |
| asupersync-h10 | Implement Region Symbol Encoding/Distribution | OPEN | P1 | Serialize region state to symbols, distribute to replicas |
| asupersync-tjd | Implement Region Recovery Protocol | OPEN | P1 | Reconstruct region state from surviving replicas |
| asupersync-p0u | Integrate with Local Region Types | OPEN | P1 | Bridge between local and distributed regions |
| asupersync-o78 | Comprehensive Distributed Region Tests | OPEN | P2 | Integration tests for distributed operation |

---

## Phases

### Phase 1: State Model and Encoding
**Duration:** 2 sprints
**Deliverables:**
- `DistributedRegionState` enum with all lifecycle states
- `RegionSnapshot` serialization format
- `StateEncoder` converting snapshots to RaptorQ symbols
- Deterministic encoding for testability

**Exit Criteria:**
- State machine transitions are well-defined and tested
- Region state can be encoded and decoded correctly
- Encoding is deterministic (same state = same symbols)

### Phase 2: Distribution and Replication
**Duration:** 2 sprints
**Deliverables:**
- `SymbolDistributor` for routing symbols to replicas
- Quorum-based write acknowledgment
- Incremental/delta state updates
- Epoch-bounded state versions

**Exit Criteria:**
- Writes succeed when quorum acknowledges
- Delta updates reduce bandwidth for incremental changes
- State versions are properly ordered by epoch

### Phase 3: Recovery and Integration
**Duration:** 2 sprints
**Deliverables:**
- `RecoveryCollector` gathering symbols from replicas
- `StateDecoder` reconstructing region state
- `RegionBridge` connecting local and distributed APIs
- Comprehensive test suite

**Exit Criteria:**
- Recovery succeeds from any quorum of replicas
- Local regions can be upgraded to distributed
- All integration tests pass

---

## Success Criteria

1. **Recovery Correctness**: Region state recovers correctly from any K' >= threshold symbols across replicas
2. **Quorum Semantics**: Writes succeed with quorum (N/2+1), reads succeed with quorum
3. **State Consistency**: Recovered state is identical to last committed state
4. **Latency Overhead**: Distributed operation adds <50ms overhead to local region operations
5. **Partition Tolerance**: System continues operating in degraded mode during partitions
6. **Cancel Propagation**: Cancellation flows correctly across distributed region boundaries
7. **Lifecycle Synchronization**: Local and distributed region states remain consistent

---

## Dependencies

### Depends On
- **asupersync-0vx** (Foundation Layer) - RaptorQ encoding/decoding infrastructure
- **asupersync-7gm** (Transport Layer) - Symbol transport to replicas
- **asupersync-bsx** (Epoch Concurrency) - Epoch boundaries for state versioning
- `src/record/region.rs` - Local region infrastructure

### Blocks
- **asupersync-zfn** (Symbolic Obligations) - Uses distributed regions for obligation tracking
- **asupersync-9mq** (Integration) - Distributed regions in unified API

---

## Acceptance Criteria Checklist

### DistributedRegion State Model (asupersync-qqw)
- [ ] `DistributedRegionState` enum: Initializing, Active, Degraded, Recovering, Closing, Closed
- [ ] State transition rules with clear triggers and guards
- [ ] `RegionSnapshot` capturing full region state (tasks, children, finalizers, metadata)
- [ ] Version tracking with epoch bounds
- [ ] Metrics for state transitions

### Region Symbol Encoding/Distribution (asupersync-h10)
- [ ] `StateEncoder` serializing `RegionSnapshot` to bytes
- [ ] RaptorQ encoding of serialized state into symbols
- [ ] `SymbolDistributor` routing symbols to configured replicas
- [ ] Quorum write acknowledgment with configurable consistency level
- [ ] Delta encoding for incremental state updates
- [ ] Symbol tagging with region ID, epoch, and version

### Region Recovery Protocol (asupersync-tjd)
- [ ] Recovery trigger detection (quorum loss, node restart, admin command)
- [ ] `RecoveryCollector` querying replicas for symbols
- [ ] Progress tracking during symbol collection
- [ ] RaptorQ decoding when threshold reached
- [ ] State reconstruction from decoded snapshot
- [ ] Partial recovery for large regions
- [ ] Cancellation-aware recovery (interruptible)

### Integration with Local Region Types (asupersync-p0u)
- [ ] `RegionBridge` connecting local Region API to distributed backend
- [ ] Transparent promotion of local regions to distributed
- [ ] Lifecycle synchronization between local and distributed states
- [ ] Type conversions preserving structured concurrency guarantees
- [ ] API compatibility (spawn, cancel, close work identically)
- [ ] Mixed region trees (local and distributed in same hierarchy)

### Test Suite (asupersync-o78)
- [ ] State machine transition tests
- [ ] Encoding/decoding roundtrip tests
- [ ] Quorum write tests
- [ ] Recovery from various failure scenarios
- [ ] Integration with local regions
- [ ] Performance benchmarks

---

## State Machine Overview

```
                    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │                                         │
                    ▼                                         │
  ┌──────────────────────┐                                    │
  │     Initializing     │────────────────┐                   │
  │  (gathering quorum)  │                │                   │
  └──────────┬───────────┘                │                   │
             │ quorum_reached             │ timeout           │
             ▼                            ▼                   │
  ┌──────────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────────┐      │
  │       Active         │      │       Failed         │      │
  │  (normal operation)  │      │  (initialization     │      │
  └──────────┬───────────┘      │   failed)            │      │
             │                  └──────────────────────┘      │
             │ quorum_lost                                    │
             ▼                                                │
  ┌──────────────────────┐                                    │
  │      Degraded        │◀───────────────────────────────────┤
  │  (partial quorum)    │                                    │
  └──────────┬───────────┘                                    │
             │ recovery_triggered                             │
             ▼                                                │
  ┌──────────────────────┐      recovery_complete             │
  │     Recovering       │────────────────────────────────────┘
  │  (rebuilding state)  │
  └──────────┬───────────┘
             │ close_requested
             ▼
  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │       Closing        │
  │  (draining tasks)    │
  └──────────┬───────────┘
             │ drained
             ▼
  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │       Closed         │
  │  (terminal state)    │
  └──────────────────────┘
```

---

## Risk Assessment

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation |
|------|------------|--------|------------|
| State serialization bloat | Medium | Medium | Delta encoding, compression, lazy serialization |
| Recovery takes too long for large regions | Medium | High | Incremental recovery, parallel collection |
| Split-brain during network partition | Medium | High | Epoch fencing, quorum validation |
| Local/distributed state divergence | Low | High | Strong lifecycle synchronization, invariant checking |
| Recovery loop (constant re-recovery) | Low | High | Backoff, circuit breaker on recovery attempts |

## Profiling Results (GentleMountain)

Created comprehensive benchmark suite: benches/raptorq_benchmark.rs

### GF(256) Primitives Baseline
| Operation | 64B | 256B | 1KB | 4KB | 16KB |
|-----------|-----|------|-----|-----|------|
| add_slice (XOR) | 10.9 GiB/s | 19.3 GiB/s | 22.8 GiB/s | 23.4 GiB/s | 21.8 GiB/s |
| mul_slice | 1.1 GiB/s | 1.1 GiB/s | 0.9 GiB/s | 1.2 GiB/s | 1.1 GiB/s |
| addmul_slice | 1.0 GiB/s | 1.0 GiB/s | 1.1 GiB/s | 1.0 GiB/s | 1.1 GiB/s |

### Key Findings
1. XOR (add_slice) is memory-bound at ~20-24 GiB/s - SIMD autovectorized by LLVM
2. addmul_slice is THE hot path at ~1 GiB/s (20x slower than XOR due to table lookups)
3. Branchless optimization tested but reverted - showed mixed results:
   - +7% at 4KB but -8% to -16% at smaller sizes
   - Branch predictor performs well when data is mostly non-zero (typical case)

### End-to-End Throughput
- Encode (k=32, 1KB symbols): ~36 MiB/s
- Decode (source only): ~70 MiB/s
- Decode (repair only): ~13 MiB/s (Gaussian elimination is O(n^3))

### Next Steps
- bd-35lp: Safe SIMD XOR acceleration (potential 2-4x for addmul with gather)
- bd-1l7k: Buffer reuse to reduce allocations

title: Instrument budget checkpoints with tracing
description:
# Task

Add tracing for budget consumption and checkpoint operations.

## Background

Budgets are the resource constraint mechanism:
- Deadline: Wall-clock time limit
- Poll quota: Maximum poll iterations
- Cost quota: Abstract cost units
- Priority: Scheduling priority

Tasks observe budgets via `cx.checkpoint()`. This is where budget exhaustion
triggers cancellation.

## What to Instrument

1. **Budget creation/propagation**: When budget is set or inherited
   - Fields: task_id, deadline, poll_quota, cost_quota, priority, source (explicit, inherited)
   
2. **Checkpoint call**: Each checkpoint observation
   - Level: TRACE (high frequency)
   - Fields: task_id, polls_used, polls_remaining, time_remaining, cost_used
   
3. **Budget exhaustion**: When budget triggers cancellation
   - Level: INFO
   - Fields: task_id, exhausted_resource (deadline/polls/cost), overage_amount
   
4. **Budget tightening**: When child budget is stricter than parent
   - Fields: task_id, resource, old_value, new_value, source

## Example Trace

```
budget_set[task=100, deadline=10s, polls=1000, source=explicit]
  checkpoint[task=100, polls_used=100, time_elapsed=1.2s] // TRACE
  checkpoint[task=100, polls_used=200, time_elapsed=2.4s] // TRACE
  ...
  budget_exhausted[task=100, resource=deadline, overage=0.3s] // INFO
    cancel_requested[task=100, reason=BudgetExhausted]
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Budget creation/inheritance is traceable
- [ ] Checkpoints recorded at TRACE level
- [ ] Exhaustion clearly identifies which resource
- [ ] Tightening shows old vs new values
- [ ] High-frequency checkpoints don't overwhelm logs (TRACE level)

title: Implement test oracle: deadline_monotone invariant checker
description:
## Purpose
Implement a test oracle that verifies the INV-DEADLINE-MONOTONE invariant: children can never have longer deadlines than their parents.

## The Invariant
From asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §5:
```
∀r ∈ dom(R), ∀r' ∈ R[r].subregions:
  deadline(R[r']) ≤ deadline(R[r])    // Tighter or equal
```

This ensures budget propagation is correct - a child region cannot escape its parent's deadline.

## Why This Matters
- Prevents orphan work that outlives its parent
- Ensures cancellation can always complete within parent's budget
- Critical for bounded cleanup guarantees

## Oracle Design
```rust
pub struct DeadlineMonotoneOracle {
    region_deadlines: HashMap<RegionId, Option<Time>>,
    parent_map: HashMap<RegionId, RegionId>,
}

impl DeadlineMonotoneOracle {
    pub fn on_region_create(
        &mut self,
        region: RegionId,
        parent: Option<RegionId>,
        budget: &Budget
    );
    
    pub fn on_budget_update(
        &mut self,
        region: RegionId,
        new_budget: &Budget
    );
    
    pub fn check(&self) -> Result<(), DeadlineMonotoneViolation>;
}
```

## Violation Detection
```rust
pub struct DeadlineMonotoneViolation {
    pub child: RegionId,
    pub child_deadline: Option<Time>,
    pub parent: RegionId,
    pub parent_deadline: Option<Time>,
}
```

A violation occurs when:
- Child region has deadline D_c
- Parent region has deadline D_p
- D_c > D_p (child deadline is LATER than parent)

## Integration
- Check on region creation
- Check on budget tightening (should always be valid by construction)
- Lab runtime validates after each step

## Testing
1. Valid: child deadline ≤ parent deadline
2. Invalid: manually construct violation → oracle catches
3. None deadline: unbounded is ≤ bounded (None ≤ Some(T)) - actually None means unbounded which is ≥ any bounded

Actually, the semantics here is:
- None = unbounded = infinity
- Some(T) = bounded to T
- So the check is: child_deadline ≤ parent_deadline where None = ∞

## References
- asupersync_v4_formal_semantics.md §5: INV-DEADLINE-MONOTONE
- asupersync_plan_v4.md §3.3: Budget product semiring

## Acceptance Criteria
- Oracle verifies deadline monotonicity: children deadlines are ≤ parent deadlines (or None semantics handled explicitly).
- Produces clear diagnostic output pointing to offending parent/child and their budgets.
- Deterministic and usable in both unit and E2E tests.
close_reason: DeadlineMonotoneOracle fully implemented with 350+ lines, 18 unit tests passing. Verifies INV-DEADLINE-MONOTONE: child deadlines must not exceed parent deadlines. Integrated into OracleSuite.

```rust
// Recording
let recorder = TraceRecorder::new(RecorderConfig::default());

trace.save("failing_test.trace")?;

let replay = LabRuntime::replay(trace);

// Step through

}
```

title: [METHODOLOGY] Capture baseline p50/p95/p99 for all primary operations
description:
Run comprehensive benchmarks for all primary Asupersync operations and capture baseline performance metrics. This is the foundation for all future optimization work -- without baselines, we cannot measure improvement or detect regressions.

BACKGROUND (section 0.11 Tail-Latency Decomposition): The Alien CS Graveyard methodology requires statistical benchmarking with p50/p95/p99 percentiles and bootstrap confidence intervals. Tail-latency decomposition identifies which subsystem contributes most to high-percentile latency. For Asupersync, the tail terms that usually dominate are: queueing (scheduler queue depth), synchronization (lock contention), and retries (cancellation retry count).

OPERATIONS TO BENCHMARK: (1) Task spawn -- measure time from spawn call to first poll. (2) Task cancellation -- measure time from cancel signal to all obligations released. (3) Channel send/recv -- measure one-way latency for both bounded and unbounded channels. (4) Cx capability check -- measure has<T>() and get<T>() latency. (5) Budget check -- measure budget remaining check and propagation latency. (6) RaptorQ encode/decode -- measure encoding and decoding throughput at various block sizes. (7) DPOR exploration -- measure exploration rate (states/second) for a standard test program.

RUST IMPLEMENTATION GUIDANCE: (1) Use criterion.rs with sample_size(100) and measurement_time(Duration::from_secs(10)) for stable results. (2) Each benchmark produces: p50, p95, p99 latencies and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. (3) Store results in artifacts/baseline.json with schema: { operation: string, p50_ns: u64, p95_ns: u64, p99_ns: u64, ci95_lower_ns: u64, ci95_upper_ns: u64, timestamp: string, git_sha: string }. (4) First mandatory counters for tail decomposition: scheduler_queue_depth (histogram), cancellation_retry_count (counter), wake_to_run_latency_us (histogram). Expose via metrics crate with prometheus exporter. (5) Use black_box() to prevent compiler optimization of benchmark targets. (6) Benchmark both cold (first run) and warm (steady state) performance.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: (1) Baselines captured for all 7 operations listed above. (2) Each baseline has valid confidence intervals (CI width < 20% of median). (3) Results are reproducible: running baseline twice produces overlapping CIs. (4) artifacts/baseline.json is committed to the repository with git SHA tag. (5) CI can compare new results against baseline and flag >5% regression. (6) Tail-latency counters (queue depth, retry count, wake-to-run) are operational and emitting.

LOGGING REQUIREMENTS: Each benchmark run logs: operation_name, sample_count, p50_ns, p95_ns, p99_ns, ci95_lower_ns, ci95_upper_ns, git_sha, timestamp, machine_info (cpu, os). Tail-latency counters are emitted as prometheus-style metrics: asupersync_scheduler_queue_depth_histogram, asupersync_cancellation_retry_count_total, asupersync_wake_to_run_latency_us_histogram. Summary report generated as Markdown for PR comments.

TESTING APPROACH: (1) Verify benchmark harness itself: a known-cost operation (sleep 1ms) should benchmark at ~1ms +/- 10%. (2) Verify baseline stability: run same benchmark 5 times, assert all p50 values are within 10% of each other. (3) Verify regression detection: artificially degrade an operation by 10%, assert CI pipeline flags it.

comments.text:
## Deep Audit: src/http/h1/codec.rs (1092 lines)

**Verdict: SOUND** — no bugs found.

### Analysis

HTTP/1.1 server-side codec implementing Decoder<Request> + Encoder<Response> with DecodeState machine (Head → Body{remaining} / Chunked{decoder}).

**Security hardening (excellent):**
- Anti-smuggling: rejects both TE+CL (AmbiguousBodyLength), rejects compound TE values (only bare 'chunked'), rejects duplicate CL/TE headers
- Header injection prevention: tchar set validation (RFC 7230), rejects \r\n in header names and values, reason phrase injection blocked
- DoS hardening: size limits on request line (8KB), headers (64KB configurable), body (16MB configurable), chunk size line (1KB), trailers, header count (128)

**Decoder path:**
- decode_head: request line length check before headers-end scan. UTF-8 validated. Header count bounded.
- body_kind: TE/CL anti-smuggling, HTTP/1.0 chunked rejection, CL parse validation
- Content-Length body: upfront BodyTooLarge check (line 569), exact remaining-bytes read
- ChunkedBodyDecoder: 4-phase state machine (SizeLine/Data/DataCrlf/Trailers). saturating_add for body size check. Chunk extensions stripped via ';' split. Trailer validation reuses parse_header_line. Trailer byte count correctly tracked (line 429-432).
- State transitions: mem::replace to Head after each complete request — no state leak

**Encoder path:**
- validate_header_field on all response headers and trailers
- TE+CL consistency rejection, TrailersNotAllowed without chunked
- CL mismatch detection (declared vs actual body length)
- Auto Content-Length insertion when absent
- Chunked: correct hex chunk-size + data + CRLF + terminal 0-chunk + trailers + terminal CRLF

**Design note (not a bug):** Line 412 trailer DoS check uses src.len() (entire remaining buffer) rather than just trailer data. With large pipelined requests following chunked trailers, this could cause false HeadersTooLarge rejection. In practice: unlikely at 64KB default, and lines 429-432 perform the correct per-trailer accounting. Defense-in-depth that errs conservative.

**Tests:** 35 tests covering GET/POST, chunked with extensions/trailers, sequential decoding, size limits, smuggling protection, encoding variants. Good coverage.
